terms.def: The four areas made by a midsagittal line and a transverse line crossing at the navel: right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower, named for the patient's own sides.

The muscles of the abdominal wall: the vertical rectus abdominis, crossed by tendinous intersections and wrapped in the rectus sheath that meets its partner at the linea alba; three flat layers, the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis; and the quadratus lumborum in the back wall. They compress the abdomen and bend and twist the trunk.
terms.say: REK-tus ab-DOM-in-iss; LIN-ee-uh AL-buh; kwad-RAY-tus lum-BOR-um

terms.def: The part of the ventral body cavity below the diaphragm: the abdominal cavity above and the pelvic cavity below, with only an imaginary boundary between them.

The nine areas made by two vertical and two horizontal lines across the abdomen: right and left hypochondriac with the epigastric between them, right and left lumbar with the umbilical between them, and right and left iliac with the hypogastric between them.

Abduction moves a limb away from the midline of the body in the frontal plane; adduction moves it back toward the midline. Fingers abduct away from the middle finger and toes away from the second toe.

Filtrate containing what a healthy filter holds back. Proteinuria is protein, usually albumin, in the urine above the normal trace; hematuria is red blood cells in the urine, from the glomeruli or anywhere further down the urinary tract.

The blood group system set by sugars added to the H antigen on red cells: type A carries the A antigen, type B the B antigen, type AB both, type O neither. From infancy, plasma holds antibodies against whichever of A and B the red cells lack.

The absolute refractory period is the time, about 1 ms from threshold through most of the falling phase, when no stimulus can start another action potential. The relative refractory period follows it, when only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can.

The fed state, about four hours after a meal, when nutrients are being absorbed. Insulin is high and glucagon low, glucose is the main fuel, and the liver, muscle and adipose tissue store the extra as glycogen, protein and fat.

The parts around the eyeball that protect and move it: the eyelids, the conjunctiva lining the lids and covering the white of the eye, the lacrimal gland and the ducts that drain tears into the nose, and the six extraocular (extrinsic eye) muscles. The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve, the superior oblique by the trochlear nerve, and the other four and the levator palpebrae superioris by the oculomotor nerve.
The neurotransmitter that motor neurons release onto skeletal muscle, made from an acetyl group and choline. It is also used by some autonomic neurons and in the brain.
roots: bile, where choline was first found

terms.term: acetylcholine receptors at the end plate
terms.def: The nicotinic receptor proteins on the motor end plate: ligand-gated channels that open when two acetylcholine molecules bind, letting sodium in (and a little potassium out), which depolarizes the end plate. A compound in tobacco also opens them, hence the name.

The enzyme anchored in the synaptic cleft that splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline within about a millisecond, ending each signal; the choline is taken back into the axon terminal and reused.
A substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) when it dissolves in water, raising the H+ concentration. A strong acid releases nearly all of them; a weak acid releases only a small share.

Acidemia is blood pH below 7.35 and alkalemia is blood pH above 7.45. Acidosis and alkalosis are the processes that push pH down or up; in everyday speech the words are often used for the blood state itself.
The release of a capacitated sperm's acrosomal enzymes by exocytosis, set off by a rise in calcium in the sperm head. The enzymes, mainly acrosin, digest a path through the zona pellucida.

A rapid, all-or-none reversal of the membrane potential: sodium rushes in (to about +30 mV), then potassium flows out, returning the membrane to rest. It travels along the membrane without shrinking; in a neuron it is also called a nerve impulse.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: The two steps that turn vitamin D into its active hormone: the liver adds a hydroxyl group (making 25-hydroxyvitamin D) and the kidneys add a second. Too little leads to poor calcium absorption; in children the soft, bowing bones of rickets.

Active immunity is made by your own immune system, after infection or a vaccine; it is slow to start, leaves memory and lasts long. Passive immunity is borrowed antibody, from mother to baby or by injection; it works at once but fades in weeks to months.
Movement of a substance across a membrane that requires the cell to supply energy, usually from ATP. It usually moves the substance against its gradient; vesicle transport also counts.

terms.term: ADH and aquaporins in the collecting duct
terms.def: ADH binds its receptor protein on principal cells, raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, which moves stored aquaporins into the apical membrane. Water then leaves the collecting duct by osmosis into the salty medulla; without ADH the duct is nearly waterproof.

The role of antidiuretic hormone in blood pressure: it makes the kidneys keep water, and at the high levels a large fall in volume produces, it also constricts arterioles. Its other name, vasopressin, reflects that effect.

Weak androgens, mainly DHEA, made by the zona reticularis under ACTH's drive. Tissues convert them into stronger androgens; they matter most in women, supporting pubic and underarm hair and sex drive.

The outer 80 to 90 percent of each adrenal gland, which makes steroid hormones from cholesterol in three zones: the zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), the zona fasciculata (cortisol) and the zona reticularis (adrenal androgens).

Addison disease is destruction of the adrenal cortex, with low cortisol and aldosterone, high ACTH and darker skin. Cushing syndrome is the effect of long-term glucocorticoid excess, usually from medication: central fat, thin skin, high blood glucose and raised blood pressure.

The inner part of each adrenal gland. Its chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic postganglionic neurons without axons: stimulated directly by preganglionic fibers, they release epinephrine (about 80 percent) and norepinephrine into the blood.

The complete breakdown of fuel using oxygen: glycolysis, then the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrion, then the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where oxygen accepts electrons and most ATP is made.

The complete breakdown of glucose, fatty acids, lactate and some amino acids with oxygen in a muscle fiber's mitochondria, yielding about 30–32 ATP per glucose. It supplies nearly all ATP in activity lasting more than a few minutes.
The route, usually a nerve, that carries information from the sensory receptor toward the control center.

The pressure a ventricle must overcome to open its semilunar valve and eject blood, set mainly by aortic pressure for the left ventricle. A higher afterload leaves more blood in the ventricle after ejection and lowers stroke volume.

The clumping of cells when antibodies, each with two or more binding sites, bind antigens on several cells and cross-link them. It is an immune process, not clotting, and is often followed by hemolysis.

The build-up of DNA damage, damaged proteins and failing mitochondria in cells, with shortening telomeres (the capped repeat sequences at chromosome ends) and senescence, a permanent stop to division in a cell that stays alive and releases inflammatory signals.

Leukocytes without visible granules: lymphocytes (a large round nucleus almost filling the cell; mostly the cells of specific immunity, from the lymphoid branch) and monocytes (the largest, with a kidney-shaped nucleus; they leave the blood and become macrophages).

The ways the airway keeps particles and microorganisms out of the alveoli: hairs in the nasal vestibule, sticky mucus with lysozyme, defensins and IgA, the mucociliary escalator (cilia that move the mucus sheet toward the pharynx to be swallowed), and the cough reflex (vagus nerve) and sneeze reflex (trigeminal nerve), which blast irritants out.

The opposition to airflow through the airways, which rises steeply as airway radius falls (resistance depends on 1 ÷ r⁴). Bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle contraction, from acetylcholine, histamine or leukotrienes) raises it; bronchodilation (relaxation, from epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins) lowers it. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease in which bronchoconstriction, wall swelling and mucus narrow the airways.

The main mineralocorticoid, a steroid from the zona glomerulosa. Released when plasma potassium rises or angiotensin II arrives, it makes the kidney reabsorb sodium, with water following, and secrete potassium.

The alimentary canal (GI tract) is the continuous tube food passes through: mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine, ending at the anus. The accessory digestive organs (teeth, tongue, glands that make saliva, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) help from outside it; food never passes through them.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: One version of a gene. A person with two identical alleles of a gene is homozygous; with two different alleles, heterozygous. A gene with multiple alleles, such as ABO, has more than two versions in the population, though each person carries only two.

Adrenergic receptor proteins of the alpha family. Alpha-1 raises calcium in smooth muscle, so vessels in skin and gut constrict, the pupil's dilator muscle contracts and sphincters tighten. Alpha-2, often on the varicosity itself, lowers cyclic AMP and turns down norepinephrine release.

The volume of fresh air that reaches the alveoli each minute: (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate, about 4.2 L/min at rest. Shallow breathing lowers it even when minute ventilation stays the same.

The tiny air sacs, about 0.2 mm across and numbering hundreds of millions, where gases cross between air and blood. They cluster in alveolar sacs. Thin type I alveolar cells form the wall; cuboidal type II cells secrete surfactant, a film that lowers surface tension, and replace type I cells; alveolar macrophages engulf particles; alveolar pores link neighbors.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: The handling of amino acids beyond protein building. Transamination moves each amino group onto glutamate; deamination in the liver releases it as ammonia; the carbon skeleton is burned or made into glucose (glucogenic amino acids) or into ketone bodies or fat (ketogenic amino acids).

Fast production of ATP in muscle by splitting glucose, mostly from the fiber's own glycogen, to pyruvate and turning pyruvate into lactate without using oxygen. It yields 2 ATP per glucose and dominates efforts of about 10 seconds to a couple of minutes.
Making ATP without using oxygen: glycolysis followed by conversion of pyruvate to lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. It yields only 2 ATP per glucose.

A severe, rapid, whole-body type I reaction in which mast cells and basophils everywhere release histamine and leukotrienes: vasodilation and leaky capillaries drop MAP (anaphylactic shock, a distributive shock) and the airways narrow. Intramuscular epinephrine is the first treatment.
A connection between two blood vessels. Where branches of two arteries join, blood can reach tissue by a second route, called collateral circulation.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: The reference posture for describing the body: standing upright and facing forward, feet flat and pointing forward, arms at the sides with the palms facing forward and the thumbs pointing away from the body. Every directional term assumes this posture.

The study of the body's structures: their shape, size, parts and position. Gross anatomy covers what you can see unaided, microscopic anatomy what needs a microscope, regional anatomy one body part at a time, and systemic anatomy one organ system at a time.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: Too little hemoglobin to carry a normal load of oxygen, from blood loss (hemorrhagic anemia), too little production (iron-deficiency, pernicious and aplastic anemia, or too little erythropoietin) or early destruction of red cells (sickle cell disease, thalassemia).

The growth of new capillaries by sprouting from existing ones, driven by growth factors such as VEGF released when tissue is low in oxygen. In muscle, endurance training triggers it, shortening the distance oxygen must diffuse to each fiber.

The role of atrial natriuretic peptide in lowering blood pressure: released when the atria are stretched, it makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water, lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH, and relaxes arterioles.
Anterior means toward the front of the body; posterior means toward the back. Ventral (belly side) and dorsal (back side) mean the same in a standing human.

The muscles of the front of the thigh: the quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris and vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius), which extends the knee through the quadriceps tendon, and the sartorius, plus the iliopsoas (psoas major and iliacus), the prime mover of hip flexion. The femoral triangle lies at the top of the front of the thigh.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: The five kinds of antibody, set by the heavy chain: IgG (main blood antibody, crosses to the fetus), IgA (in secretions), IgM (first made, a pentamer), IgE (on mast cells) and IgD (on naïve B cells). Class switching changes a B cell's class while keeping its variable region.

An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. The variable regions at the arm tips form two antigen-binding sites; the constant regions, including the Fc region of the stem, set the class and bind Fc receptor proteins and complement.

Substances that slow or stop coagulation: the body's own antithrombin, protein C and the heparin-like molecules on the vessel lining, and drugs such as heparin (boosts antithrombin; works in minutes) and warfarin (blocks vitamin K recycling; works over days).

Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): a peptide made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolarity rises or blood volume falls sharply. It makes kidney cells insert aquaporins so less urine is made, and at high levels it constricts small arteries.

An antigen is a molecule the immune system recognizes as a specific target, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a surface. An antibody is a Y-shaped plasma protein, released by cells descended from lymphocytes, that binds one antigen; with two or more binding sites it can link and clump cells.

Any molecule that a lymphocyte's antigen receptor or an antibody binds specifically. Each antigen receptor binds one small part of it, an epitope (antigenic determinant), and a large antigen carries many epitopes.

A cell that takes in antigen, breaks it into peptides and loads them onto MHC class II (antigen processing), then displays them for T cells (antigen presentation): dendritic cells, which start naive T cell responses, macrophages and B cells.

Proteins made in advance that kill microbes directly: lysozyme, an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks bacterial cell walls, and defensins, small proteins that punch holes in microbial membranes.

A 0-to-10 score of a newborn's condition at 1 and 5 minutes after birth, rating appearance (color), pulse, grimace (reflex response), activity (muscle tone) and respiration from 0 to 2 each. 7 to 10 is reassuring.
Programmed cell death: an orderly self-destruction in which the cell's own enzymes dismantle it into membrane-wrapped pieces that neighboring cells engulf, without spilling its contents.

The control of hunger and eating by the hypothalamus. Ghrelin from the empty stomach raises hunger; stomach stretch and gut hormones produce satiety, the fullness that ends a meal; leptin from fat reports long-term stores.
A membrane protein that forms a water channel, letting water molecules cross in single file far faster than through the bare bilayer. Water still moves in the direction osmosis sets.
A small bundle of smooth muscle running from a hair follicle to the papillary dermis. Cold or fear makes it contract involuntarily, pulling the slanted hair upright and raising a goose bump.

Any heart rhythm that is abnormal in rate, regularity, starting point or conduction; also called dysrhythmia. Examples are tachycardia (above 100 per minute at rest), bradycardia (below 60), heart block, atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation, which is treated by defibrillation. An artificial pacemaker fires when the heart's own rate is too slow.

Reading an arterial blood gas (ABG): pH, PaCO2 (the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood, normally 35 to 45 mm Hg) and bicarbonate (22 to 26 mmol/L). Read the pH, find which number matches it to name the primary disorder, then check whether the other number has moved to compensate.

terms.term: arteries of the abdomen and pelvis
terms.def: The branches of the abdominal aorta: three single gut arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric) and paired renal and gonadal arteries, ending in the common iliac arteries, which split into internal iliacs for the pelvis and external iliacs for the legs. The celiac trunk splits into the left gastric artery, the splenic artery and the common hepatic artery.

terms.term: arteries of the head and neck
terms.def: The brachiocephalic trunk (right side only), the common carotid arteries, which split into external carotids for the face and scalp and internal carotids for the brain, and the vertebral arteries from the subclavians. The carotid sinus is the pressure-sensing bulge at the start of each internal carotid.

In the arm, one artery renamed at landmarks: subclavian, axillary, brachial, then the radial and ulnar arteries, which join in the palmar arches. In the leg: femoral (with its deep femoral branch), popliteal, then the anterior tibial, which becomes the dorsalis pedis, and the posterior tibial.

The smallest artery, under about 0.1 mm across, with one to a few layers of smooth muscle. Arterioles are the main resistance vessels; their steady partial contraction, vascular tone, sets how much blood enters each capillary bed.

The three kinds of blood vessel. An artery carries blood away from the heart, a vein carries blood back toward the heart, and a capillary is the thinnest vessel, where materials pass between blood and cells.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The bundles of axons in the spinal cord's white columns. Ascending tracts carry sensory information up to the brain; descending tracts carry motor commands down. Their names give origin then destination, and most cross the midline somewhere along their path.

Chains of neurons that carry sensory signals up the spinal cord and brainstem. Conscious pathways use a first-order neuron (sensory receptor to CNS), a second-order neuron (crosses the midline, a decussation, and rises to the thalamus) and a third-order neuron (thalamus to cortex). The dorsal column system (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus, then the medial lemniscus) carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception and crosses in the medulla; the spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and crosses in the spinal cord; the spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum.
The buildup of plaques of fat, foam cells and fibrous tissue in the tunica intima of large and medium arteries. Plaques narrow the lumen and can rupture, triggering a thrombus that blocks the artery.
The first two cervical vertebrae. The atlas (C1) is a ring with no body or spinous process that carries the skull; the axis (C2) has an upward peg, the dens, around which the atlas and skull turn.
roots: the giant who held up the heavens

terms.term: atomic number, mass number and isotopes
terms.def: The atomic number is an atom's proton count, which defines the element; the mass number is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons, and radioisotopes are isotopes whose unstable nuclei give off radiation.
The smallest unit of an element that still behaves like that element: a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it.

Adenosine triphosphate: a nucleotide of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups. Splitting off the outer phosphate by hydrolysis leaves ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and releases energy that cells use for work.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: The splitting of ATP by water into ADP and phosphate, which releases energy because the products are more stable than ATP. An ATPase is an enzyme that does this; phosphorylation is attaching a phosphate group to another molecule, which changes its energy and shape.

The ATP made from one glucose broken down fully with oxygen: about 30–32, using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2. Only 4 are made directly; the rest come from oxidative phosphorylation. Older texts give 36–38.

Atrial natriuretic peptide, a hormone released by stretched muscle cells of the heart's upper chambers. It makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH release, and dilates vessels, so blood volume and pressure fall.
A reflex in which stretch of the atria and nearby large veins, from more venous return, raises heart rate through the cardiovascular center. Also called the Bainbridge reflex.

The atrioventricular node: autorhythmic tissue in the lower interatrial septum, and the only normal electrical doorway from atria to ventricles. It conducts slowly, causing the AV nodal delay of about 0.1 second, during which the atria finish contracting.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: The valves between each atrium and its ventricle: the tricuspid valve on the right and the mitral (bicuspid) valve on the left. Chordae tendineae tie their cusps to papillary muscles, which keep the cusps from flipping into the atria when the ventricles contract.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: The route from the cochlea to the cortex: cochlear nerve, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary nuclei (where the two ears are first compared), inferior colliculus, medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Each ear reaches both hemispheres.

An adaptive immune response against self antigens after self-tolerance fails; autoimmune disease is the damage it causes. It can be organ-specific, as in type 1 diabetes, or systemic, as in rheumatoid arthritis (inflamed synovial membranes) and systemic lupus erythematosus (antibodies against nuclear contents forming immune complexes).

The part of the motor division that controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, mostly without conscious control. Its sympathetic division (fight-or-flight) dominates in stress and exercise; its parasympathetic division (rest-and-digest) dominates at rest.

The steady background firing of autonomic neurons at rest, which lets one division change an effector in both directions. Vagal tone holds the resting heart well below its own rate of about 100 beats a minute; sympathetic tone keeps most blood vessels partly constricted.

The kidney's own control that keeps GFR nearly constant between a mean arterial pressure of about 80 and 180 mm Hg by adjusting the afferent arteriole: the myogenic mechanism (stretch makes it constrict) and tubuloglomerular feedback (more sodium chloride at the macula densa makes it constrict).

A specialized cardiac muscle cell, also called a pacemaker cell, that depolarizes to threshold on its own with no outside stimulus. About 1 percent of heart cells are autorhythmic; they start and conduct each heartbeat's signal and contract only weakly.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: The two divisions of the skeleton. The axial skeleton (80 bones) is the upright core: skull, hyoid, ear bones, backbone and rib cage. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) is the limbs plus the shoulder and hip bones that attach them to the trunk.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: A lymphocyte that matures in the red bone marrow and binds intact antigen with a membrane-bound antibody as its antigen receptor; when activated, its descendants release antibodies.

The negative feedback loop that corrects fast changes in blood pressure: baroreceptor signals reach the cardiovascular center, which adjusts sympathetic and vagal output to the heart, arterioles and veins. Also called the baroreflex; on standing it is the orthostatic reflex.

Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the walls of the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch (the arch group is sometimes called the aortic sinuses, a name anatomists give to the bulges at the root of the aorta). They fire faster when arterial pressure stretches the wall more, and they reset to a new pressure within a day or two.

Masses of gray matter deep in the cerebrum (the caudate and putamen, together the striatum, and the globus pallidus), working with the subthalamus and substantia nigra. They help select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones; the older name is basal ganglia.
A substance that takes up hydrogen ions, lowering a fluid's H+ concentration, either directly or by releasing hydroxide ions (OH−) that join H+ to form water. Also called alkaline.

The thin mat of proteins under every epithelium that anchors it to the tissue below. It has two parts: the basal lamina, made by the epithelial cells, and the reticular lamina, made by the tissue beneath.

Adrenergic receptor proteins of the beta family, which raise cyclic AMP. Beta-1 speeds the heart and strengthens its contraction. Beta-2, reached mainly by circulating epinephrine, relaxes smooth muscle (widening the small airways and dilating vessels in skeletal muscle) and makes the liver release glucose.

The breakdown of a fatty acid inside mitochondria, two carbons at a time, into acetyl CoA; each turn also makes one FADH2 and one NADH. It needs oxygen, because the carriers must be reoxidized by the electron transport chain.
roots: second letter of the Greek alphabet: the carbon being oxidized

terms.def: A yellow-green, slightly alkaline fluid made by hepatocytes: water, bicarbonate, bile salts, bilirubin, cholesterol and phospholipids. Its bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets; it has no digestive enzymes. It drains through the hepatic ducts and the common bile duct, and its bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and reused (the enterohepatic circulation).

The hollow ball of cells an embryo becomes around day 5: an outer layer, the trophoblast, which attaches to the uterus and forms supporting tissues; a cluster inside, the inner cell mass, which forms the embryo; and a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel.

Bleeding inside the skull around the brain. An epidural hematoma is usually arterial, between skull and dura, and lens-shaped; a subdural hematoma is usually from torn bridging veins, between dura and arachnoid, and crescent-shaped; a subarachnoid hemorrhage puts blood into the CSF.

The oocyte's defenses against polyspermy, the entry of more than one sperm. After one sperm fuses, the cortical reaction releases enzymes that alter the zona pellucida so no other sperm can bind, and the membrane sheds its sperm-binding receptor protein. The corona radiata (the ring of granulosa cells) and the zona pellucida (the glycoprotein coat) are the layers sperm cross; the altered zona is sometimes called the fertilization membrane.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue: red cells, white cells and platelets carried in a liquid matrix, plasma. Its fiber-forming protein stays dissolved until a clot forms.
A jelly-like plug that seals a cut vessel: platelets clump at the damage, and a protein dissolved in the plasma forms sticky threads that trap red cells.

terms.term: blood flow and the flow equation (vessels)
terms.def: The volume of blood passing a point per minute. In any vessel, organ or the whole circuit it follows F = ΔP / R: the pressure difference between the two ends divided by the resistance.

terms.term: blood potassium and the resting potential
terms.def: Because potassium leak sets most of the resting potential, blood potassium changes it. Hyperkalemia (high blood potassium) shrinks the potassium gradient and depolarizes cells; hypokalemia (low blood potassium) hyperpolarizes most cells.

The pressure of blood in the large systemic arteries, which swings with each heartbeat between systolic pressure, the peak during ejection, and diastolic pressure, the lowest point just before the next ejection. It is written systolic over diastolic, for example 120/80 mm Hg.

Blood pressure is the pressure blood exerts on the walls of the blood vessels, usually measured in a large artery and written as the peak over the lowest value, such as 120/80 mm Hg. Blood volume is the total amount of blood, about 5 liters in an adult; less blood volume means less stretch of the vessel walls and a lower blood pressure.

Blood enters each kidney by the renal artery and branches in order into segmental, interlobar, arcuate and cortical radiate arteries; veins with matching names return it to the renal vein. The kidneys receive about 20 to 25 percent of resting cardiac output.

The lungs' two blood supplies. The pulmonary arteries bring deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the alveolar capillaries for gas exchange. The bronchial arteries, systemic branches mostly of the thoracic aorta, bring oxygenated blood to the airway walls, connective tissue and visceral pleura; bronchial veins drain partly to the azygos system and partly into pulmonary veins.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: The two capillary beds of a nephron in series: the afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus, the efferent arteriole carries it out, and it then flows through the peritubular capillaries around the tubules, and in juxtamedullary nephrons also the vasa recta in the medulla.

terms.term: blood volume and blood pressure (in detail)
terms.def: The link between how much blood you have and your long-term blood pressure: more volume raises venous return, stroke volume and cardiac output, so MAP rises; less volume lowers them. Only restoring volume corrects a lasting change.

The brain capillary wall's control of what enters brain tissue: endothelial cells sealed by tight junctions, with no pores and few vesicles, maintained by astrocyte end-feet. Small lipid-soluble molecules cross freely, glucose and amino acids need carrier proteins, and most proteins, ions and water-soluble drugs are kept out.

The regions of body water, each separated by a barrier: the intracellular fluid inside cells (about two thirds of total body water) and the extracellular fluid outside them (one third), which is three quarters interstitial fluid and one quarter plasma. Total body water is about 60% of body mass in a young man.
terms.topicTitle: Body fluid compartments and water balance

terms.def: Osseous tissue: hard connective tissue whose matrix is collagen hardened by calcium-containing mineral crystals. It is rich in blood vessels, so it heals well.

The four cells of bone tissue: osteogenic cells (dividing stem cells), osteoblasts (build matrix), osteocytes (osteoblasts trapped in lacunae that maintain matrix and sense load) and osteoclasts (huge fused cells of the macrophage line that resorb bone).

terms.term: bone growth in length and width
terms.def: Long bones lengthen by interstitial growth of cartilage at the epiphyseal plates, which bone then replaces, and widen by appositional growth: osteoblasts add bone under the periosteum while osteoclasts remove bone inside.

Named surface features of bones. Projections for tendons and ligaments include tuberosities, tubercles, trochanters, crests, spines and epicondyles; joint-forming projections include heads, condyles and facets; a fossa is a shallow depression and a meatus is a canal.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: The extracellular material of bone: about one third collagen and ground substance, which resists pulling, and two thirds hydroxyapatite crystals of calcium phosphate, which resist squeezing. Osteoid is new matrix before it mineralizes.

The continual replacement of old bone by new at the same site: osteoclasts resorb, then osteoblasts refill, with little change in shape. Bone modeling instead builds and removes on different surfaces, changing shape. Wolff's law: bone adapts its mass and structure to the loads placed on it.

The 26 bones of the ankle and foot: 7 tarsals (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms), 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges (two in the big toe, the hallux). They form longitudinal and transverse arches held up in part by the plantar aponeurosis.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.def: The 27 bones of the wrist and hand: 8 carpals in two rows (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate), 5 metacarpals in the palm and 14 phalanges in the fingers and thumb (pollex). The carpals and the flexor retinaculum form the carpal tunnel.
terms.topicTitle: The pectoral girdle and upper limb

terms.def: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related: P₁ × V₁ = P₂ × V₂. Enlarging the alveoli lowers the pressure of the air inside them; shrinking them raises it.

The neural plate folds into the neural tube (neurulation); its front end forms three primary brain vesicles (prosencephalon or forebrain, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon or hindbrain), then five secondary vesicles that become the cerebrum, diencephalon, midbrain, pons and cerebellum, and medulla. Neural crest cells form structures outside the CNS.

The stalk linking the cerebrum and diencephalon to the spinal cord: the midbrain (with the cerebral peduncles and the superior and inferior colliculi), the pons and the medulla oblongata. Its nuclei control heart rate, blood vessel diameter and breathing rhythm.

Motor tracts from brainstem upper motor neurons to the spinal cord: the vestibulospinal tract (balance and antigravity posture), the reticulospinal tracts (tone, posture and walking), the tectospinal tract (turning the head toward a sight or sound) and the rubrospinal tract from the red nucleus (arm flexors; small in humans).
roots: entrance hall, named for a balance chamber deep in the skull

terms.term: breathing during exercise and at altitude
terms.def: In exercise, ventilation rises to match carbon dioxide production with little change in blood gases (hyperpnea). At altitude, low PO2 drives ventilation through the carotid bodies, and acclimatization over days and weeks raises ventilation further and adds red blood cells; going up too fast can cause acute mountain sickness.

The branching airways of the lungs: primary (main) bronchi, secondary (lobar) and tertiary (segmental) bronchi, smaller bronchi, then bronchioles without cartilage, terminal bronchioles (the end of the conducting zone), respiratory bronchioles (the first with alveoli) and alveolar ducts. Down the tree, cartilage disappears, smooth muscle becomes relatively thicker and the epithelium thins.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: Enzymes built into the membrane of the microvilli that finish digestion at the absorbing surface: lactase (lactose to glucose and galactose), sucrase (sucrose to glucose and fructose), maltase (maltose to two glucose) and peptidases (short peptides to amino acids).
A pair of substances, a weak acid and the weak base it becomes after releasing H+, that resists changes in pH by taking up or releasing hydrogen ions. It holds acid temporarily and can be used up.
The movement of a whole fluid, with everything dissolved or carried in it, from higher to lower pressure. Blood moving through vessels and air moving into the lungs are examples.

terms.term: bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers
terms.def: The fast conducting path through the ventricles: the AV bundle (bundle of His) crosses the cardiac skeleton, splits into right and left bundle branches down the interventricular septum, and feeds the Purkinje fibers, a subendocardial conducting network. The moderator band carries part of the right branch to the right ventricle's front papillary muscle.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: Naming a burn by the deepest layer destroyed: superficial (first-degree, epidermis only), partial-thickness (second-degree, into the dermis, blistered and painful), full-thickness (third-degree, through the dermis, leathery and painless), and fourth-degree (into muscle, tendon or bone).

A flattened sac of synovial membrane holding a film of synovial fluid, placed where skin, a tendon or a muscle slides over bone (subcutaneous, submuscular or subtendinous bursae). A tendon sheath is a tube-shaped bursa wrapped around a tendon.
A peptide hormone released by the thyroid gland's parafollicular (C) cells when blood calcium rises. It inhibits osteoclasts and so lowers blood calcium, but in adults its effect is small.

The active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made when the liver and then the kidneys each add a hydroxyl group; PTH switches on the kidney step. It makes the intestine absorb calcium and phosphate. Too little in adults causes osteomalacia, soft poorly mineralized bone.

The control of plasma calcium and phosphate by PTH and calcitriol (calcitonin plays a minor part in adults), through absorption from the intestine, exchange with bone and excretion by the kidneys. Only ionized calcium is active. Hyperphosphatemia (above about 4.5 mg/dL) is usually from kidney failure and lowers free calcium; hypophosphatemia (below about 2.5 mg/dL) often follows refeeding and weakens muscles by limiting ATP.

terms.term: calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
terms.def: The outflow of calcium ions from the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. In skeletal muscle, voltage-sensing DHP receptors in the T tubule are linked to ryanodine receptors (release channels) in the SR and pull them open when the T tubule depolarizes.

Calcium-induced calcium release: calcium entering a cardiac muscle cell through L-type channels opens calcium release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases a much larger amount of calcium into the cytosol and starts contraction.
terms.topicTitle: Cardiac muscle cells and their action potential

terms.def: The release of neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles, small sacs in an axon terminal, when an action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels and entering calcium triggers the vesicles to fuse with the membrane by exocytosis.
Disease in which cells that have gathered mutations divide without control and escape apoptosis. The resulting mass is a tumor (neoplasm); spread of its cells to distant sites is metastasis.

The changes a sperm undergoes over several hours in the female reproductive tract that make it able to fertilize: cholesterol leaves its plasma membrane, calcium and bicarbonate enter, and its tail switches to hyperactivated beating.

The pressure of blood against the inside of a capillary wall (CHP), also called blood hydrostatic pressure. It pushes fluid out of the capillary, and falls from about 35 mm Hg at the arteriole end to about 15 mm Hg at the venule end.

Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelium; fenestrated capillaries have pores through their cells; sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. An arteriole feeds a capillary bed; metarterioles, thoroughfare channels and arteriovenous anastomoses can shunt blood past it; pericytes wrap the wall; vasomotion is rhythmic arteriolar contraction. Precapillary sphincters are described classically, but their role in humans is unsettled.

A molecule of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, roughly one carbon to two hydrogens to one oxygen. Monosaccharides are single sugar units, disaccharides are two joined, and polysaccharides are long chains; sugars are the small ones.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Salivary and pancreatic amylase cut starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins; brush border enzymes (α-dextrinase, maltase, sucrase, lactase) finish them into glucose, galactose and fructose. Glucose and galactose enter absorptive cells with sodium through SGLT1, the sodium-glucose cotransporter (secondary active transport); fructose enters by facilitated diffusion. All three leave into the villus capillaries.
Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions, so a higher PCO2 lowers blood pH and a lower PCO2 raises it. Normal arterial PCO2 is about 40 mm Hg (35–45).

terms.term: carbon dioxide as a waste product of metabolism
terms.def: The carbon dioxide cells make as they break down fuel, released when pyruvate loses a carbon and in the citric acid cycle. It diffuses into the blood and is breathed out; one glucose yields 6 CO2.

terms.term: carbon dioxide as the main drive to breathe
terms.def: Minute to minute, breathing is set mainly to hold arterial PCO2 near 40 mm Hg: a small rise in PCO2 sharply increases ventilation, while low oxygen drives breathing strongly only once arterial PO2 falls below about 60 mm Hg.

Harm from carbon monoxide (CO), a colorless, odorless gas from incomplete burning. It binds heme about 200 to 250 times more tightly than oxygen (forming carboxyhemoglobin), lowers oxygen content, shifts the curve left and blocks mitochondria, while PO2 and a standard pulse oximeter reading stay normal. It is treated with 100% oxygen.

The main buffer of blood: carbonic acid (H2CO3), a weak acid, paired with bicarbonate (HCO3−), a weak base. Bicarbonate takes up added H+ to form carbonic acid, which splits into water and carbon dioxide that is breathed out.

The enzyme in red blood cells that speeds the reaction CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 by thousands of times, in whichever direction the concentrations push it: toward bicarbonate in the tissues and back to carbon dioxide in the lungs.
Muscle tissue found only in the heart wall: short, branched, striated fibers with one central nucleus, joined by intercalated discs. It is involuntary.
The volume of blood one ventricle pumps per minute: heart rate times stroke volume (CO = HR × SV). It is about 5 L/min in a resting adult.
The difference between a person's highest cardiac output and their cardiac output at rest: the extra pumping available on demand. Training raises it; age and heart disease lower it.

Four rings of dense connective tissue around the heart valves, joined into one sheet between the atria and the ventricles. It holds the valve openings in shape, anchors the heart muscle, and blocks electrical signals from crossing straight from atria to ventricles.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: Compression of the heart by blood or fluid collecting in the pericardial cavity. Because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch quickly, pressure in the sac rises, the heart cannot fill between beats, and blood pressure falls.
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: The changes exercise brings: higher heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output, arteriole dilation in working muscle, less flow to the gut and kidneys, and a modest rise in MAP. Target heart rate is a chosen percentage of maximum heart rate, which is roughly 220 minus age.
The point at which every carrier protein in a membrane is occupied, so raising the concentration gradient no longer speeds transport. The rate at that point is the transport maximum.

Firm, flexible, avascular connective tissue whose chondrocytes sit in pockets in a water-rich matrix, usually wrapped in a perichondrium. Its types are hyaline cartilage (smooth), fibrocartilage (thick collagen) and elastic cartilage (elastic fibers).
The smallest unit that can carry out the activities of life on its own. Cells are built from molecules and are the units that make up tissues.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The cell body holds a neuron's nucleus and makes its proteins; dendrites are short branches that receive signals; the single axon carries the signal away, ending in axon terminals (synaptic end bulbs) that release chemicals onto the next cell.
The ordered series of events from a cell's formation to its division: interphase (G1, S and G2, with DNA replicated in S) followed by the mitotic phase. A cell that stops cycling rests in G0.
The process by which a cell becomes specialized in structure and function, by switching on one set of genes and keeping others off. The genome itself is not changed.
A specialized spot where membrane proteins connect a cell to a neighboring cell or to the material around it. The three main types are tight junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions.

The controlled breakdown of fuel molecules, such as glucose, inside cells, with the energy released captured as ATP. Broken down fully with oxygen, one glucose yields 6 CO2, 6 water and about 30–32 ATP.

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord, where integration happens. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything else: the nerves, the ganglia along them and the sensory receptors at their ends.

Neurons near the front surface of the medulla oblongata that respond to hydrogen ions in the brain's fluid. Because carbon dioxide crosses the blood–brain barrier and hydrogen ions do not, they track arterial PCO2.

The hierarchy that runs the ANS: the spinal cord holds preganglionic neurons and simple visceral reflexes; brainstem centers integrate reflexes for the heart, vessels, breathing and pupils; the hypothalamus integrates body temperature, water balance and energy stores; and the limbic system and cortex feed emotions and thoughts into the hypothalamus.

The folded structure behind the brainstem that compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects force, timing and direction, and helps keep balance. Damage causes ataxia, clumsy uncoordinated movement on the same side.

A ring of connected arteries under the brain, also called the circle of Willis: the anterior communicating artery, the anterior cerebral arteries, the internal carotids, the posterior communicating arteries and the posterior cerebral arteries from the basilar artery. It is an anastomosis that can reroute blood around a slowly narrowed artery.

Differences in function between the two cerebral hemispheres: language is handled mainly by the left hemisphere in most people, and spatial attention, face recognition and the emotional tone of speech mainly by the right. The corpus callosum shares information between them.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: Cerebrospinal fluid: the clear fluid secreted mainly by the choroid plexuses (about 500 mL a day) that fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space, floats and cushions the brain, and returns to venous blood, classically through the arachnoid granulations. Excess CSF enlarging the ventricles is hydrocephalus; a lumbar puncture samples it.

The largest part of the brain: two cerebral hemispheres separated by the longitudinal fissure and joined by the corpus callosum. Its outer layer, the cerebral cortex, is gray matter folded into gyri and sulci over a core of white matter that includes the internal capsule.

The four spaces inside the heart: two upper atria that receive blood from veins and two lower ventricles that pump blood into arteries. Surface grooves (the coronary and interventricular sulci) mark their boundaries; auricles, pectinate muscles and trabeculae carneae are features of their walls.
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: The features all living things share: organization, metabolism (the sum of all chemical changes in the body), responsiveness, movement, growth, development and reproduction. Staying alive also depends on oxygen, nutrients, water, a narrow temperature range and suitable air pressure.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A state in which positive and negative charges are held apart by a barrier, so one region has extra positive charge and a nearby region extra negative charge. Separating charge takes energy, which is stored as potential energy; in your cells, a very thin layer of separated charge lines the two faces of the membrane.

The three main buffers in body fluids: the bicarbonate buffer (main buffer of extracellular fluid), the phosphate buffer (inside cells and in urine) and the protein buffer (hemoglobin, albumin and proteins inside cells). They act within seconds but remove no acid from the body.
The smallest level of organization: atoms, the smallest units of an element, and molecules, the units formed when atoms bond together.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A molecule that one cell releases to change the activity of another cell (also called a signaling molecule). It acts only on cells with receptor proteins that bind it.

A process that breaks and forms chemical bonds, turning reactants into products without creating or destroying atoms. A synthesis reaction joins reactants into a larger product; a decomposition reaction splits a reactant into smaller products.

Signaling across a synaptic cleft by a neurotransmitter: an action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal, calcium triggers exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, the neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, and it is then removed.

Chloride, the main ECF anion (98–106 mmol/L), follows sodium and trades places with bicarbonate: vomiting causes hypochloremia, and large volumes of saline cause hyperchloremia. Magnesium, mostly in bone and cells, is set by reabsorption in the thick ascending limb; hypomagnesemia causes tremor, tetany and arrhythmias and keeps potassium and calcium low.
roots: magnesium, from Magnesia, a region of Greece

terms.def: The one-for-one exchange of bicarbonate for chloride across the red blood cell membrane through the carrier protein band 3. In the tissues bicarbonate leaves and chloride enters; in the lungs the exchange reverses. It is passive and uses no ATP.

Autonomic neurons named for their transmitter. Cholinergic neurons release acetylcholine: every preganglionic neuron, every parasympathetic postganglionic neuron, and the sympathetic postganglionic neurons to eccrine sweat glands. Adrenergic neurons release norepinephrine: most sympathetic postganglionic neurons.

Chromatin is DNA wound around histone proteins into nucleosomes and folded further. A chromosome is one DNA molecule with its proteins; once copied, it has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

Disorders caused by an extra, missing or rearranged chromosome, seen on a karyotype (the chromosomes photographed in metaphase and arranged in pairs). A trisomy is three copies of one chromosome; trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome, whose risk rises with maternal age.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: long-lasting lung disease with airflow obstruction that does not fully reverse (FEV1 ÷ FVC below 0.70 after a drug that opens the airways), mainly from smoking. Its two main forms are emphysema, the destruction of alveolar walls, and chronic bronchitis, a daily cough with excess mucus for at least three months in two years in a row.

Mixing waves of the stomach grind and mix food into chyme, a soupy acidic paste, and push a few milliliters at a time through the pylorus. Gastric emptying takes about 2 to 4 hours for a mixed meal; the enterogastric reflex and the hormones CCK and secretin slow it when acid, fat or concentrated chyme reach the small intestine.

Mobile projections of the cell surface with a core of microtubules. Cilia are short and numerous and move fluid across the cell surface; a flagellum is long and single and moves the cell, as in a sperm.

A body rhythm with a cycle of about 24 hours that persists without time cues, such as melatonin, cortisol and body temperature. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master (biological) clock, reset daily by light.

The three levels that multiply the small intestine's absorptive surface: circular folds (permanent ridges of mucosa and submucosa), villi (finger-like projections of the mucosa, each with blood capillaries and a central lacteal for fat) and microvilli on each absorptive cell. Intestinal glands between the villi renew the lining and secrete watery intestinal juice.

Failure of the circulation to deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, so cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactate rises. Hypovolemic shock comes from too little volume, cardiogenic shock from a failing pump, and obstructive shock from a blockage of flow into or out of the heart.

A loop of eight reactions in the mitochondrial matrix, also called the Krebs or TCA cycle, that joins acetyl CoA to oxaloacetate and rebuilds oxaloacetate. Each turn releases 2 CO2 and makes 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP.

The four chemical classes of hormones: amine hormones (single changed amino acids), peptide hormones (short amino acid chains), protein hormones (long folded chains) and steroid hormones (built from cholesterol). Androgens are steroid hormones that drive male characteristics.

The six kinds of substance food supplies: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and water. Macronutrients (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and water) are needed in grams a day; micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) in milligrams or micrograms.

Sorting bones by shape into long (a shaft and two ends), short (cube-like), flat (thin, with two broad surfaces), irregular (complex shapes) and sesamoid (small round bones inside tendons). Shape, not size, decides the group.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: Epithelia are named by layers and by the shape of the surface cells. Simple means one layer and stratified means two or more; squamous cells are flat, cuboidal cells are cube-shaped and columnar cells are tall.

By shape, neurons are multipolar (one axon, many dendrites), bipolar (one axon, one dendrite) or unipolar, also called pseudounipolar (one process that splits in two). By job, they are sensory neurons (toward the CNS), interneurons (within the CNS) or motor neurons (out to effectors).

The rapid mitotic divisions of the zygote in its first days, which make more and smaller cells (blastomeres) without any growth. By day 3 to 4 they form a solid ball of about 16 to 32 cells, the morula.

Activation of only the rare naive lymphocytes whose ready-made antigen receptors fit an antigen, followed by clonal expansion into a clone of identical cells; many clones responding to one microbe's many epitopes make a polyclonal response.

Clot retraction: platelets pull on fibrin with actin and myosin, squeezing out serum and drawing the vessel edges together. Fibrinolysis: tPA converts plasminogen, built into the clot, into plasmin, which cuts fibrin and dissolves the clot over days.

Too little clotting: thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count), hemophilia (an inherited lack of factor VIII or IX), von Willebrand disease. Too much: thrombosis, forming a thrombus in an unbroken vessel; an embolus is a mass carried in the blood, and the blockage it causes is an embolism. Thrombocytosis is a high platelet count.

The conversion of blood into a gel as the enzyme thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin threads. In the body, tissue factor with factor VIIa starts it and activated platelets host the burst of thrombin; in the lab model, the extrinsic (PT) and intrinsic (aPTT) pathways meet at factor X and the common pathway. Factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K.

The snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear. Its three channels are the scala vestibuli (from the oval window), the cochlear duct and the scala tympani (to the round window). The spiral organ (organ of Corti), with its hair cells, sits on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane.

The osmotic pressure made by dissolved proteins that cannot cross the wall between two fluids; also called oncotic pressure. In plasma (blood colloid osmotic pressure, BCOP) it is about 25 mm Hg, mostly from albumin, and it pulls fluid into capillaries.

Common skin conditions: pressure injury (bedsore) from compressed capillaries over bone; acne from plugged, inflamed follicles; stretch marks from torn dermal fibers; callus and corn from thickened stratum corneum; albinism (melanocytes make little or no melanin); vitiligo (melanocytes destroyed in patches); eczema (weak barrier with inflammation).

The most common urinary problems: urinary tract infection (UTI), usually gut bacteria climbing the urethra; kidney stones (renal calculi), crystals of concentrated solute, mostly calcium oxalate; and incontinence, involuntary leakage of urine, sorted into stress, urge, overflow and functional types.
Dense bone built of osteons, forming the shaft wall of long bones and the outer shell of every bone. Also called cortical bone; about 80% of the skeleton's mass.

The response of the system that did not cause an acid–base disorder: the lungs change PCO2 (respiratory compensation, within hours) or the kidneys change bicarbonate (renal compensation, over 3 to 5 days), in the same direction as the primary change. It is uncompensated, partially compensated or fully compensated depending on how far the pH has returned toward 7.35 to 7.45.

The body's responses to blood loss: the baroreceptor reflex within seconds, movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma over hours, the RAAS, ADH and thirst over a day, and replacement of plasma proteins and red blood cells over days to weeks.

About 30 plasma proteins that, once activated by the classical, lectin or alternative pathway, split C3 and then coat microbes for phagocytes (opsonization), promote inflammation, and build the membrane attack complex that bursts microbes.

Problems of pregnancy that include ectopic pregnancy (implantation outside the uterine cavity, usually in a uterine tube), placenta previa (a placenta over or near the cervix, causing painless bleeding), preeclampsia (new high blood pressure after week 20 with organ damage, from endothelial injury) and gestational diabetes (diabetes that appears in pregnancy as placental hormones cause insulin resistance).
The amount of solute in a given volume of solution: amount divided by volume. For electrolytes it is usually given in millimoles per liter (mmol/L), a unit that counts particles.

The two functional divisions of the respiratory tract. The conducting zone (nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea and the air tubes down to the last ones without alveoli) filters, warms, humidifies and delivers air; the respiratory zone (the smallest airways that carry alveoli, and the alveoli) is where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between air and blood.

The speed at which an action potential travels along an axon, from about 0.5 m/s in thin unmyelinated fibers to about 120 m/s in wide myelinated ones. It rises with axon diameter, myelination and temperature.

Structural problems of the heart or great vessels present at birth, in about 1 baby in 100. Examples include a patent foramen ovale (a flap that never seals), septal defects (holes in the wall between the atria or ventricles) and a patent ductus arteriosus.

Tissue made of relatively few cells scattered in a large extracellular matrix of ground substance and fibers. Its groups are connective tissue proper (loose and dense), supportive connective tissue (cartilage and bone) and fluid connective tissue (blood).

Protein fibers in the matrix: collagen fibers are strong when pulled but barely stretch, elastic fibers (made of elastin) stretch and recoil, and reticular fibers are thin collagen strands that form supporting nets.

The three connective tissue layers of a skeletal muscle: the epimysium around the whole muscle, the perimysium around each fascicle (a bundle of fibers), and the endomysium around each fiber. They merge at the ends of the muscle into its tendon.

Consciousness needs the reticular activating system and the cerebral cortex. The EEG records the cortex's summed synaptic potentials: fast small waves when awake, slow large waves in deep sleep. Sleep cycles about every 90 minutes through non-REM stages N1, N2 and N3 and REM sleep, when the EEG looks awake, the eyes dart, dreams are vivid and most skeletal muscles are paralyzed.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: The way an action potential travels along an unmyelinated axon: every patch of membrane fires in turn, each next to the last. It is slow, about 0.5 to 2 m/s.

A working muscle cell of the heart wall (a cardiomyocyte): short, branched and striated, with one or two central nuclei, many mitochondria, and intercalated discs whose gap junctions pass action potentials to its neighbors. It rests at about −90 mV and fires only when charge from a neighbor brings it to threshold.
terms.topicTitle: Cardiac muscle cells and their action potential

terms.def: The strength of contraction at any given stretch, set by how much calcium reaches the cross-bridges. Positive inotropic factors such as norepinephrine and epinephrine raise it; negative inotropic factors such as beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, acidosis and hyperkalemia lower it.
The part of a feedback loop that receives input from the afferent pathway, compares it with the set point, and sends commands along the efferent pathway (also called the integrating center).

Heart rate is set by the cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata. Its cardioaccelerator center speeds the SA node through sympathetic nerves and the cardiac plexus; its cardioinhibitory center slows it through the vagus nerves. Factors that change heart rate are called chronotropic.

The system that decides when a cell moves through the cell cycle. Cyclins bind and switch on cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which push the cell forward, and checkpoints pause it until conditions are met. Oncogenes are overactive division-promoting genes; tumor suppressor genes normally restrain division.

The temperature of the deep tissues (brain, chest and abdominal organs), held near 36.6 to 37 °C, as opposed to the shell of skin and limbs, whose temperature varies widely with blood flow and surroundings.

The heart muscle's own blood supply. The right and left coronary arteries leave the aorta just above the aortic valve and branch (left anterior descending, circumflex, marginal and posterior interventricular arteries); cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: The temporary endocrine gland formed from a follicle's granulosa and theca cells after ovulation. It secretes progesterone, estradiol and inhibin for about 12 to 14 days, then shrinks into a pale scar, the corpus albicans, unless a pregnancy keeps it alive.

Cortical nephrons (about 85%) have their renal corpuscles in the outer cortex and short loops. Juxtamedullary nephrons (about 15%) have their corpuscles next to the medulla and long loops reaching deep into it, which let the kidney make concentrated urine.

The main tract for voluntary movement, running from the cerebral cortex through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, pons and pyramids of the medulla. About 85–90% of its axons cross at the pyramidal decussation and descend as the lateral corticospinal tract; the rest form the anterior corticospinal tract. The corticobulbar tract is its branch to the cranial nerve motor nuclei.
roots: bulb, the old name for the brainstem

terms.def: The main glucocorticoid, a steroid from the zona fasciculata released under control of CRH and ACTH, with negative feedback, a morning peak and a rise with stress. It raises blood glucose through gluconeogenesis, damps inflammation and keeps vessels responsive to sympathetic signals.

terms.term: countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta
terms.def: The passive exchange of solute and water in the hairpin vasa recta. Blood gains salt and urea and loses water on the way down, then reverses on the way up, so it carries off reabsorbed water without washing out the medullary gradient.

The nephron loop's way of building the medullary gradient. Fluid flows in opposite directions in its two limbs; the thick ascending limb pumps salt out without water and the descending limb loses water, so a small difference at each level is multiplied into a large one from top to bottom.
A bond in which two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons (single, double or triple bonds). The strongest bonds in the molecules of your body.
The eight bones of the brain case (cranium): the frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones. Its domed top is the calvaria.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: A small molecule in muscle that stores a high-energy phosphate group, also called phosphocreatine. The enzyme creatine kinase moves the phosphate to ADP to remake ATP in one step, covering about the first 10 seconds of all-out effort, and rebuilds creatine phosphate at rest.
A myosin head bound to actin, bridging from a thick filament to a thin filament. It exists only while the head is attached.
terms.topicTitle: The sliding filament model and cross-bridge cycle

terms.def: The repeating sequence by which a myosin head moves a thin filament: the cocked head binds actin; releasing phosphate drives the power stroke, which pulls the thin filament toward the M line; a new ATP binding frees the head; and splitting that ATP recocks it. It runs while calcium is on troponin and ATP is available.
terms.topicTitle: The sliding filament model and cross-bridge cycle

terms.def: The four side-view curves of the adult spine: cervical and lumbar curves bow forward (lordosis), thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves bow backward (kyphosis). The thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves are primary, present before birth; the cervical and lumbar curves are secondary, forming after birth. Scoliosis is an abnormal sideways bend.
The skin: a keratinized stratified squamous epidermis on a dermis of dense irregular connective tissue. It is the only dry membrane.
Division of the cytoplasm at the end of the mitotic phase. A ring of actin and myosin tightens around the middle of the cell, deepening a cleavage furrow until the cell pinches in two.

The network of protein fibers in the cytoplasm: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments and microtubules. It shapes the cell, holds organelles, provides tracks for transport and, with motor proteins such as myosin, produces movement. Microtubules grow from the centrosome, which holds a pair of centrioles.

A CD8 T cell that recognizes antigen in MHC class I and kills the cell showing it, by releasing perforin (which makes pores) and granzymes (which trigger caspases) or by binding Fas with its Fas ligand, so the target dies by apoptosis.

Air that is breathed in and out but takes no part in gas exchange. Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting airways, about 150 mL; alveolar dead space is alveoli that get air but no blood flow; total dead space is the two added together.

The muscles along the vertebral column. The erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis groups, lateral to medial) runs from the pelvis and lower spine to the ribs, vertebrae and skull and extends the spine; the splenius extends the head and turns it to the same side.

A visceral reflex: stretch of the rectum, usually after a mass movement, signals the sacral spinal cord, which makes the rectum contract and the internal anal sphincter relax. The external anal sphincter is voluntary, so you choose when defecation happens, often helped by a Valsalva's maneuver.

terms.term: defenses against each type of pathogen
terms.def: A pathogen is a microbe or parasite that can cause disease. Each type meets the defenses that can reach it: antibodies and complement for bacteria outside cells, Th1 cells and macrophages for bacteria inside cells, interferons, NK cells, antibodies and cytotoxic T cells for viruses, and Th2 cells, IgE and eosinophils for worms. Immune evasion is a pathogen's ways around them.

Damage to or loss of the myelin sheath, which lets current leak out between nodes so conduction slows or fails. Multiple sclerosis, in which the immune system attacks CNS myelin, is the commonest demyelinating disease.

Connective tissue packed with thick collagen bundles and few cells. In dense regular tissue the bundles run parallel (tendons, ligaments); in dense irregular tissue they run every way (dermis, organ capsules).
Depolarization: the membrane potential becomes less negative than rest. Repolarization: it returns toward rest after a depolarization. Hyperpolarization: it becomes more negative than rest.

A dermatome is the strip of skin whose sensory axons travel in one spinal nerve and enter the cord through one dorsal root. Neighboring dermatomes overlap, so damage to one root reduces sensation rather than abolishing it.

The connective tissue layer of the skin beneath the epidermis. Its thin papillary layer (areolar tissue) rises into dermal papillae; its thick reticular layer (dense irregular tissue) gives the skin strength and stretch and holds the larger vessels, nerves and glands.
A button-shaped anchoring junction in which cadherins grip across the gap between two cells and dense plaques anchor intermediate filaments on each side. It holds cells together against pulling.

The formation of the first blood vessels by vasculogenesis: mesoderm cells become hemangioblasts, which cluster into blood islands; angioblasts at their edges form endothelium, cells in their centers form the first blood cells, and the islands join into vascular tubes. Later vessels sprout from existing ones by angiogenesis.

The lower airway grows from the laryngotracheal bud, an outpouching of the foregut, which splits into two lung buds (bronchial buds) that branch repeatedly; the upper airway begins as the olfactory pits on the face. Fetal breathing movements and lung fluid stretch the lungs, which is needed for their growth.

terms.term: development of the skeleton, joints and limbs
terms.def: Limbs grow from limb buds under the apical ectodermal ridge, which keeps the tip growing; cartilage models become bone by endochondral ossification; joints form where a joint interzone stays uncommitted; and the limbs rotate in weeks 7 and 8.

A group of diseases with chronically high blood glucose (hyperglycemia) from too little insulin, too little response to it, or both. Type 1 is loss of beta cells to the immune system; type 2 is insulin resistance with beta cells that cannot keep up. Polyuria and polydipsia are its classic signs.

A dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. When it contracts, the dome flattens and moves down, which enlarges the thoracic cavity; it is the main muscle of breathing.

Diarrhea is three or more loose or watery stools a day, from secretion, unabsorbed solutes, inflammation or fast transit; it loses water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate. Constipation is infrequent, hard stools, usually from slow transit, which lets the colon absorb more water.
The central part of the brain between the cerebrum and the brainstem, made of the thalamus, hypothalamus and epithalamus. The thalamus relays and filters almost all input to the cerebral cortex.

The spreading of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated, driven by their own random motion. Net diffusion is the overall movement left after subtracting the particles crossing one way from those crossing the other; it stops at equilibrium, though the particles keep moving.

The net movement of each solute between plasma and interstitial fluid, down its own concentration gradient. Lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass through the endothelial cells; small water-soluble ones pass through the clefts between them.

The six things that happen to food: ingestion (taking it in), propulsion (moving it along), mechanical digestion (breaking and mixing it without changing its molecules), chemical digestion (enzymes splitting molecules by hydrolysis), absorption (moving nutrients from the lumen into blood or lymph) and defecation (expelling the remains).
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: Shock caused by widespread vasodilation, which drops TPR and pools blood in dilated vessels; also called vascular shock. Its main forms are septic shock (from sepsis, the body's poorly controlled response to an infection), neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone) and shock from a severe allergic reaction.

Substances that increase urine output, most by blocking sodium reabsorption. A loop diuretic blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and is the strongest; a thiazide diuretic blocks the sodium–chloride symporter of the distal tubule; an osmotic diuretic such as mannitol is filtered but not reabsorbed and holds water in the tubule.

The cerebellum has a midline vermis, two lateral hemispheres and a small flocculonodular lobe underneath. Functionally, the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) handles balance and eye movement, the spinocerebellum (vermis and nearby strip) posture and ongoing movement, and the cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) planning skilled movement. Inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles join it to the medulla, pons and midbrain.
Deoxyribonucleic acid: two antiparallel strands of nucleotides twisted into a double helix, held together by base pairing (A with T, G with C). Its base sequence stores inherited information.

The copying of DNA before a cell divides. Helicase separates the strands, and DNA polymerase builds a new complementary strand on each old one, giving two identical molecules that each keep one old strand.

A dominant allele shows its effect with one copy; a recessive allele only with two. A carrier is a healthy heterozygote with one recessive disease allele. Autosomal dominant and recessive patterns involve genes on autosomes; a recessive lethal allele kills only homozygotes, a dominant lethal allele anyone with one copy.

The branches a spinal nerve splits into just outside the intervertebral foramen. The dorsal ramus supplies the deep back muscles and the skin of the back; the larger ventral ramus supplies the front and sides of the trunk and the limbs. Both are mixed.

The two roots connecting each side of a spinal cord segment to the body. The dorsal (posterior) root carries sensory axons in and has a dorsal root ganglion holding their cell bodies; the ventral (anterior) root carries motor axons out. Beyond the ganglion they join into one nerve.

The two routes visual information takes beyond the primary visual cortex: the dorsal stream into the parietal lobe works out where things are and guides movement toward them, and the ventral stream into the temporal lobe recognizes what they are.
The posterior main body cavity: the cranial cavity inside the skull, which holds the brain, and the vertebral canal inside the backbone, which holds the spinal cord. Both parts are walled in by bone.

terms.term: drugs that act on autonomic receptors
terms.def: Drugs that bind autonomic receptor proteins. An agonist activates a receptor protein and an antagonist blocks it. Sympathomimetic drugs (albuterol, phenylephrine) mimic sympathetic effects; sympatholytic drugs (beta blockers) block them; parasympathomimetic drugs (pilocarpine) mimic acetylcholine; anticholinergic drugs (atropine) block it; nicotine activates the nicotinic receptor proteins of every ganglion.

Supply of one organ by both autonomic divisions. The divisions usually have opposite effects (sympathetic speeds the heart, parasympathetic slows it) and sometimes cooperate (both stimulate the glands that make saliva). Most blood vessels, sweat glands, arrector pili muscles and the adrenal medulla lack it and get sympathetic fibers only.

Timed stretches of the ECG. The PR interval (start of P to start of QRS, 0.12 to 0.20 second) is mostly AV nodal delay; the ST segment (end of QRS to start of T) is the flat plateau when the ventricles are fully depolarized; the QT interval (start of QRS to end of T) spans the ventricular action potential.

The three deflections of a normal beat: the P wave (atrial depolarization), the QRS complex (ventricular depolarization, which hides atrial repolarization) and the T wave (ventricular repolarization).

An excess of fluid in the interstitial spaces, which forms when fluid filters out of capillaries faster than it drains away. Causes are higher capillary pressure, lower plasma protein, leaky capillary walls, or blocked drainage; widespread swelling is systemic edema.
The cell, tissue or organ that carries out the control center's command and so changes the regulated variable; almost always a muscle or a gland.

Estrogen (mainly estradiol) builds the endometrium, thins cervical mucus, drives female secondary sex characteristics, protects bone and gives negative or, when high and sustained, positive feedback. Progesterone makes the endometrium secretory, thickens cervical mucus, quiets the myometrium, raises resting body temperature and gives negative feedback.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: The rest-and-digest pattern: slower heart rate, narrowed pupils and near focusing, tears and watery saliva, more movement and secretion in the stomach and intestines, relaxed sphincters, emptying of the bladder and rectum, and narrowed airways. Effects are local and brief.

The fight-or-flight pattern: faster, stronger heartbeat (through the cardiac accelerator nerves), constricted skin and gut vessels (through the vasomotor nerves) and dilated vessels in working skeletal muscle (through local chemicals and epinephrine), wider airways and pupils, glucose release from the liver, sweating, and slowed gut and bladder emptying. It can be widespread and is prolonged by adrenal epinephrine.

Testosterone, directly or after conversion to DHT or estradiol, shapes the male reproductive tract before birth, drives the changes of puberty, and maintains sperm production, sex drive, muscle, bone and red cell production. Secondary sex characteristics are the features it produces that differ between the sexes but are not part of the reproductive tract, such as facial hair and a deeper voice.
The route that carries commands away from the control center to the effector: nerves carrying action potentials, or a hormone traveling in the blood.
