Local lipid messengers made on demand from a 20-carbon fatty acid cut out of membrane phospholipids. They include prostaglandins, which sensitize pain-sensing nerve endings and dilate small vessels, and leukotrienes, which constrict airways.
The share of the end-diastolic volume that a ventricle ejects in one beat: EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100. A normal left ventricular value is about 50 to 70 percent.

Elastic arteries, the largest arteries near the heart, have many elastic fibers in the tunica media; they stretch during ejection and recoil in diastole. Muscular arteries, farther out, have a thick smooth muscle media and distribute blood to organs.
A property of particles that makes them push or pull on each other. Protons carry positive charge and electrons negative charge; opposite charges attract and like charges repel.

The flow of electric charge, measured in amperes. In your body it is an ion current, carried by ions moving through fluid or across a membrane; by convention its direction is the direction positive charge moves, and current equals voltage divided by electrical resistance.
A synapse where gap junctions join two neurons, so ions and current pass directly from one to the other. It is almost instant, usually two-way, and makes coupled neurons fire in step.

The electrocardiogram (ECG, also EKG): a graph over time of the summed voltage changes of the heart, recorded from electrodes on the skin. Each lead is one view, the voltage between a positive electrode and a reference; a standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 electrodes.

The total push on an ion: its concentration gradient combined with the electrical gradient (the voltage), which pushes positive ions toward the negative side and negative ions toward the positive side. The two parts can add together or oppose each other.
A substance that separates into ions when it dissolves in water, so the water conducts electricity. In clinical use, the dissolved ions themselves, such as sodium, potassium, chloride and calcium.

The protein complexes of the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 to oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor, and pump H+ into the intermembrane space. H+ flowing back through ATP synthase makes ATP (chemiosmosis); together this is oxidative phosphorylation.

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. An element is a substance made of one kind of atom, listed in the periodic table by atomic number; a compound is two or more different elements joined in a fixed ratio.

The four membranes around the embryo that are not part of its body: the amnion, which encloses the amniotic cavity and its fluid; the yolk sac, where the first blood cells form; the allantois, whose vessels become those of the cord; and the chorion (chorionic membrane), the outermost, which makes hCG.

The graded depolarization of the motor end plate caused by acetylcholine opening the end plate's acetylcholine-gated channels. In a healthy junction it is several times larger than needed to bring the neighboring sarcolemma to threshold.

End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the volume in a ventricle at the end of diastole, just before it contracts (about 120 mL at rest). End-systolic volume (ESV) is the volume left at the end of systole, after ejection (about 50 mL at rest).

The clearing of a neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft, which ends its signal: by diffusion away, by degradation (enzymes such as acetylcholinesterase break it down), or by reuptake (transporter proteins carry it back into the axon terminal or nearby astrocytes).

Bone formation in which a hyaline cartilage model is broken down and replaced by bone, starting at a primary ossification center in the diaphysis and later at secondary ossification centers in the epiphyses. It forms most of the skeleton.
A ductless gland that releases hormones into the interstitial fluid, from where they diffuse into capillaries and travel in the blood to target cells.

All the hormone-secreting glands and cells of the body taken together: dedicated glands such as the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands, organs with a hormone-making part such as the pancreas, and scattered hormone-secreting cells in organs such as the stomach, heart and kidneys. Its parts are linked only by the blood.

Taking material into a cell by folding a patch of plasma membrane around it and pinching it off as a vesicle. Its forms are phagocytosis (large particles), pinocytosis (droplets of fluid) and receptor-mediated endocytosis (specific substances bound to matching membrane proteins).

A network of membrane sacs and tubes in the cytoplasm. Rough ER is studded with ribosomes and folds new proteins; smooth ER has no ribosomes and makes lipids, breaks down some drugs and stores calcium ions.

Energy is the capacity to do work. Potential energy is stored energy (chemical energy is potential energy held in the arrangement of atoms and bonds); kinetic energy is the energy of motion, including heat. An exergonic reaction releases energy, and an endergonic reaction takes energy in.

The relation between energy taken in as food and energy spent. A positive balance is stored, mostly as fat; a negative balance draws stores down. Body mass index (kg/m²) screens body weight, and dietary guidelines give official advice on healthy eating.

The energy food releases when broken down, measured in kilocalories: the heat that raises 1 kg of water by 1 °C. Carbohydrate and protein supply about 4 kcal per gram, fat about 9, and alcohol about 7.

The nervous system in the gut wall: the myenteric plexus between the two muscle layers (motility) and the submucosal plexus in the submucosa (secretion and local blood flow). It can run peristalsis and secretion by itself; the autonomic nervous system adjusts it.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: A biological catalyst, almost always a protein. Its substrate binds a pocket called the active site, and the enzyme lowers the activation energy, the energy the reactants must gain before they can react.
The surface layer of the skin: a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with no blood vessels, fed by diffusion from the dermis. About 90% of its cells are keratinocytes.

The main hormone of the adrenal medulla (also called adrenaline). Released into the blood during sympathetic activation, it reaches cells throughout the body, including cells no sympathetic fiber touches, and keeps acting for a few minutes after the nerve signal stops.

The disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a growing long bone (the growth plate). Its four zones (reserve zone, proliferative zone, zone of maturation and hypertrophy, zone of calcified matrix) add cartilage that bone replaces; when growth ends it becomes the epiphyseal line.

A sheet of tightly joined cells that covers a body surface or lines a lumen. Its apical surface faces the open space, its basal surface rests on a basement membrane, and it has no blood vessels of its own.
roots: originally nipple; a thin covering layer

terms.def: The membrane voltage at which one ion has no net movement, because its electrical gradient exactly cancels its concentration gradient. About −90 mV for potassium and +60 mV for sodium.

Erection is the filling of erectile tissue with blood when parasympathetic nerves release nitric oxide and its smooth muscle relaxes. Ejaculation is the release of semen: sympathetic nerves move it into the urethra (emission), then a somatic reflex through the pudendal nerve expels it (expulsion).
A red blood cell: a flexible biconcave disc about 7.5 µm across with no nucleus or organelles, packed with hemoglobin. It makes ATP by glycolysis and lives about 120 days.

The making of red blood cells in red bone marrow, from proerythroblasts through erythroblasts to reticulocytes, which lose their ribosomes in a day or two in the blood. Erythropoietin from the kidneys drives it in a negative feedback loop that senses the oxygen reaching the kidneys.
Erythropoietin, a hormone released by oxygen-sensing cells of the kidney when oxygen delivery falls. It acts on the red bone marrow to raise red blood cell production.

The muscular tube, about 25 cm long, from the pharynx through the chest and diaphragm to the stomach. It is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, its muscle changes from skeletal above to smooth below, and it is closed at the top by the upper esophageal sphincter and at the bottom by the lower esophageal sphincter. Reflux of stomach contents past the lower sphincter causes heartburn; frequent reflux is GERD.

Nutrients the body cannot make, or cannot make fast enough, so they must come from food: the nine essential amino acids, the essential fatty acids linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid, and every vitamin and mineral.

Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption: the extra oxygen used after exercise, above resting use, to rebuild ATP and creatine phosphate, reload myoglobin, clear lactate and pay for a warmer body, raised hormones and repair. The older name is oxygen debt.
A cell whose membrane can produce an action potential, because it has voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. Neurons and muscle fibers are the main excitable cells.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: The sequence that links an action potential on the sarcolemma to contraction: the action potential travels down the T tubules, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and calcium binding to troponin lets myosin pull on actin.

Graded potentials caused by a neurotransmitter in a postsynaptic neuron. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is a small depolarization toward threshold; an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) hyperpolarizes the membrane or holds it near rest, away from threshold.

A gland whose product travels through a duct, or for a single-cell gland directly, onto a surface such as the skin or the inside of the gut. A serous gland releases watery, enzyme-rich fluid; a mucous gland releases mucus.

Release of material from a cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and empties its contents outside. It is how cells secrete products, and it adds the vesicle's membrane and proteins to the cell surface.

Breathing out (exhalation). Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall, which raises alveolar pressure above atmospheric. Forced expiration adds the internal intercostals and abdominal wall muscles. One inspiration plus one expiration is a respiratory cycle.
Gas exchange between alveolar air and blood in the pulmonary capillaries: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, each down its partial pressure gradient.

The fourteen bones of the face: two each of the maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal and palatine bones and the inferior nasal conchae, plus the single vomer and mandible. The mandible is the only skull bone that moves freely.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull
terms.say: mak-SIL-uh; zy-go-MAT-ik; LAK-rih-mul; PAL-uh-tine; KONG-kee; VOH-mer; MAN-dih-bul

terms.def: Passive movement of a substance down its gradient through a specific membrane protein: a channel, or a carrier protein that binds the substance, changes shape and releases it on the other side. Glucose enters most cells this way.

Temperature, pH, the amounts of substrate and enzyme, helpers and inhibitors all change how fast an enzyme works. A cofactor is a non-protein helper, often a metal ion; a coenzyme is an organic cofactor, often made from a vitamin.

Net diffusion is faster with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature, smaller particles, a larger surface area to cross, a shorter diffusion distance and a barrier that the particle crosses easily. The time to diffuse grows with the square of the distance, so diffusion works only over very short distances.

Spaces in each limb segment enclosed by deep fascia, intermuscular septa and bone, each holding muscles with a shared action. Because fascia barely stretches, swelling inside one raises its pressure until blood flow stops: compartment syndrome.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: The pattern of fascicles in a muscle: parallel (strap-like or spindle-shaped fusiform), convergent (a fan), pennate (angled onto a tendon: unipennate, bipennate or multipennate) or circular (a ring around an opening, a sphincter). Pennate muscles are stronger for their size; parallel muscles shorten farther and faster.

Cardiac muscle is striated and uses troponin, but its fibers are linked by gap junctions so the heart contracts as a unit, some fibers fire on their own (autorhythmicity), calcium entering from outside triggers release from the SR, its long action potential prevents tetanus, and it relies almost entirely on aerobic respiration.

The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its head fits the acetabulum on an angled neck; the greater and lesser trochanters anchor hip muscles, the linea aspera runs down its back, and its medial and lateral condyles rest on the tibia.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.def: The joining of a sperm and a secondary oocyte, from the sperm binding the zona pellucida to the combining of their chromosomes, normally in the ampulla of the uterine tube. It is also called conception, and its product is the zygote, a single diploid cell.

The pattern of blood flow before birth, when the placenta, not the lungs, exchanges gases. Three fetal shunts carry it: the ductus venosus (umbilical vein to inferior vena cava, past the liver), the foramen ovale (right atrium to left), and the ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk to aorta, past the lungs).

The hemoglobin of a fetus (HbF), with two alpha and two gamma chains. It binds 2,3-BPG weakly, so it holds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin (P50 about 19 mm Hg) and can take oxygen from maternal blood. It is mostly replaced by adult hemoglobin by about six months after birth.

The stage from the end of the embryonic period to birth: about week 10 to week 40 of pregnancy on the clinical count, a time of growth and maturation. Pregnancy is split into three trimesters; quickening is the mother's first feeling of movement, lanugo is fine body hair, and vernix caseosa is the greasy coating that protects the skin.

A rise in body temperature, usually to 38 °C or more, caused by pyrogens raising the hypothalamic set point through prostaglandin E2; heat-gain responses then raise temperature to meet the new set point.
The main cell of connective tissue proper, which makes fibers and ground substance. A less active one that maintains the matrix is called a fibrocyte.

The subtypes of fibrous joint (suture between skull bones; syndesmosis, where a ligament or interosseous membrane joins two bones; gomphosis, a tooth held in its socket by the periodontal ligament) and of cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis, joined by hyaline cartilage; symphysis, joined by fibrocartilage). A joint that has turned to bone is a synostosis.
Movement of water and small solutes through a membrane or thin barrier, pushed by a hydrostatic pressure gradient. Particles too large for the openings, such as blood cells, stay behind.

The three-layer filter between glomerular blood and the capsular space: the fenestrated endothelium (its fenestrations stop blood cells), the thick, negatively charged glomerular basement membrane, and the podocyte pedicels with filtration slits between them. It passes water and small solutes and holds back almost all protein.

Flexion is a sagittal-plane movement that decreases the angle between two bones or bends the trunk or neck forward; extension increases the angle and returns the part toward anatomical position. Hyperextension is extension past anatomical position, and hyperflexion is flexion beyond the normal range.

terms.term: flow equals pressure gradient divided by resistance
terms.def: Flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance: F = ΔP/R. Doubling the pressure gradient doubles flow; doubling the resistance halves it.

Blood velocity equals flow divided by the total cross-sectional area of the vessels at that level. The capillaries together have the largest total area, so blood moves slowest there, about 0.3 mm/s, compared with about 30 cm/s in the aorta.

A disturbance of the volume or concentration of the body fluids. Hypovolemia and hypervolemia are losses and gains of salt and water together, which change only the extracellular fluid; dehydration and overhydration (water intoxication when severe) are losses and gains of water in excess of solute, which change osmolality and shrink or swell cells. A fluid shift moves fluid between compartments without changing the total.
terms.topicTitle: Body fluid compartments and water balance

terms.def: The loss of water, salts and proteins from the blood after a large burn: water evaporates through the lost barrier and plasma leaks through damaged, leaky capillaries into the tissues, so blood volume and blood pressure fall, most in the first day.

Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between clear materials; the cornea does most of it and the lens the rest. Accommodation rounds the lens for near vision: the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule fibers go slack and the lens bulges. Myopia focuses distant light in front of the retina, hyperopia behind it, and presbyopia is the age-related stiffening of the lens. Visual acuity is measured with a Snellen chart.

The growth of an ovarian follicle through the primordial, primary, secondary, tertiary and mature vesicular (Graafian) stages: granulosa cells multiply around the oocyte, theca cells form outside them, and a fluid-filled antrum appears. The late stages need FSH; most growing follicles die by atresia.

A soft spot of a newborn's skull: an area covered by tough membrane where several skull bones have not yet grown to meet. The anterior fontanelle is the largest and usually closes by about 1 to 2 years.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: An opening in the wall between the fetal atria, left by the septum secundum and covered from the left side by a flap of the septum primum. It lets blood pass only from the right atrium to the left, and after birth the flap is pressed shut and usually seals, leaving the fossa ovalis.

The heart's earliest development: mesoderm at the head end of the embryonic disc (the cardiogenic area) forms two cardiogenic cords, which hollow into two endocardial tubes. As the embryo folds, they fuse into one primitive heart tube, which begins beating at about day 22 after fertilization.

The cells and cell fragments of blood: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, about 45% of blood volume. Platelets are fragments, not whole cells, which is why the group is called elements.
A shallow oval dip in the interatrial septum, seen from the right atrium. It marks where an opening between the atria sealed after birth.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: The four stages of healing a broken bone: fracture hematoma, fibrocartilaginous callus (internal and external callus), bony callus of spongy bone, and remodeling. Closed or open reduction puts the ends back in line.

The heart's built-in property that a more-filled, more-stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully and ejects more, so stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume. It keeps the outputs of the two ventricles matched.
A vertical plane that divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) parts. It is also called the coronal plane.

Areas of the cerebral cortex with particular jobs (localization of function), many known by Brodmann's area numbers. Primary areas send out movement (primary motor cortex, precentral gyrus) or first receive a sense (primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, primary visual and auditory cortex); association areas plan movement or interpret one sense; multimodal integration areas combine senses; the prefrontal cortex runs executive function.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: The three kinds of joint sorted by how much they move: a synarthrosis is immobile or nearly so, an amphiarthrosis is slightly movable, and a diarthrosis is freely movable.

What blood does: it transports gases, nutrients, wastes, hormones and heat; it regulates pH, body temperature and fluid balance; and it protects against blood loss (clotting) and infection (white blood cells and immune proteins).

The liver's jobs: storing and releasing glucose, making plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, handling the nitrogen from broken-down amino acids, chemically processing drugs and toxins (detoxification), excreting bilirubin, storing iron and vitamins, and making bile.

The six jobs of the skeleton: support, protection of organs, movement (muscles pull on bones), mineral storage (about 99% of the body's calcium), blood cell formation in red marrow, and fat storage in yellow marrow.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: A small muscular sac under the liver that stores bile between meals and concentrates it by absorbing salt and water. Cholecystokinin makes it contract and empty bile into the duodenum. Gallstones form in it, most often from cholesterol.
A sex cell with one set of chromosomes: a sperm in males, an oocyte (egg) in females. An oocyte that has finished meiosis is called an ovum.
A cluster of neuron cell bodies is a nucleus in the CNS and a ganglion in the PNS. A bundle of axons is a tract in the CNS and a nerve in the PNS.

A cluster of protein tunnels, each made of two docked connexons of six connexins, that connects the cytoplasm of neighboring cells. Water, ions and small molecules pass through, so electrical current can spread from cell to cell.

Tube-shaped glands that open into the gastric pits of the stomach lining. They contain mucous neck cells (thin mucus), parietal cells (hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor), chief cells (pepsinogen and gastric lipase) and enteroendocrine cells, including G cells, which release gastrin.

Hormones released from the lining of the stomach and small intestine that coordinate digestion: gastrin (raises stomach acid), secretin (bicarbonate from the pancreas and the ducts that carry bile), cholecystokinin or CCK (gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes; slows stomach emptying) and motilin (clearing contractions between meals).
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: A segment of DNA whose base sequence codes for a working product, usually a protein. The genome is all the DNA in one set of chromosomes: about 3.1 billion base pairs and roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes in humans.

Using a gene to make its product. Cells control which genes they express, mainly through transcription factors, proteins that bind DNA near a gene and raise or lower its transcription. The proteome is the full set of proteins a cell holds at a given time.

The general senses use sensory receptors spread through the body: somatosensation (touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain and position) and the visceral senses from internal organs. The special senses (smell, taste, vision, hearing and balance) have sensory receptors gathered in organs in the head. A sensory modality is one kind of sense; a submodality is a variety within it.
The table that matches each three-base codon in mRNA to one amino acid or to a stop signal: 64 codons, 61 naming amino acids and 3 stops. A tRNA's anticodon pairs with its codon.

Genotype is the set of alleles a person carries for a gene or trait; phenotype is what is expressed and can be observed or measured, such as a blood type or a disease. Phenotype depends on genotype and environment. A trait is any inherited characteristic.

The three layers formed from the epiblast by gastrulation in week 3, as cells move through the primitive streak: ectoderm (outer covering and nervous system), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood, heart, kidneys and most connective tissue) and endoderm (linings of the gut and airways and the glands that bud from them). The hypoblast, the lower layer of the earlier two-layered disc, is replaced.
One cell or a group of epithelial cells that makes a product and releases it (secretion).

The Glasgow Coma Scale scores consciousness by adding the best eye-opening (1 to 4), verbal (1 to 5) and motor (1 to 6) responses, for a total from 3 to 15. A total of 8 or less is severe impairment, the usual working definition of coma.

The four glial cells of the CNS: astrocytes (regulate the fluid around neurons, wrap capillaries, form scars), oligodendrocytes (myelinate segments of many axons), microglia (resident immune cells that engulf debris) and ependymal cells (line the fluid-filled spaces of the brain and spinal cord).

The two glial cells of the PNS: Schwann cells, which myelinate one segment of one axon or cradle several unmyelinated axons and guide axon regrowth, and satellite cells, which cover neuron cell bodies in ganglia.

A support cell of nervous tissue (also called glia or neuroglia). Glial cells hold neurons in place, wrap and insulate axons, control the fluid around neurons and engulf debris, and unlike mature neurons they can divide.

The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of glomerular filtrate both kidneys make per minute, about 125 mL/min or 180 L a day in a healthy young adult. GFR = filtration coefficient × net filtration pressure.
The peptide hormone of the pancreatic alpha cells, released when blood glucose falls. It acts mainly on the liver, switching on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so blood glucose rises.
A six-carbon monosaccharide (C6H12O6) that dissolves in the liquid part of your blood and is the main fuel your cells, especially brain cells, break down for energy.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Muscles of the buttock and side of the hip: the gluteus maximus (extends and laterally rotates the thigh), the gluteus medius and minimus (abduct and medially rotate it and hold the pelvis level), the tensor fasciae latae (pulls on the iliotibial tract) and deep lateral rotators such as the piriformis.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: The coat of sugar chains attached to proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids on the outer surface of the plasma membrane. It marks cell identity, cushions the cell and helps cells recognize each other.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: A heavily branched polysaccharide of glucose that your liver and muscles build after meals. Liver glycogen is split to release glucose into the blood between meals; muscle glycogen fuels only the muscle that stores it.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.term: glycogen metabolism and gluconeogenesis in detail
terms.def: The steps of glucose storage and release. Glycogen synthase builds glycogen from activated glucose; glycogen phosphorylase clips glucose off by phosphorolysis, and glucose-6-phosphatase in liver and kidney frees it into the blood. Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from lactate, amino acids and glycerol, bypassing glycolysis's three one-way steps.

Glycogenesis is building glycogen from glucose; glycogenolysis is breaking glycogen down to glucose; gluconeogenesis is making new glucose from non-carbohydrates such as lactate, glycerol and amino acids, mainly in the liver.
The first stage of glucose breakdown: ten enzyme reactions in the cytosol that split one glucose into two pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. It does not use oxygen.

The ten steps of glycolysis in two phases. In the energy-consuming phase, hexokinase traps glucose as glucose-6-phosphate and 2 ATP are spent; in the energy-yielding phase, each three-carbon half is oxidized, making NADH, and 4 ATP are made, for a net 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.
roots: enzyme that adds a phosphate from ATP

terms.def: A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts and packages proteins arriving from the ER and sends them in vesicles to the plasma membrane, out of the cell, or to lysosomes. With the ER, vesicles, lysosomes and plasma membrane it forms the endomembrane system.
The steroid sex hormones made by the gonads: testosterone from the testes, driven by LH, and estrogens and progesterone from the ovaries, driven by FSH and LH.

A small, short-lived change in membrane potential whose size depends on the strength of the stimulus. It can depolarize or hyperpolarize, fades within a millimeter or two, and can add to other graded potentials.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: A difference in some quantity between two places, such as a concentration gradient (a difference in concentration) or a temperature gradient. Things move down a gradient, from more to less, without an energy input; its steepness is the difference divided by the distance.

Leukocytes with visible stained granules, all from the myeloblast: neutrophils (most numerous, many-lobed or polymorphonuclear nucleus, engulf bacteria), eosinophils (red-orange granules, attack parasitic worms) and basophils (dark granules holding histamine).

Gray matter is CNS tissue rich in neuron cell bodies, dendrites and axon terminals, where integration happens. White matter is CNS tissue made mostly of axon bundles wrapped in fatty glial layers, which carry signals between regions.

The large vessels at the base of the heart: the superior and inferior venae cavae (into the right atrium), the pulmonary trunk (out of the right ventricle, splitting into the right and left pulmonary arteries), the pulmonary veins (into the left atrium) and the aorta (out of the left ventricle, rising as the ascending aorta and curving over as the aortic arch).
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: Too much growth hormone causes gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults; too little in childhood causes pituitary dwarfism. Too little ADH effect causes diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine); too much causes SIADH (water retention and low plasma sodium).

A protein hormone of the anterior pituitary (GH, somatotropin). It drives growth mostly by making the liver and tissues release insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which makes epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide and tissues build protein; directly, it breaks down stored fat and raises the glucose in the blood.

The sense of taste. Taste buds hold gustatory receptor cells, epithelial cells with no axon that detect five taste qualities (salty, sour, sweet, umami and bitter) and pass the signal to sensory neurons in the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Umami is the savory taste of glutamate.

The community of trillions of bacteria living mainly in the colon (also called normal flora). They ferment fiber (saccharolytic fermentation) into short-chain fatty acids and gas (flatus), turn bilirubin into stercobilin, make some vitamins, and crowd out harmful microbes.

A hair is a strand of dead cells filled with hard keratin; it grows from a hair follicle, a tube of epidermis that dips into the dermis. The shaft projects above the skin and the root lies in the follicle; the matrix in the bulb, over the hair papilla, divides to make the hair, whose layers are the medulla, cortex and cuticle.

Hair cells are epithelial sensory receptor cells topped with a staircase of stereocilia joined by tip links. Bending toward the tallest stereocilium opens mechanically gated channels, K+ flows in and the cell releases more glutamate; bending away closes them and the cell releases less.

The repeating cycle of a hair follicle: anagen (growth, years on the scalp), catagen (a few weeks in which the follicle shrinks and a club hair forms) and telogen (about 3 months of rest before the old hair is pushed out by a new one).

The less oxygen hemoglobin carries, the more carbon dioxide the blood can carry, because deoxyhemoglobin binds more hydrogen ions and more carbon dioxide. It helps blood load carbon dioxide in the tissues and unload it in the lungs.

The hamstrings: the biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the back of the thigh. They start on the ischial tuberosity, flex the knee and extend the hip, and their tendons form the upper borders of the popliteal fossa behind the knee.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: A diploid (2n) cell holds both members of every chromosome pair, 46 in humans; a haploid (n) cell holds one of each pair, 23. Homologous chromosomes are the two members of a pair, one from each parent, with the same genes in the same order; the versions of a gene they carry are alleles.

The pouches of the colon wall (singular haustrum), formed because the colon's outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three ribbons, the teniae coli, whose tone bunches the wall. Epiploic appendages are small fat-filled tags of peritoneum on the surface. Haustral contractions slowly squeeze contents from one pouch to the next.

A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, or can only do so at abnormally high filling pressures. Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs; right-sided failure backs it up into the systemic veins; congestive heart failure names the resulting congestion.

The sounds of each beat, heard as lub-dub: S1 (lub) from closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole, and S2 (dub) from closure of the semilunar valves at its end. A murmur is the sound of turbulent flow, usually through a narrowed (stenotic) or leaking (regurgitant) valve.

Illness when temperature control is overwhelmed. Hyperthermia (heat gain beyond heat loss) ranges from heat exhaustion, with a normal brain, to heat stroke, a core above about 40 °C with brain dysfunction. Hypothermia is a core below 35 °C; frostbite is frozen tissue.

The four routes by which the body trades heat with its surroundings, each driven by a gradient: radiation (infrared rays to cooler surfaces), conduction (direct contact), convection (moving air or water) and evaporation (water turning to vapor, about 580 kcal per liter of sweat).

A CD4 T cell that recognizes antigen in MHC class II and, once activated, directs other immune cells with cytokines and surface contact. Th1 cells arm macrophages and cytotoxic T cells against microbes inside cells; Th2 cells direct the response to parasitic worms.

The percentage of a blood sample's volume made up of red blood cells, read from the packed red column of a spun sample (the packed cell volume): about 37–47% in women and 42–52% in men. The thin pale layer above the red column is the buffy coat of white blood cells and platelets.
Blood cell formation: stem cells in red bone marrow divide and differentiate into red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Also called hemopoiesis.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: The making of blood cells in red bone marrow. A hematopoietic stem cell (hemocytoblast) gives rise to myeloid stem cells, which make red blood cells, megakaryocytes (which shed platelets) and most white blood cells, and to lymphoid stem cells, which make the immune system's central white blood cells. Growth factors such as erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and colony-stimulating factors steer it.

The iron-containing protein that fills red blood cells and carries oxygen. Each molecule has four globin chains (two alpha and two beta in adults), and each chain holds a heme ring with an iron ion that binds one oxygen molecule.

The percentage of hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites that are occupied, normally 95 to 100% in arterial blood. SaO2 is measured in an arterial blood sample; SpO2 is estimated by pulse oximetry, which shines red and infrared light through a finger.

Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis): a mother's antibodies cross to the fetus and destroy its red cells. The severe form occurs when an Rh-negative mother, sensitized by an earlier Rh-positive baby, makes anti-D that attacks a later Rh-positive fetus; anti-D immune globulin prevents it.
The stopping of bleeding from a damaged vessel, in three overlapping steps: vascular spasm, the platelet plug and coagulation.
The amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid is proportional to that gas's partial pressure and its solubility. Carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble in plasma than oxygen.

The route that carries blood from the capillaries of the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas through the hepatic portal vein to a second capillary bed, the liver's sinusoids, before it leaves through the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava.
The maintenance of fairly stable conditions inside your body while conditions outside change. Each regulated variable moves within a normal range and is pulled back whenever it drifts.

Keeping internal conditions, such as body temperature and the water content of the blood, within a normal range even when the outside world changes. A change is detected and triggers a response that pushes the value back.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A state in which a regulated variable stays outside its normal range because some part of its feedback loop (sensor, control center, pathway or effector) has failed or been overwhelmed. Many diseases are failed regulation of this kind.

Prevention of pregnancy. Hormonal contraception, such as the combined birth control pill of a synthetic estrogen and a progestin, keeps negative feedback on GnRH, FSH and LH so no follicle dominates and no LH surge or ovulation occurs; progestins also thicken cervical mucus and thin the endometrium.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in males: pulses of GnRH drive LH and FSH; LH makes Leydig cells produce testosterone, and FSH with testosterone drives the Sertoli cells. Testosterone brakes GnRH and LH, and inhibin from the Sertoli cells brakes FSH.

Growth in length at the epiphyseal plates is driven by growth hormone through IGF-1, needs thyroid hormones, speeds up with the sex hormones at puberty, and ends when estrogen closes the plates in both sexes.

terms.term: hormonal control of the ovarian cycle
terms.def: The control of the ovarian cycle by GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus, FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary, and estradiol, progesterone and inhibin from the ovary. In the follicular phase follicles grow and one dominates; after ovulation, in the luteal phase, the corpus luteum's hormones hold FSH and LH low.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: A chemical messenger released into the blood that acts on target cells elsewhere in the body. It reaches nearly every cell, but only its target cells respond.

The ways hormones combine at a target: permissive (one hormone is needed for another's full effect), synergistic (together they give more than the sum of each alone) and antagonistic (they push the same variable in opposite directions).

Water-soluble hormones travel dissolved in the plasma; lipid-soluble hormones travel mostly bound to carrier proteins. Only free (unbound) hormone reaches target cells. A hormone's half-life is the time for half of it to be cleared from the blood.

terms.term: hormones that act on the kidney
terms.def: The signals that direct the kidney: ADH keeps water, aldosterone keeps sodium and loses potassium, ANP loses sodium and water, and PTH keeps calcium and loses phosphate. Angiotensin II, sympathetic nerves and endothelin, a vasoconstrictor peptide from endothelial cells, narrow renal arterioles; the kidney itself makes renin, EPO and calcitriol.

The hormones that decide whether fuel is stored or released. Insulin is the main anabolic hormone (building and storing); glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol are catabolic hormones that release fuel and raise blood glucose; growth hormone builds protein but releases fat.

Blood carries carbon dioxide in three forms: about 70% as bicarbonate ions, about 20–23% as carbaminohemoglobin (carbon dioxide bound to the amino groups of globin, not the heme iron) and about 7–10% dissolved.

Blood carries about 98.5% of its oxygen bound to hemoglobin, four molecules per hemoglobin, and about 1.5% dissolved in plasma. Hemoglobin with oxygen bound is oxyhemoglobin; hemoglobin without it is deoxyhemoglobin.

terms.term: how each system changes with age
terms.def: The changes in each organ system with age: working units such as nephrons, motor units, elastic fibers and naive T cells are lost, so resting function is usually kept but reserve, the extra capacity available under stress, shrinks.

A lipid-soluble hormone crosses the plasma membrane (steroids diffuse through it; the thyroid gland's hormones use transporter proteins) and binds an intracellular receptor protein. The hormone–receptor complex binds a hormone response element on DNA and changes transcription, so the cell makes new proteins over hours.
Muscle names are built from word parts describing location, shape, size, direction of the fascicles, number of heads at the origin, attachments (origin first) and action.

Audition, the sense of hearing, turns sound into nerve signals. Frequency is heard as pitch and coded by the place of greatest vibration on the basilar membrane; amplitude is heard as loudness and coded by firing rate. Conductive hearing loss blocks sound in the external or middle ear; sensorineural loss damages the cochlea or cochlear nerve. The Weber and Rinne tuning fork tests tell them apart.

terms.term: how the basal nuclei and cerebellum shape movement
terms.def: The basal nuclei and cerebellum shape movement without sending commands to the spinal cord. The basal nuclei select movements through a direct (go) pathway and an indirect (stop) pathway acting on the thalamus; the cerebellum compares intended and actual movement and corrects it. Motor pathways outside the pyramidal tract were once called the extrapyramidal system.

A water-soluble hormone binds a receptor protein in the plasma membrane. A G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP; cAMP switches on protein kinase A, which phosphorylates target proteins in a phosphorylation cascade. Phosphodiesterase ends the signal by breaking cAMP down. Other pathways use IP3, DAG and calcium.

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a glycoprotein hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from implantation onward. It acts like LH on the corpus luteum, keeping it alive and making progesterone so the endometrium is not shed; pregnancy tests detect it.

The long bone of the arm, from shoulder to elbow. Its head fits the glenoid cavity; below it are the anatomical neck, the greater and lesser tubercles with the intertubercular groove between them, and the surgical neck. Its lower end has the medial and lateral epicondyles, the capitulum, the trochlea and the olecranon fossa.
terms.topicTitle: The pectoral girdle and upper limb

terms.def: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid: carbonic anhydrase forms H+ and bicarbonate, the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) moves H+ into the lumen, and Cl− follows through channels. The bicarbonate goes to the blood, making it slightly alkaline after a meal (the alkaline tide). Acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine stimulate it.
A weak attraction between a partly positive hydrogen atom, covalently bonded to oxygen or nitrogen, and a partly negative oxygen or nitrogen atom nearby. No electrons are shared or transferred.

Hydrophilic (water soluble) substances are ions and polar molecules, which attract water and dissolve. Hydrophobic substances are nonpolar and are pushed into clusters by water molecules bonding with each other.
The pressure a fluid exerts, for example on the walls of its container. In a column of fluid it rises with depth, by about 0.74 mm Hg for each centimeter of water.
A small U-shaped bone in the upper neck, just above the voice box. It touches no other bone: ligaments hang it from the styloid processes, and muscles and the tongue attach to it.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: An immune response that damages your own tissues, usually against a harmless antigen (an allergen), usually after a symptom-free first exposure (sensitization). Type I is IgE on mast cells (immediate; allergy), type II antibody against cell-surface antigens, type III immune complexes, and type IV T cells (delayed).

Arterial blood pressure that stays above normal on repeated measurements; by the American ACC/AHA guidelines (set in 2017 and kept in 2025), 130/80 mm Hg or more (stage 2 at 140/90 or more). Also called high blood pressure, it usually causes no symptoms but thickens the left ventricle and damages arteries over years.

Hypertrophy is growth of a tissue by enlargement of its existing cells, as when muscle fibers add myofibrils after resistance training. Atrophy is shrinking as cells lose size, as with disuse, loss of the motor neuron or aging. Hyperplasia is growth by adding cells, which adds few if any fibers in adult skeletal muscle.

Hyperventilation is breathing more than carbon dioxide production requires, so arterial PCO2 falls below 35 mm Hg (hypocapnia). Hypoventilation is breathing less, so PCO2 rises above 45 mm Hg (hypercapnia). Both are defined by PCO2, not breathing rate.

The layer of areolar and adipose tissue beneath the dermis, also called the subcutaneous layer or superficial fascia. It anchors the skin loosely to the deep fascia over the muscles, stores fat, and insulates and cushions.

A blood glucose below 70 mg/dL. It triggers glucagon and epinephrine release (shakiness, sweating, a fast heart) and, as the brain runs short of glucose, confusion, seizures and loss of consciousness.

Blood vessels that link the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary: a first network of capillaries in the hypothalamus, portal veins down the infundibulum, and a second network among the anterior pituitary cells. A portal system is any arrangement of two capillary networks in a row joined by veins.

A hormonal axis is a chain of hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and target gland, each driving the next. In long-loop feedback the target gland's hormone inhibits both the hypothalamus and the pituitary; in short-loop feedback the pituitary hormone inhibits the hypothalamus.
A small region of the diencephalon below and in front of the thalamus, just above the pituitary gland. Its nuclei act as control centers for many homeostatic loops.
Hypoxia is too little oxygen reaching the tissues; hypoxemia is too little oxygen in the arterial blood. Altitude and lung disease cause both; a large bleed can cause hypoxia without hypoxemia.

Too little oxygen reaching the tissues, or reaching them and not being used. Its four types are hypoxemic (low arterial PO2), anemic (low oxygen content), stagnant or circulatory (too little blood flow) and histotoxic (cells unable to use oxygen, as with cyanide).

The attack on tumor cells by cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells and other immune cells, which recognize mutated, viral or overabundant proteins. Cancers escape by losing MHC class I, using brake proteins such as PD-L1 and recruiting regulatory T cells; checkpoint inhibitors and CAR T cells turn the attack back on.

A weakened or absent immune response, leading to frequent, severe or opportunistic infections. Primary forms are inherited, such as SCID (no working T cells, so both arms fail); secondary forms are acquired, such as HIV infection, which destroys helper T cells and progresses to AIDS (CD4 count below 200 per microliter or a defining illness).

The ability to respond faster and more strongly to an antigen met before, carried by long-lived memory B cells and memory T cells left after clonal expansion, which are more numerous and quicker to switch on than the naive cells they came from.

The embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium, from about day 6 to day 12 after fertilization. The outer trophoblast forms the syncytiotrophoblast, a many-nucleated mass without cell boundaries that digests its way in and reaches maternal blood.

In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote's phenotype falls between the two homozygotes'. In codominance, the heterozygote fully expresses both alleles, as in blood type AB, where A and B are codominant.

The response of tissue to injury: chemical messengers such as histamine from mast cells dilate small arteries and make small vessels leaky, causing redness, heat, swelling and pain, and white blood cells move in to clear debris.

The local response to injury or infection: chemical messengers widen and open small vessels (redness, heat, swelling, pain), leukocytes leave the blood by rolling, sticking, diapedesis and chemotaxis toward chemokines, and phagocytes clear the site, leaving pus. Acute inflammation lasts days; chronic inflammation lasts weeks or more and scars.

Innate immunity is the defense present from birth that acts within minutes to hours against patterns shared by groups of microbes, the same way each time. Adaptive immunity is built by lymphocytes that each recognize one antigen; it takes days on first exposure and responds faster the next time.

An organic compound contains carbon covalently bonded to hydrogen; an inorganic compound, such as water, sodium chloride or carbon dioxide, does not. Functional groups are small clusters of atoms, such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino and phosphate, that give organic molecules predictable behavior.

Breathing in (inhalation). In quiet breathing, the diaphragm and external intercostals contract and enlarge the thorax; intrapleural pressure falls, the lungs expand, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric, and air flows in. Forced inspiration adds accessory muscles such as the scalenes, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor.

The protein hormone of the pancreatic beta cells, released when blood glucose rises. It lowers blood glucose by moving GLUT4 carriers into muscle and fat cell membranes, driving glycogenesis and blocking glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; it also stores fat and moves potassium into cells.
The skin: the body's outer covering, made of the epidermis and dermis. With the hair, nails and skin glands it forms the integumentary system.
The zigzag joint where two cardiac muscle fibers meet end to end. Its desmosomes hold the fibers together and its gap junctions let the electrical change pass from fiber to fiber.

Cytokines released by virus-infected cells (interferon alpha and beta) that make neighboring cells produce antiviral proteins; interferon gamma, from NK cells and some lymphocytes, activates macrophages.
roots: to get in the way of (named for interfering with virus growth)

terms.def: The regions of a kidney cut in a frontal plane: the outer renal cortex; the renal medulla, split into cone-shaped renal pyramids with renal columns between them; the renal papilla at each pyramid's tip; and the minor calyces, major calyces and renal pelvis that collect urine and leave at the renal hilum.

Gas exchange between blood in systemic capillaries and the tissue cells: oxygen diffuses into the cells and carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood. It is not the same as cellular respiration, which uses the oxygen.

The fibrocartilage pad between two vertebral bodies: a tough outer ring, the anulus fibrosus, around a soft gel core, the nucleus pulposus. In a herniated disc, the core pushes out through a tear in the ring.
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is the fluid inside cells. Extracellular fluid (ECF) is all fluid outside cells; its main parts are interstitial fluid, which bathes the cells, and plasma.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: A receptor protein in the cytosol or nucleus (a nuclear receptor) that binds a lipid-soluble messenger. The pair binds DNA and switches genes on or off, so the response starts in hours and lasts hours to days.
Bone formation directly within a sheet of mesenchyme, with no cartilage stage. It forms the flat bones of the skull roof, most bones of the face and the collarbones.

The three standard sites for injecting into muscle: the deltoid site (two to three finger widths below the acromion; small volumes), the ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius and minimus, found from the greater trochanter, anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest) and the vastus lateralis site (middle third of the outer thigh; preferred in infants).
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: A glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells that binds vitamin B12 in the small intestine; only the combination can be absorbed, in the last part of the small intestine. Without it, B12 deficiency causes pernicious anemia.

The rate each part of the conduction system fires at when left on its own: SA node about 60 to 100 per minute (about 100 with no nerve input), AV node and AV bundle about 40 to 60, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers about 20 to 40. Any site other than the SA node that sets the rhythm is an ectopic pacemaker, or ectopic focus.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: An atom or group of atoms with unequal numbers of protons and electrons, so it carries a net charge. A cation has lost electrons and is positive; an anion has gained electrons and is negative. The hydrogen ion, H+, is a lone proton.

An integral membrane protein that forms a water-filled tunnel through which one kind of ion passes quickly, down its electrochemical gradient. Leak channels are open most of the time; gated channels open and close in response to a trigger.
The different ion contents of the fluids on each side of the plasma membrane: extracellular fluid is high in sodium and chloride, and intracellular fluid is high in potassium.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: The electrical attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion, formed after one atom transfers electrons to another. Strong in a dry crystal, weak in water, which separates the ions.

The two classes of receptor protein for neurotransmitters. An ionotropic receptor protein is a ligand-gated channel: fast and brief. A metabotropic receptor protein acts through a G protein and often a second messenger: slower, longer-lasting and amplified.
Ipsilateral means on the same side of the body; contralateral means on the opposite side. The right arm and right leg are ipsilateral.

How the body moves and keeps iron: transferrin carries it in plasma to the marrow and other cells; ferritin stores it safely inside liver cells, macrophages and marrow; hemosiderin is a clumped, slowly released store. Most iron is recycled from old red cells.

Muscle tension is the force a contracting muscle exerts on its attachments. In an isotonic contraction the muscle's length changes: it shortens in a concentric contraction and lengthens under load in an eccentric one. In an isometric contraction tension rises but length does not change.
Yellowing of the skin, the whites of the eyes and mucous membranes when bilirubin builds up in the blood, from fast red cell breakdown, liver damage or blocked outflow of bile.
A joint: any place where a bone meets another bone, a cartilage or a tooth. Some joints move freely and some do not move at all.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus is where a nephron's tubule touches its own afferent and efferent arterioles: the macula densa in the tubule wall senses sodium chloride, the juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole release renin, and mesangial cells lie between them and inside the glomerulus.

The main cell of the epidermis. It is made in the stratum basale, fills with keratin as it is pushed toward the surface, seals the spaces around it with lipid, and dies as a flat cell of the stratum corneum.

The liver's conversion of excess acetyl CoA into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a little acetone), which other tissues burn. A raised blood level is ketosis; enough to acidify the blood is ketoacidosis.

Loss of the kidneys' ability to keep the blood steady. Acute kidney injury develops over hours to days; chronic kidney disease lasts more than 3 months, with stage 5 (GFR below 15) being kidney failure. Retained wastes cause uremia, and dialysis replaces filtration by diffusion across a semipermeable membrane.

Voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcolemma and T tubules of cardiac muscle cells that open slowly on depolarization and stay open a long time. The calcium entering through them holds the plateau and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
terms.topicTitle: Cardiac muscle cells and their action potential

terms.def: Making and releasing milk. Prolactin, which rises when suckling lowers dopamine, makes the milk; oxytocin, released in the milk ejection (let-down) reflex, contracts the myoepithelial cells and ejects it. Colostrum is the first, IgA-rich milk; foremilk is thinner and hindmilk richer in fat.

Bloating, cramps, gas and diarrhea after eating more lactose than the remaining lactase can digest. Undigested lactose holds water in the gut and is fermented by colon bacteria. Low adult lactase (lactase non-persistence) is the pattern in most of the world's adults; it is not an allergy.

Broca's area in the lower left frontal lobe (producing fluent, grammatical speech) and Wernicke's area in the upper left temporal lobe (understanding language), joined by a band of white matter. Damage causes aphasia: expressive (Broca's), receptive (Wernicke's) or conduction aphasia.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: The voice box: a cartilage tube between the laryngopharynx and the trachea that keeps the airway open, seals it during swallowing and makes sound. Its framework includes the thyroid cartilage (with the laryngeal prominence, or Adam's apple), the ring-shaped cricoid cartilage and the epiglottis. Inside, the vocal folds (true vocal cords) vibrate to make sound; the glottis is the vocal folds and the gap between them; the vestibular folds above do not make sound.

The three layers of a blood vessel wall: the tunica intima (endothelium on a basement membrane; in arteries, bounded by the internal elastic membrane), the tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic fibers; in arteries, bounded by the external elastic membrane) and the tunica externa, also called tunica adventitia (collagen). Large vessels carry their own small vessels and nerves, the vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum.

The layers of the epidermis, deep to superficial: stratum basale (dividing basal cells), stratum spinosum (keratin-making cells joined by desmosomes), stratum granulosum (keratohyalin and lipid granules; cells die), stratum lucidum (clear, eleiden-filled, thick skin only) and stratum corneum (flat dead cells, shed).

The three layers of the eyeball's wall: the fibrous tunic (the white sclera and the clear cornea), the vascular tunic (the choroid, the ciliary body and the iris around the pupil) and the neural tunic (the retina).

The four layers of the alimentary canal wall, from the lumen outward: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae), submucosa (connective tissue with vessels and a nerve plexus), muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle) and serosa (visceral peritoneum), replaced by a fibrous adventitia where there is no peritoneum.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: The three layers of the heart wall: the epicardium on the outside (the same layer as the visceral pericardium), the thick myocardium of cardiac muscle in the middle, and the endocardium, an endothelial lining, on the inside.
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: The dependence of the tension a muscle fiber can produce on its sarcomere length. Tension is greatest at the optimal length, near resting length, where thick and thin filaments overlap best, and falls when the sarcomere is shorter or much longer.

The lens is the clear, flexible disc behind the iris, held by zonule fibers. Aqueous humor, made by the ciliary processes, fills the space in front of it and drains into the scleral venous sinus; vitreous humor is the gel behind it. Glaucoma is damage to the optic nerve, most often linked to poor drainage of aqueous humor and raised pressure in the eye.

A hormone released by fat cells in proportion to fat stores. It acts on the hypothalamus to lower food intake and allow energy use, and it permits reproduction; most obesity involves leptin resistance, not a lack of leptin.

A white blood cell. Leukocytes keep their nucleus and organelles, number about 4,500–11,000 per µL of blood, and do most of their work in the tissues, squeezing out through capillary walls toward chemical signals.

A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a pivot, the fulcrum. In the body a bone is the bar, a joint is the fulcrum, the muscle's pull is the effort and the part moved is the load. The fulcrum is in the middle of a first-class lever, the load in a second-class and the effort in a third-class lever.

The long ligaments that tie the vertebrae together: the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments along the front and back of the bodies, the elastic ligamentum flavum between laminae, the supraspinous ligament along the spinous process tips, and its neck version, the nuchal ligament.
Any molecule that binds specifically to a site on a protein. A chemical messenger is a ligand for its receptor protein, and so is a drug that binds the same site.

A ring of structures at the inner border of the cerebrum, including the hippocampus, amygdala and cingulate gyrus (the limbic lobe), linked to the hypothalamus. It links emotion, memory and the body's responses to them.

A molecule made mostly of carbon and hydrogen with few oxygen atoms, so it is nonpolar and does not dissolve in water. Fats, phospholipids and steroids are lipids; a substance that dissolves in them is lipid soluble.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Bile salts emulsify fat; pancreatic lipase splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides; micelles carry these to the brush border; absorptive cells rebuild triglycerides and package them into chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals as chyle and reach the blood through the thoracic duct.
The building of fatty acids and triglycerides from acetyl CoA, mainly in the liver and adipose tissue when fuel is plentiful and insulin is high.
The hydrolysis of stored triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids inside fat cells. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol and growth hormone switch it on; insulin switches it off.

Particles that carry lipids in the blood: a core of triglycerides and cholesterol inside a shell of phospholipids and apolipoproteins. VLDL carries liver-made triglycerides, which lipoprotein lipase unloads into tissues; LDL carries cholesterol to cells; HDL returns cholesterol to the liver.

The divisions of each cerebral hemisphere: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, named for the skull bones over them, plus the insula buried in the lateral sulcus. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal, the lateral sulcus lies above the temporal lobe, and the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital.

A tissue's ability to adjust its own blood flow by changing the radius of its arterioles, without nerves or hormones. Metabolic autoregulation dilates arterioles when metabolites build up; the myogenic response constricts them when pressure stretches them.

Your heart sits in the mediastinum, between the lungs, behind the sternum and on the diaphragm, with about two thirds of its mass left of the midline. Its apex is the pointed lower tip, at about the fifth intercostal space on the left; its base is the broad upper, back end where the large vessels attach.
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, on either side of the spine from about T12 to L3, the right a little lower than the left. From outside in, each is wrapped by the renal fascia, the adipose capsule (renal fat pad) and the renal capsule.

Connective tissue with few, loosely woven fibers and plenty of ground substance. Its forms are areolar tissue (packing under epithelia), adipose tissue (fat cells, called adipocytes; brown fat makes heat) and reticular tissue (nets in soft organs).

Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per change in transpulmonary pressure (ΔV ÷ ΔP): how easily the lungs stretch. It is set by elastic fibers and by the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli, which surfactant lowers, so surfactant raises compliance. Thoracic wall compliance is how easily the chest wall expands.

The paired, spongy organs of gas exchange on either side of the mediastinum. Each has an apex, a base on the diaphragm and a hilum where the bronchus, vessels and nerves enter. Fissures divide the right lung into three lobes and the left into two; the left has a cardiac notch for the heart.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: Interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel: mostly water and small solutes, with some protein, lymphocytes and anything picked up from the tissues.

A small, bean-shaped organ along the lymphatic vessels that filters lymph. Lymph enters through afferent vessels, trickles through macrophage-lined sinuses past a cortex of lymphoid nodules (with germinal centers) and a paracortex, and leaves through efferent vessels at the hilum; lymphocytes enter from the blood through high endothelial venules.

The one-way vessels that return filtered fluid to the blood: blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, valved collecting vessels, lymphatic trunks, and the thoracic duct (from the cisterna chyli) and right lymphatic duct, which empty where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.

Protein-rich swelling of a region whose lymphatic drainage has failed, most often after lymph nodes are removed or irradiated, or from parasitic worms blocking the vessels. Over time the tissue becomes firm and non-pitting.
A membrane sac of digestive enzymes that work in acid. It digests material taken into the cell and recycles worn-out parts (autophagy); if lysosomes burst, the cell digests itself (autolysis).
A large cell in connective tissue that engulfs bacteria, dead cells and debris by phagocytosis and digests them. Any cell that eats this way is a phagocyte.

The major nerves that leave the plexuses: phrenic (diaphragm), axillary (deltoid), radial (arm and forearm extensors), median (most forearm flexors and the thumb), ulnar (small hand muscles), femoral (quadriceps), sciatic (back of the thigh), dividing into the tibial and fibular nerves, plus the intercostal nerves between the ribs. Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve's path, usually from a compressed lower lumbar or sacral root.

The main neurotransmitters, grouped by chemistry: acetylcholine; amino acids (glutamate, the main excitatory one, and GABA and glycine, the main inhibitory ones); biogenic amines (norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin); neuropeptides such as endorphins; and gases such as nitric oxide.

The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands, exocrine glands that add fluid to sperm to make semen. The seminal vesicles supply most of the volume (alkaline, with fructose); the prostate adds a milky fluid with PSA; the bulbourethral glands add mucus before ejaculation.

On average, the female pelvis is lighter, wider and shallower than the male pelvis, with a round pelvic inlet, a wide subpubic angle (about 80 to 90 degrees or more) and a shorter, wider sacrum. The pelvic brim divides the greater pelvis above from the lesser pelvis below.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.def: Exocrine glands in the breast that can make milk. Milk-making alveoli, grouped into lobules and lobes, drain through branching ducts into lactiferous ducts that open at the nipple (older texts describe a widening under the areola, the lactiferous sinus); the pigmented areola surrounds the nipple.

The rule that the amount of a substance in your body stays constant only when input (intake plus production) equals output (excretion plus use). If input exceeds output, the amount rises; if output exceeds input, it falls.

Chewing: mechanical digestion in the mouth by the teeth, the muscles of mastication, the tongue and the cheeks, which breaks food into small pieces, mixes it with saliva and shapes it into a bolus, a soft ball ready to swallow.

The changes in the mother's body during pregnancy, driven by placental hormones, the growing uterus and the fetus's demands: blood volume up 40 to 50% with a lower hematocrit, cardiac output up 30 to 50% with lower total peripheral resistance, higher minute ventilation with a lower PaCO2, GFR up about 50%, a slower gut, and insulin resistance in the second half.

The average pressure in the arteries over a whole cardiac cycle, which drives blood through the organs. At rest it is estimated as diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure; the estimate runs low at fast heart rates.

terms.term: mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times resistance
terms.def: The rule MAP = CO × TPR: mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. Because CO = heart rate × stroke volume, blood pressure can change only through heart rate, stroke volume or resistance.

Measuring arterial pressure with a sphygmomanometer: a cuff squeezes the brachial artery shut and is slowly let down. The first Korotkoff sound marks systolic pressure and the last marks diastolic pressure. A cuff that is too small or an arm below heart level gives a reading that is too high.

Medial means closer to the midline that divides the body into equal right and left halves; lateral means farther from it, toward the side. Intermediate means between a more medial and a more lateral structure.
The muscles of the inner thigh: the adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, gracilis and pectineus. They start on the pubis (and ischium) and adduct the thigh.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: The central compartment of the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs, from the breastbone to the backbone and from the neck to the diaphragm. It holds the heart, the large vessels, the trachea, the esophagus and the thymus.
Ways of making pictures of the inside of a living body without opening it. A radiograph (X-ray) is a flat projection; CT, MRI, PET and ultrasound produce sections.

The division that makes gametes: one round of DNA copying, then two divisions. Meiosis I pairs the homologs, lets them cross over and separates them; meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, giving four haploid cells that all differ. Failure of chromosomes to separate is nondisjunction.

A pigment cell in the stratum basale that makes melanin from tyrosine, packs it into melanosomes and passes them along its branches to keratinocytes, where melanin caps the nucleus and absorbs UV light.
The voltage across a cell's plasma membrane, always read as the inside compared with the outside. A value of −70 mV means the inside is 70 millivolts more negative than the outside.
roots: power (Latin); a stored ability to push charge

terms.def: Proteins in or on a membrane. Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer, most spanning it; peripheral proteins sit loosely on one surface. They transport substances, act as enzymes, bind signals, anchor the cell and mark its identity.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: A small molecule made inside a cell that carries the signal of a first messenger bound outside. In the usual arrangement, a G-protein-coupled receptor switches on a G protein, which switches on a membrane enzyme that turns ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP).

The storing and recall of information. Short-term and working memory hold a few items briefly; long-term memory is declarative (episodic and factual) or procedural (skills). The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories into the cortex by strengthening synapses. Anterograde amnesia is loss of new memory formation; retrograde amnesia is loss of memories from before an injury.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: The three membranes around the brain and spinal cord: the tough dura mater outside, the web-like arachnoid mater, and the thin pia mater on the nervous tissue. The epidural space lies outside the dura, the subdural space between dura and arachnoid, and the CSF-filled subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

The permanent end of menstrual periods, confirmed after 12 months with none, at about 51 on average. The ovaries run out of follicles, estradiol and inhibin fall, and loss of their negative feedback makes FSH and LH rise.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: Loose embryonic connective tissue of star-shaped mesenchymal cells in a watery ground substance. These stem cells give rise to fibroblasts, fat cells, chondrocytes and the cells that build bone.

A fall in blood pH caused by a fall in bicarbonate below 22 mmol/L, either because a fixed acid was gained (high anion gap, as in diabetic ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis) or because bicarbonate was lost (normal anion gap, as in diarrhea). The anion gap is Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8 to 12 mmol/L. The lungs compensate by lowering PCO2.

A rise in blood pH caused by a rise in bicarbonate above 26 mmol/L, most often from vomiting, stomach suction or diuretics, and kept up by loss of volume, chloride and potassium. The lungs compensate, to a limited extent, by slowing breathing and raising PCO2.

The rate at which the body uses energy, and so makes heat. The basal metabolic rate (BMR), measured awake at rest after a 12-hour fast in a warm room, is about 60 to 70% of the total metabolic rate, which also includes handling food and physical activity.
All the chemical reactions in your body. Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones and usually releases energy; anabolism builds large molecules from smaller ones and usually needs energy.

Membrane glycoproteins coded by the major histocompatibility complex that hold peptides for T cells to inspect. Class I, on nearly all nucleated cells, shows peptides made inside the cell; class II, mainly on antigen-presenting cells, shows peptides from material taken in. Their genes vary enormously between people (MHC polymorphism).
Tiny, nonmoving, finger-like folds of the plasma membrane with a core of actin that increase surface area for absorption. A dense layer of them forms a brush border.

Micturition (urination) is the emptying of the bladder. In the micturition reflex, stretch signals from the bladder reach the pons; when the cortex allows it, the pons drives the sacral micturition center (S2 to S4), whose parasympathetic fibers contract the detrusor while both urethral sphincters relax.
Inorganic elements needed from food. Major minerals, such as calcium, sodium and potassium, are needed at more than 100 mg a day; trace minerals, such as iron, zinc and iodine, at less.

The total volume of air moved into or out of the lungs each minute: tidal volume times respiratory rate, about 6 L/min at rest. The respiratory rate is the number of breaths per minute, 12 to 20 in a resting adult.
A bean-shaped organelle with a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane that uses oxygen to oxidize fuel molecules and captures the released energy as ATP.

Division of the nucleus of a somatic cell into two nuclei with identical chromosome sets, in four phases: prophase, metaphase (chromosomes on the metaphase plate), anaphase (sister chromatids pulled apart by the mitotic spindle via their kinetochores) and telophase.

The three ways an exocrine cell releases its product: merocrine (by exocytosis; the cell stays whole), apocrine (the product-filled apical end pinches off) and holocrine (the whole cell breaks apart and becomes the secretion).

A monomer is a small unit that can link to others like it; a polymer is a chain of many monomers joined by covalent bonds, and a macromolecule is any very large molecule. Dehydration synthesis joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis adds water and splits them apart.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: A neuron that carries commands from the brain or spinal cord out to an effector. Those that supply skeletal muscle send one long axon to the muscle, where it branches, each branch ending on one muscle fiber.

One motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibers it supplies. One action potential in the neuron makes every fiber in the unit contract; small units allow fine control and large units produce great force.

An epithelial membrane (mucosa) lining a tract that opens to the outside of the body, such as the digestive and respiratory tracts. Its epithelium rests on the lamina propria, a layer of loose connective tissue, and in most places it is coated with mucus.

The G protein–coupled acetylcholine receptor protein on every parasympathetic target and on eccrine sweat glands. Depending on subtype it inhibits (slowing the heart by opening potassium channels) or excites (contracting gut smooth muscle, stimulating glands). Atropine blocks it.
roots: fly (the fly agaric mushroom, where muscarine was first found)

terms.def: A decline in a muscle's ability to produce force during repeated or sustained activity, which recovers with rest. It comes from weaker drive from the nervous system and from changes in the fibers, mainly phosphate buildup, reduced calcium release and, in long events, glycogen depletion; ATP does not run out.
A single muscle cell, also called a myocyte. It is a whole living cell, unlike the nonliving protein fibers of connective tissue.

The return of a muscle fiber to rest: the motor neuron stops firing, the SR release channels close, and calcium pumps (calcium ATPases in the SR membrane) use ATP to move calcium back into the SR, so calcium leaves troponin and tropomyosin covers actin again.

Skeletal muscle forms when myoblasts fuse into myotubes that mature into fibers, and it is repaired by muscle stem cells lying on each fiber's surface that become myoblasts and fuse with damaged fibers. Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength; muscular dystrophy is a group of inherited diseases in which fibers degenerate and are replaced by fat and connective tissue.
The primary tissue type made of muscle cells, which contract, shortening with force by using myosin to pull on actin filaments. It comes in three kinds: skeletal, cardiac and smooth.
roots: little mouse (the shape of a flexing muscle)

terms.def: The slight tension and resistance to stretch of a relaxed skeletal muscle, from its passive elasticity plus low-level motor unit firing in postural and stretched muscles. Hypotonia is abnormally low tone; hypertonia is abnormally high tone.

A single brief contraction and relaxation of a muscle fiber or motor unit in response to one action potential. On a myogram it shows a latent period, a contraction phase and a longer relaxation phase.
