The diaphragm, which flattens as it contracts and enlarges the chest, and the intercostal muscles between the ribs: the external intercostals lift the ribs as you breathe in, and the internal and innermost intercostals pull them down in forceful breathing out.

Muscles that originate mostly on skull bones and insert into the skin of the face and scalp, so they move skin rather than bones. They include the occipitofrontalis (frontalis and occipitalis joined by the epicranial aponeurosis), orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, zygomaticus major and buccinator.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the head and neck

terms.def: The four chewing muscles, which originate on the skull and insert on the mandible: the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid close the jaw, and the lateral pterygoid protracts it, helps open it and grinds side to side.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the head and neck

terms.def: Muscles of the leg below the knee: the front group (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus) dorsiflexes the foot, the side group (fibularis longus and brevis) everts it, and the back group (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior) plantar flexes it, the gastrocnemius and soleus through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

terms.def: Muscles that move the forearm: the biceps brachii, brachialis and brachioradialis flex the elbow; the triceps brachii extends it; the pronator teres and pronator quadratus turn the palm down; the supinator and biceps brachii turn it up.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb

terms.def: Muscles that position the scapula (trapezius, rhomboid major and minor, serratus anterior, pectoralis minor) and muscles that move the humerus (pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, deltoid, teres major, coracobrachialis). The deltoid is the prime mover of abduction, the pectoralis major of flexion and the latissimus dorsi of extension.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb

terms.term: muscles that move the wrist and fingers
terms.def: Forearm muscles that move the wrist and fingers: flexors on the palm side, most from the medial epicondyle (flexor carpi radialis and ulnaris, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis), plus the deeper flexor digitorum profundus from the ulna and extensors on the back from the lateral epicondyle (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digitorum). These are the extrinsic hand muscles; the intrinsic hand muscles, including the thenar and hypothenar eminences, lie in the hand.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb

terms.def: A lasting change in the base sequence of DNA. Depending on how it alters the codons, it can leave the protein unchanged (silent), swap one amino acid (missense), end the protein early (nonsense) or shift the reading frame.

An autoimmune disease in which antibodies reduce the acetylcholine receptor proteins at the motor end plate, so end plate potentials shrink and fall below threshold with repeated firing. Weakness worsens with use, often starting in the eye muscles; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors help.

Many tightly wrapped layers of a glial cell's plasma membrane around an axon segment, mostly lipid, which insulate it and speed signals along it. The bare gaps between segments are nodes of Ranvier; axons with this wrapping are myelinated, those without it unmyelinated.

Myocardial ischemia is blood flow to heart muscle too low for its oxygen demand; when it reverses it causes angina. A myocardial infarction (heart attack) is death of heart muscle from ischemia that lasts too long, usually a clot on a cracked fatty plaque.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: A long rod of contractile protein filaments inside a muscle fiber, running the fiber's length. It is a chain of sarcomeres, and hundreds to thousands of myofibrils fill each fiber.

A red, iron-containing protein in muscle fibers that binds oxygen more tightly than the blood's oxygen carrier. It stores a little oxygen, releasing it when oxygen in the fiber falls low, and speeds oxygen's movement to the mitochondria.

A plate of hard keratin made by the nail matrix under the nail root. The visible nail body slides over the nail bed; the lunula is the visible white edge of the matrix, the eponychium (cuticle) seals its base, and the hyponychium seals under its free edge.

terms.term: named joints of the girdles, spine, wrist, hand and foot
terms.def: Joints named for the bones they join, such as the sternoclavicular (saddle), acromioclavicular (plane), sacroiliac, atlanto-occipital (condyloid), atlantoaxial (pivot), zygapophysial (facet), radioulnar (pivot), radiocarpal (condyloid), carpometacarpal, metacarpophalangeal, interphalangeal (hinge), subtalar and metatarsophalangeal joints; the distal tibiofibular joint is a syndesmosis.

Named features of the skull, such as the orbit (eye socket), mastoid and styloid processes, zygomatic arch, sella turcica, cribriform plate, the three cranial fossae and the pterion. Each is described by the bone it belongs to.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull
aka: perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone
terms.say: MAS-toyd; STY-loyd; SEL-uh TUR-sih-kuh; KRIB-rih-form; TEER-ee-on

terms.def: A large granular lymphocyte of innate immunity that kills virus-infected and cancer cells without earlier exposure, when they show stress proteins or lack the normal self-identity protein; it releases granules that trigger the target's apoptosis.

Muscles of the neck: the sternocleidomastoid (one side turns the face to the opposite side; both flex the neck), the scalenes (lift the first two ribs and flex the neck), the suprahyoid muscles that raise the hyoid, and the infrahyoid strap muscles that lower and steady it.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the head and neck

terms.def: Cell death caused by injury, such as lost blood supply, crushing, burns or poisons. The cells swell and burst, and their spilled contents trigger inflammation.
A loop in which the response opposes the stimulus, moving the regulated variable back toward the set point; the loop switches itself off as the change shrinks. Most homeostatic loops work this way.

The microscopic unit of the kidney that makes urine: a renal corpuscle, which filters blood plasma, and a renal tubule, which takes back most of the filtered fluid and adds some substances to it. Each kidney has about a million, and lost nephrons are not replaced.
A cable of many axons, bundled with connective tissue and blood vessels, that runs outside the brain and spinal cord. It usually carries signals in both directions, in different axons.

Networks where the ventral rami of neighboring spinal nerves branch, join and exchange axons before giving off named nerves: the cervical (C1–C4), brachial (C5–T1), lumbar (L1–L4) and sacral (L4–S4) plexuses.

terms.term: nervous and hormonal control of GFR
terms.def: Nerves and hormones that override autoregulation: strong sympathetic activation constricts the afferent arterioles and lowers GFR; angiotensin II constricts the efferent arterioles and protects GFR; ANP and local prostaglandins widen the afferent arterioles and raise it.

The two long-distance messaging systems. Nervous signaling sends action potentials along axons and a neurotransmitter across a synapse to one cell, acting in milliseconds; endocrine signaling sends a hormone through the blood to every target cell, acting in seconds to hours and lasting longer.

terms.term: net filtration pressure at the glomerulus
terms.def: The net pressure driving filtration at the glomerulus: NFP = glomerular hydrostatic pressure − (capsular hydrostatic pressure + blood colloid osmotic pressure), about 55 − (15 + 30) = 10 mm Hg.

The sum of the four Starling forces across a capillary wall: NFP = (CHP + IFCOP) − (BCOP + IFHP). A positive value means capillary filtration, fluid moving out; a negative value means capillary reabsorption, fluid moving in.
Patterns of connection among neurons. In divergence one neuron synapses on many, spreading its signal; in convergence many neurons synapse on one, which sums their inputs.

The synapse between a motor neuron's axon terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber: the terminal, a synaptic cleft about 50 nm wide, and the motor end plate, a folded patch of sarcolemma packed with acetylcholine receptor proteins. Each fiber normally has one.
A cell of nervous tissue that receives signals, combines them and sends a signal of its own to other cells; also called a nerve cell. Mature neurons do not divide.

The soma (cell body) holds the nucleus and Nissl bodies (rough ER); the axon hillock is where the axon leaves it; the initial segment just beyond is the trigger zone, where action potentials start; the axon's cytoplasm is axoplasm, and its side branches are axon collaterals.
A chemical messenger that a neuron releases from its axon terminal at a synapse. It crosses the synaptic cleft and binds receptor proteins on the postsynaptic cell; it is cleared within milliseconds.

Trouble breathing in a newborn's first hours: fast breathing, grunting, nostril flaring, chest wall sinking in and a bluish color. Its main cause in preterm babies is respiratory distress syndrome, a shortage of surfactant that lets alveoli collapse after each breath.

The acetylcholine receptor protein on every autonomic postganglionic neuron and on adrenal chromaffin cells. It is a ligand-gated ion channel, so it is fast and always excitatory; it differs in subunits from the nicotinic type at the neuromuscular junction.

The transmitter (NE, also called noradrenaline) released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons from their varicosities. It binds alpha and beta-1 receptor proteins strongly and beta-2 weakly, and its signal ends mainly by reuptake into the varicosity.
7.35 to 7.45 in blood from an artery, a hydrogen ion concentration of about 35 to 45 nmol/L. Blood is slightly basic.

Typical partial pressures at rest at sea level: alveolar air PO2 about 100 and PCO2 about 40 mm Hg; arterial blood PO2 about 95 (80 to 100) and PCO2 40 (35 to 45); venous blood PO2 about 40 and PCO2 about 46 mm Hg.

The external nose is the part of the nose on the face, supported by bone above and cartilage below; air enters it through the two nares (nostrils). Behind them, the nasal cavity is the air space divided by the nasal septum, floored by the roof of the mouth, roofed by the cribriform plate and walled by the conchae. Its blood-rich, mucus-covered lining filters, warms and humidifies air.

The notochord is a rod of mesoderm along the embryo's midline whose signals induce the neural tube; its remnant is the nucleus pulposus. Somites are the paired blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube; each forms a sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), a myotome (skeletal muscle) and a dermatome (dermis of the back).

A polymer of nucleotides, each a phosphate, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base. Deoxyribonucleic acid stores hereditary instructions and ribonucleic acid carries them out; purines (A, G) have two rings and pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Pancreatic nucleases (ribonuclease for RNA, deoxyribonuclease for DNA) cut nucleic acids into nucleotides; brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases split these into pentose sugars, nitrogenous bases and phosphate, which are absorbed by active transport.
The organelle that holds a cell's DNA. A double-membrane nuclear envelope with nuclear pores surrounds it, and a dense nucleolus inside it assembles ribosome parts.

What bone needs from the diet: dietary calcium (about 1,000 mg a day for adults, 1,300 mg for teenagers), vitamin D to absorb it, protein for the collagen matrix, and phosphorus and magnesium, together with weight-bearing exercise.

Obligatory water reabsorption is the water that follows solute out of the proximal tubule and descending limb whatever the body needs, roughly 80 to 85% of what is filtered. Facultative water reabsorption is the adjustable rest, in the late distal tubule and collecting duct, and happens only when ADH is present.

The sense of smell. An odorant dissolves in the mucus of the olfactory epithelium and binds an odorant receptor protein on an olfactory sensory neuron, whose axon passes through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb. Anosmia is the loss of smell.

The making of oocytes by meiosis. Oogonia multiply by mitosis before birth and become primary oocytes that pause in prophase I; just before ovulation one finishes meiosis I into a secondary oocyte and a small polar body, and it finishes meiosis II only if a sperm enters.

The mouth: the oral vestibule between the lips, cheeks and teeth, and the cavity proper inside the teeth. Its roof is the bony hard palate in front and the muscular soft palate behind, with the uvula hanging from it; the fauces opens into the oropharynx. The tongue is skeletal muscle whose papillae grip food or carry taste buds, anchored by the lingual frenulum; the gingiva (gums) cover the bone around the teeth.
A structure made of two or more kinds of tissue that has a recognizable shape and does a specific job, such as the stomach or a kidney.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A group of organs that work together on a shared job, such as the digestive system.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A structure in the cytoplasm with a specific job; most are wrapped in their own membrane. The cytosol is the fluid part of the cytoplasm in which the organelles sit.
A whole living individual. In humans, all eleven organ systems working together make the organism.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The formation of the organs from the germ layers, from week 3 to the end of week 8, the embryonic period. Folding in week 4 turns the flat disc into a body with a gut tube (foregut, midgut and hindgut). It is the time when a drug, an infection or a missing nutrient is most likely to cause a major defect.

The origin is a muscle's attachment on the bone that stays still, usually proximal; the insertion is its attachment on the bone that moves. Contraction pulls the insertion toward the origin. The belly is the fleshy middle of the muscle.

A sustained fall in blood pressure on standing: at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes. Also called postural hypotension, it causes lightheadedness or fainting when the baroreceptor reflex cannot keep up.

The total concentration of all dissolved particles in a solution, counting each ion separately, in milliosmoles per liter (mOsm/L). Osmolality is the same count per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg); normal blood osmolality is about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg.
Neurons in the front of the hypothalamus that sense plasma osmolarity. When it rises, they lose water, shrink and fire faster, driving ADH release and thirst.

The net movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from the side with fewer dissolved particles to the side with more (from lower to higher osmolarity). Only particles the membrane holds back count: water follows solute.

The pressure needed to stop water moving into a solution by osmosis. It rises with the number of dissolved particles the membrane holds back, by about 19 mm Hg for each mOsm/L at body temperature, and water moves toward the side where it is higher.
The formation of bone tissue by osteoblasts, also called osteogenesis. It begins at an ossification center and follows one of two routes: intramembranous or endochondral.

The most common joint disease: articular cartilage thins and wears through, the bone beneath thickens and grows spurs, and the synovial membrane becomes mildly inflamed, causing pain with use, stiffness and less movement.

The cylindrical unit of compact bone: rings of matrix (lamellae) around a central canal carrying vessels and nerves, with osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi. Perforating canals join neighboring osteons.

A disease of low bone mass and weakened inner structure, from years of resorption outpacing formation, so bones break from minor falls or ordinary loads, typically the vertebrae, hip and wrist. The bone that remains is normally mineralized.

Besides growth hormone, the anterior pituitary releases TSH (to the thyroid gland), ACTH (to the adrenal gland's outer layer), the gonadotropins FSH and LH (to the ovaries and testes), and prolactin (to the milk-producing glands of the breast).

Inputs besides the chemoreceptors that change breathing: lung stretch receptors (the Hering–Breuer reflex, which limits inflation), irritant receptors in the airways (cough, bronchoconstriction), proprioceptors, the cerebral cortex (voluntary control) and the hypothalamus and limbic system (emotion, pain, temperature).

The temporomandibular joint (jaw, with an articular disc), the elbow joint (humeroulnar and humeroradial joints, the annular ligament around the radial head, and ulnar and radial collateral ligaments), the hip joint (deep acetabulum, acetabular labrum, iliofemoral ligament), and the ankle or talocrural joint (a hinge braced by the deltoid ligament inside and the anterior talofibular ligament outside).

The repeating sequence of changes in the ovary, about once a month in an adult woman: a follicle grows and matures, ovulation releases its oocyte, and the corpus luteum forms from the follicle, works for about 12 to 14 days and then breaks down into the corpus albicans unless a pregnancy keeps it alive.

The paired female gonads, almond-sized organs against the pelvic side walls. Their cortex holds ovarian follicles (each an oocyte wrapped in supporting cells) and they make estrogen and progesterone; the ovarian ligament ties each to the uterus and the suspensory ligament, which carries its vessels, ties it to the pelvic wall.
The release of a secondary oocyte, with a ring of granulosa cells, from a mature follicle onto the surface of the ovary. A sudden rise in LH triggers it about 34 to 36 hours later.

Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons; they always happen together in an oxidation-reduction reaction. Electron carriers such as NAD+ (which becomes NADH) and FAD pick up electrons in one reaction and deliver them in another.

The S-shaped graph of hemoglobin saturation against PO2. Cooperative binding, where each oxygen that binds makes the other sites bind more readily, makes it flat above about 60 mm Hg and steep below about 50. Hemoglobin is 50% saturated at about 27 mm Hg (the P50).

Oxygenated (oxygen-rich) blood has just left the lungs, with its hemoglobin about 97 to 98 percent loaded with oxygen. Deoxygenated (oxygen-poor) blood has passed through the tissues and given up some oxygen, but at rest it is still about 75 percent loaded; both are red.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: A peptide made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary. It strengthens contractions of the uterus in labor through positive feedback and makes milk flow out of the breast during nursing.

The slow, spontaneous depolarization of an autorhythmic cell between action potentials, also called the prepotential. It is driven by the funny current (Na⁺ in through HCN channels), falling K⁺ exit, and late T-type Ca²⁺ entry; its slope sets how often the cell fires.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: Nociception is the detection and signaling of tissue damage; pain is the unpleasant experience the brain produces from it. Referred pain is pain from an internal organ felt in skin or muscle, because both send axons into the same spinal segments and converge on shared second-order neurons.

Small clusters of endocrine cells scattered through the pancreas, about 1 to 2 percent of its mass. Beta cells make insulin, alpha cells make glucagon, delta cells make somatostatin and PP cells make pancreatic polypeptide. Also called the islets of Langerhans.

The alkaline fluid the exocrine pancreas secretes into the duodenum, about 1.2 to 1.5 L a day. Duct cells add bicarbonate, which neutralizes stomach acid; acinar cells add enzymes: pancreatic amylase, pancreatic lipase, and protein-digesting enzymes released as inactive precursors (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen) that enteropeptidase and trypsin activate in the duodenum.

Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas, often from trypsin activated inside the gland by a gallstone blockage or alcohol. Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, from viruses, alcohol, fat buildup, drugs or autoimmunity. Cirrhosis is scarring after years of liver injury, which raises portal vein pressure and leaves too few working hepatocytes.

Local signaling. In paracrine signaling a messenger, such as nitric oxide, diffuses to neighboring cells; in autocrine signaling it binds receptor proteins on the same cell that released it. Cytokines, including interleukins, are small proteins used this way.
Air-filled spaces inside the frontal, maxillary, sphenoid and ethmoid bones, lined by mucous membrane and draining into the nose. The maxillary sinus is the largest.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: The craniosacral division: preganglionic neurons in brainstem nuclei (leaving in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X) and in sacral segments S2–S4 send long axons to terminal ganglia beside or inside the target organ (intramural ganglia), where short postganglionic axons reach the effector. It does not supply the skin, limbs or most blood vessels.
Usually four rice-sized glands on the back of the thyroid gland. Their chief cells sense blood calcium through a calcium-sensing receptor protein and release parathyroid hormone when it falls.

Parathyroid hormone (PTH): the main hormone that raises blood calcium. It drives bone breakdown by acting on osteoblasts, which signal osteoclasts; makes the kidneys keep calcium and lose phosphate; and switches on calcitriol production. Too much is hyperparathyroidism; too little, hypoparathyroidism.

The pressure one gas in a mixture exerts: the total pressure times that gas's fraction of the mixture, written PO2 for oxygen and PCO2 for carbon dioxide. By Dalton's law, the partial pressures add up to the total pressure.

The regions of a long bone: the diaphysis (shaft) around the medullary cavity, the flared metaphyses, and the epiphyses (widened ends) capped with articular cartilage. A nutrient artery enters the shaft through a nutrient foramen.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: The shared plan of a vertebra: a weight-bearing body in front and a vertebral arch (two pedicles and two laminae) behind, enclosing the vertebral foramen. One spinous, two transverse and four articular processes stick out from the arch, and nerves leave between vertebrae through the intervertebral foramina.

The named sections of the aorta: the ascending aorta rising from the left ventricle, the aortic arch curving over to the left, and the descending aorta, which is the thoracic aorta in the chest and, after it passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, the abdominal aorta.

The neurological exam is a structured set of bedside tests used to localize a problem in the nervous system. Its parts are the mental status exam (cerebrum), cranial nerve exam (brainstem and its nerves, including the corneal reflex), sensory exam (ascending pathways, including stereognosis and graphesthesia), motor exam (strength, tone, pronator drift and reflexes) and coordination and gait exam (cerebellum, including the Romberg test).

The stomach's regions: the cardia around the esophageal opening, the dome-shaped fundus, the large body, and the pyloric part (the wide pyloric antrum, the narrow pyloric canal and the pylorus, whose pyloric sphincter controls emptying). Rugae are folds of the lining that flatten as it fills.

Giving birth: the process by which the uterus pushes out the fetus and then the placenta. True labor is contractions that progressively thin and open the cervix; the irregular Braxton Hicks contractions of false labor do not. Lightening is the fetal head dropping into the pelvis in the weeks before.

Movement of a substance across a membrane down its gradient, powered by the gradient itself, with no ATP spent by the cell. Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis and filtration are all passive transport.

The kneecap: a triangular sesamoid bone, the largest in the body, inside the tendon of the large muscle group on the front of the thigh. It glides on the front of the femur and gives that muscle more leverage.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.term: path of blood through the heart
terms.def: The order blood takes: venae cavae, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk and arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, body.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: Receptor proteins, such as the Toll-like receptors, that bind molecular patterns shared by groups of microbes (or released by damaged cells) and switch on cytokine release, starting the early induced immune response.

The shoulder girdle: the clavicle and scapula on each side, which attach the upper limb to the trunk. The clavicle meets the sternum; the scapula is held to the back of the rib cage by muscles and carries the spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity and three fossae.
terms.topicTitle: The pectoral girdle and upper limb

terms.def: The sling of muscle that closes the bottom of the pelvis and supports the pelvic organs: the pelvic diaphragm, made of the levator ani and coccygeus. Below it lies the perineum, a diamond-shaped region divided into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.

The two hip bones (coxal bones), which attach the lower limbs to the trunk. Each forms from the ilium, ischium and pubis, fused at the acetabulum. The hip bones meet the sacrum at the back and each other at the pubic symphysis; with the sacrum and coccyx they make the bony pelvis.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.def: The male organ that carries the urethra and delivers semen. It is made mostly of erectile tissue in three columns: two corpora cavernosa on top and a corpus spongiosum below, around the urethra, which widens into the glans penis; the prepuce (foreskin) covers the glans.

The stomach's protein-digesting enzyme, which splits proteins into polypeptides and works best near pH 2. Chief cells secrete it as inactive pepsinogen, which acid converts to pepsin; pepsin then activates more pepsinogen.

Substances used to improve athletic performance, banned in sport (doping). Anabolic steroids, copies of testosterone, cause muscle hypertrophy but suppress the user's own reproductive axis; EPO thickens the blood; growth hormone misuse mimics acromegaly.
The thin, fluid-filled space around the heart, between the serous layer on the heart's surface and the outer layer of the sac that encloses it. It lies in the mediastinum.

The covering around the heart: a tough outer fibrous pericardium of dense connective tissue, and an inner serous pericardium folded into a parietal layer and a visceral layer with a film of serous fluid (the pericardial cavity) between them. The fibrous layer plus the parietal layer form the pericardial sac.
terms.topicTitle: Heart location, coverings, chambers and great vessels

terms.def: The periosteum is the two-layered membrane covering a bone's outer surface except at joints: an outer fibrous layer that anchors tendons and ligaments, and an inner cellular layer that can build bone. The endosteum is a thin cell layer lining the bone's inner surfaces.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: Sensory cells in the carotid bodies (at the fork of each common carotid artery) and the aortic bodies (on the aortic arch) that respond to low arterial PO2, high PCO2 and low pH, and signal the medulla through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

The movements of the GI wall. Peristalsis is a wave of contraction behind the contents with relaxation ahead of them, which pushes them along. Segmentation is alternating rings of contraction that mix the contents with little forward movement.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: The thin, fluid-filled space in the abdominopelvic cavity between the layer of peritoneum lining the abdominal wall and the layer covering the organs. The peritoneum is the largest serous membrane in the body.

The peritoneum lines the abdominal wall (parietal layer) and covers the organs (visceral layer). A mesentery is a double fold of it that holds an organ to the back wall and carries its vessels and nerves. The greater omentum hangs from the stomach over the intestines; the lesser omentum joins the stomach to the liver. Retroperitoneal organs, such as the pancreas and kidneys, lie behind it.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: A small membrane sac of oxidizing enzymes that breaks down very long fatty acids and some toxins. Catalase inside it destroys the hydrogen peroxide these reactions make. Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species; free radicals are reactive molecules with an unpaired electron.
A number for the hydrogen ion concentration of a fluid: the negative log of [H+] in mol/L. pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic; each whole unit is a tenfold change in H+.

Killing of microbes by phagocytes, mainly neutrophils and macrophages: they find, bind, engulf and digest the microbe in a vesicle fused with lysosomes, using enzymes and an oxidative burst that makes superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and bleach.

The muscular throat tube from the back of the nasal cavity to the esophagus. The nasopharynx (behind the nose) carries only air and holds the pharyngeal tonsil and the auditory tube openings; the oropharynx (behind the mouth) and laryngopharynx (behind the larynx) carry air and food and are lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

The three phases that control gastric secretion: the cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste and thought of food act through the vagus nerves), the gastric phase (stretch and protein in the stomach act through reflexes and gastrin; the largest share) and the intestinal phase (chyme in the small intestine mostly inhibits the stomach).

The five phases of each heartbeat: ventricular filling, atrial contraction (atrial systole), isovolumetric contraction (both valves closed, pressure rising), ventricular ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation (both valves closed, pressure falling). Isovolumic is another name for isovolumetric.

terms.term: phases of the neuron action potential
terms.def: The stages of a neuron action potential: rest at about −70 mV, depolarization to threshold at about −55 mV, a rising phase to about +30 mV as sodium enters, a falling phase as potassium leaves, and an afterhyperpolarization to about −80 mV before the membrane returns to rest.

A lipid with two fatty acid tails and a charged, phosphate-containing head. It is amphipathic, with a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails, so in water it forms a two-layer sheet: the basic structure of the boundary around every cell.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Two sheets of phospholipids arranged tail to tail, with hydrophilic heads facing the water on each side and hydrophobic tails forming an oily core. It is the basic structure of every cell membrane.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: The light-sensitive cells of the retina. Rods work in dim light, have one pigment and give no color; cones work in bright light, come in three kinds and give color and fine detail, and are packed into the fovea. Photoreceptors signal to bipolar cells, which signal to retinal ganglion cells, whose axons leave at the optic disc, the blind spot.

The conversion of light into a change in a photoreceptor's membrane potential. Light changes retinal from 11-cis to all-trans (photoisomerization), activating the pigment (rhodopsin in rods: opsin plus retinal). A G protein lowers cGMP, cation channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate.

Blood's physical characteristics: about 5 L in an adult (7–8% of body weight), always red (bright when full of oxygen, dark when not), pH 7.35–7.45, roughly four to five times as viscous as water, and, deep in the trunk, at the temperature of the organs around it. Whole blood is blood with nothing added or removed.
The study of how the body's structures work: the chemical and physical events that make them do their jobs.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The pineal gland is a small gland in the epithalamus whose pinealocytes make melatonin from serotonin. Melatonin is released in darkness and switched off by light, through a pathway from the retina via the suprachiasmatic nucleus; it signals night to the body's clocks.

A pea-sized gland in the sella turcica, hung from the hypothalamus by a stalk, the infundibulum. The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is glandular epithelium that makes six hormones; the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is nervous tissue that stores and releases two hormones made in the hypothalamus.

The organ of exchange between fetal and maternal blood, formed from the chorion and the endometrium at the implantation site (placentation). Its chorionic villi, holding fetal capillaries, hang in a pool of maternal blood; the placental barrier between the two bloods is thin and large, so substances cross while the bloods stay apart. It is also a major endocrine gland.

The hormones the placenta makes: hCG, which peaks near week 10; progesterone and estrogens, which it takes over from the corpus luteum by weeks 7 to 9 and raises steadily; human placental lactogen (hPL), which reduces the mother's response to insulin and helps prepare the breasts; and some relaxin, which in humans comes mostly from the corpus luteum.

A plane is an imaginary flat surface passed through the body; a section is the cut surface produced when the body or an organ is divided along a plane. An oblique plane runs at an angle between the three main planes.
The fluid part of blood: mostly water, with dissolved salts, nutrients, wastes and proteins. It is the part of the extracellular fluid that travels through blood vessels.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: A fully differentiated B cell, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, that releases large amounts of one antibody. Activation needs helper T cell help for T cell-dependent (protein) antigens but not for T cell-independent antigens such as repeating capsule sugars.
The thin outer boundary of a cell, also called the cell membrane: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins set into it. It controls what enters and leaves the cell.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: The proteins dissolved in plasma, about 7% of it: albumin (most abundant, made by the liver; its osmotic pull holds water in the blood), globulins (transport proteins, plus immune gamma globulins made by white blood cells) and fibrinogen (the clotting protein that forms the threads of a clot).

A thrombocyte: a nucleus-free fragment of a megakaryocyte, 2–4 µm across, 150,000–450,000 per µL, living 7–10 days. Its granules and contractile proteins let it seal breaks in vessel walls and give clotting proteins a surface to work on.

A soft plug of platelets over a break in a vessel wall. Platelets adhere to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor, activate and release ADP and thromboxane A2, and aggregate as fibrinogen bridges them, a positive feedback that healthy lining confines.

The serous membrane around each lung: the visceral pleura covers the lung surface, the parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum, and they meet at the hilum. Between them, a film of pleural fluid lubricates the layers and holds the lung against the chest wall.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: The thin, fluid-filled space around each lung, between the layer of pleura on the lung and the layer on the inside of the chest wall. There are two, right and left, separated by the mediastinum.

Air in a pleural cavity, from a chest wound or a leak from the lung. Intrapleural pressure rises toward atmospheric, transpulmonary pressure is lost and the lung on that side collapses. In a tension pneumothorax, trapped air builds pressure that compresses the other lung and the great veins.

An uneven spread of charge. A polar covalent bond shares electrons unequally, leaving partial charges; a nonpolar bond shares them evenly. A polar molecule has a partly positive and a partly negative end, which depends on both its bonds and its shape.

An abnormally high red cell count and hematocrit: primary (a marrow mutation, polycythemia vera, with low erythropoietin), secondary (raised erythropoietin, as at altitude or with lung disease) or relative (lost plasma). It thickens the blood and raises resistance to flow.
Inheritance of a trait shaped by many genes, each with a small effect, plus the environment, such as height or blood pressure. It gives a continuous, bell-shaped range rather than distinct types.
A loop in which the response strengthens the stimulus, pushing the variable further in the same direction until an event outside the loop ends it, as in childbirth and blood clotting.

The fasting state between meals and overnight, when no nutrients are arriving from the gut. Insulin is low and glucagon high, the liver releases glucose from glycogen and gluconeogenesis, and most tissues burn fatty acids, sparing glucose for the brain and red blood cells.

The roughly six weeks after birth, also called the puerperium, while the reproductive organs return to their nonpregnant state. The uterus shrinks back (uterine involution) and the placental site heals, shedding lochia.

The control of the body's potassium, about 98% of it inside cells. Insulin and epinephrine move potassium into cells within minutes (internal balance), and principal cells secrete it into the urine under aldosterone (external balance), keeping plasma potassium at 3.5–5.0 mmol/L.

terms.term: potassium leak and the resting potential
terms.def: At rest, many potassium leak channels are open. Potassium diffuses out through them and leaves trapped negative proteins behind, which makes the inside negative; this is the main source of the resting potential.
A word part placed before a root that modifies its meaning, often telling where, how much, how many or how fast, such as tachy- (fast) in tachypnea.

The two neurons in series in every autonomic motor pathway. The preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the brainstem or spinal cord and a thinly myelinated axon that ends in an autonomic ganglion; the postganglionic neuron has its cell body in that ganglion and an unmyelinated axon that releases transmitter from swellings (varicosities) onto cardiac muscle, smooth muscle or glands.
The stretch on ventricular muscle at the end of filling, just before contraction, indexed by end-diastolic volume. It rises with greater venous return and with a longer filling time.

Force per unit area. In physiology it is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) and usually given relative to atmospheric pressure, the pressure of the surrounding air (about 760 mm Hg at sea level).

The way blood pressure changes along the systemic circulation: high and pulsing in the arteries, falling most steeply across the arterioles, lower through the capillaries, and falling slowly to near zero in the veins and at the right atrium.
A difference in pressure between two points, written ΔP. Fluids flow from higher toward lower pressure, and flow depends on the difference, not on how high the pressures are.

The kidney's direct response to arterial pressure: a rise in pressure makes the proximal tubule reabsorb less sodium, so more sodium and water (pressure diuresis) are excreted and blood volume and pressure fall, without any hormone.
A graph of left ventricular pressure against left ventricular volume over one beat. It traces a counterclockwise loop whose corners are the four valve events and whose width is the stroke volume.

The forces across the glomerular capillary wall: glomerular hydrostatic pressure (GBHP, about 55 mm Hg) pushes fluid out; capsular hydrostatic pressure (CHP, about 15 mm Hg) and blood colloid osmotic pressure (about 30 mm Hg on average) push it back.

Pulmonary ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure differences. Alveolar (intrapulmonary, intra-alveolar) pressure is the pressure inside the alveoli and returns to atmospheric whenever airflow stops. Intrapleural pressure, in the pleural fluid film, is about 4 mm Hg below atmospheric at rest. Transpulmonary pressure, alveolar minus intrapleural, holds the lungs open.
Active transport in which the carrier, called a pump, splits ATP itself and uses the energy to move a substance against its gradient. The sodium–potassium pump and calcium pumps are examples.

The primary response to a first exposure has a lag of about 5–10 days and a low peak, mostly IgM then IgG. The secondary response to a later exposure comes from memory cells: faster, much higher, mostly IgG and better fitting. Seroconversion is when antibody first becomes detectable in the blood.

Primary lymphoid organs (red bone marrow and the thymus) are where lymphocytes are made and mature; secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, the spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue such as the tonsils, Peyer's patches and BALT) are where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.
roots: Latin name for the tonsils, of uncertain origin

terms.term: prime movers, antagonists, synergists and fixators
terms.def: The jobs muscles take in a movement: the prime mover (agonist) does most of the work, synergists help or steady it, fixators hold the base bone still, and the antagonist makes the opposite movement. A muscle's role depends on the movement.

The travel of an action potential along a membrane. Charge from a firing patch depolarizes the next patch to threshold, so each patch regenerates a full-sized action potential; the refractory patch behind keeps it moving one way.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: The four properties all muscle shares: responsiveness to signals, the ability to contract, extensibility (being stretched without damage) and elasticity (recoiling to resting length).

The behaviors that follow from water's polarity and hydrogen bonds: it absorbs much heat with little warming, takes much heat to evaporate, clings to itself (cohesion and surface tension, the inward pull at a water surface), lubricates and cushions, takes part in reactions and dissolves many substances.
A polymer of amino acids folded into a working shape. Each amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain; peptide bonds join them into a chain called a polypeptide.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: Proteolysis, the splitting of proteins at their peptide bonds: pepsin in the stomach, then trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidase from the pancreas, then aminopeptidase and dipeptidase at the brush border. Amino acids enter absorptive cells with sodium, and dipeptides and tripeptides with hydrogen ions; they reach the blood as amino acids.

A protein's structure: its amino acid sequence, local coils and sheets, overall fold and, in some, several chains fitted together, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and covalent disulfide bonds. Denaturation is the loss of that shape, and with it the protein's function, without breaking the peptide bonds.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: The three particles of an atom. Protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) form the nucleus; electrons (negative, very light) occupy shells around it, and the outermost occupied shell is the valence shell.
Proximal means closer to where a limb attaches to the trunk, or to where a tube begins; distal means farther from that point. The elbow is proximal to the wrist.

A single layer of columnar cells of different heights, so the nuclei sit at different levels and the sheet looks layered. The ciliated form with goblet cells lines the inside of the nose, the trachea and the larger airways.

The transition to a body able to reproduce, which begins when the hypothalamus's GnRH pulses reawaken and drive FSH, LH and the sex hormones. In girls it usually starts with breast budding and reaches menarche, the first period, at about 12 to 13 years.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: The loop that carries blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the pulmonary capillaries around the alveoli, where it picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, and back through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It works at low pressure.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: Fluid buildup in the lung tissue and then the alveoli, caused by high pressure in the pulmonary capillaries (as in left-sided heart failure) or by a leaky respiratory membrane (as in sepsis or pneumonia). It slows diffusion, stiffens the lungs and floods alveoli.

Places where an artery runs near the skin over firm tissue, so its pulse, the pressure wave from each heartbeat, can be felt: temporal, facial, carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis.
Systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure: the size of each beat's pressure swing. It widens with a larger stroke volume or a stiffer aorta and narrows when stroke volume is small.

A grid that lists every equally likely combination of two parents' gametes, giving the chance of each genotype in a child. It rests on Mendelian inheritance and the law of segregation: each gamete carries one allele of each gene, each with a 1 in 2 chance.

The narrowing of both pupils when light enters either eye: optic nerve in, a midbrain relay, and parasympathetic fibers of both oculomotor nerves out to the iris sphincter. Miosis is a narrowed pupil; mydriasis is a widened one.

The step in the mitochondrial matrix that removes one carbon from pyruvate as CO2, makes NADH, and attaches the remaining two-carbon acetyl group to coenzyme A, a carrier made from vitamin B5. The step cannot run backward.

The role of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system in raising blood pressure: low pressure makes the kidneys release renin, leading to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles, releases aldosterone so the kidneys keep sodium and water, and triggers ADH and thirst.
Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius (Poiseuille's law), so halving a tube's radius makes its resistance 16 times larger and its flow 16 times smaller at the same pressure gradient.

The two forearm bones. The ulna, on the little-finger side, is large at the elbow, where its olecranon and trochlear notch wrap the humerus. The radius, on the thumb side, is large at the wrist; its disc-shaped head spins against the capitulum, and it crosses the ulna when the palm turns down.
terms.topicTitle: The pectoral girdle and upper limb

terms.def: The bulk reabsorption done by the proximal convoluted tubule: about 65% of filtered sodium and water, nearly all glucose and amino acids, most bicarbonate and phosphate, and about half the urea. Solute and water leave together, so the fluid leaving it is still about 300 mOsm/L.

The reaction rate is how fast reactants become products; more reactant, higher temperature or a catalyst raises it. A reversible reaction runs both ways, and at chemical equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the amounts stop changing. In an exchange reaction, parts of two molecules trade places.

The local, graded change in membrane potential produced when a stimulus opens ion channels in a sensory receptor, a step called sensory transduction. In the ending of a sensory neuron it is also called a generator potential; if it reaches threshold at the trigger zone, action potentials fire, faster for a stronger stimulus.

A protein that binds a specific chemical messenger and, by changing shape, starts a response in the cell. Binding is specific and reversible, and the receptor protein, not the messenger, decides what the cell does.

A stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is the sudden loss of function in part of the brain when its blood supply is interrupted: ischemic when an artery is blocked, hemorrhagic when one bursts. Its warning signs are taught as BE FAST (balance, eyes, face, arm, speech, time). A transient ischemic attack is a brief episode of the same signs with no dead brain tissue on a scan.
Increasing a muscle's force by activating more motor units, from the smallest to the largest (the size principle). Together with faster firing, it produces the graded muscle response.

The soft tissue inside bones. Red bone marrow makes blood cells; yellow bone marrow is mostly fat. In adults, red marrow remains mainly in flat bones, vertebrae, hip bones and the upper ends of the thigh and upper arm bones, and yellow marrow fills long-bone shafts.
terms.topicTitle: Functions of bone and long bone structure

terms.def: After about 120 days, macrophages in the spleen, liver and marrow engulf old red cells. Globin becomes amino acids, iron is recycled, and heme becomes green biliverdin and then yellow bilirubin, which travels on albumin to the liver, is conjugated and leaves in bile.

terms.term: red cells, white cells and platelets (basic)
terms.def: The formed elements of blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen and lose their nucleus as they mature; white blood cells defend against infection; platelets are cell fragments that help seal breaks in blood vessels.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: A rapid, involuntary, predictable response to a particular stimulus, produced by a fixed circuit of neurons. The same stimulus gives the same response each time, and a spinal reflex runs without the brain.

The five-part circuit every reflex runs on, in order: sensory receptor, sensory neuron, integration center (one or more synapses in the spinal cord or brainstem), motor neuron and effector. Damage to any part can abolish the reflex.
A short time during and just after an action potential when the membrane cannot fire again, or fires only with a stronger stimulus, because its sodium channels cannot reopen until it repolarizes.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: Regrowth of a cut axon. In the PNS, the part beyond the cut breaks down, Schwann cells form a tube and the axon regrows along it at about 1 mm per day; in the CNS, missing guidance, growth-blocking myelin proteins and the astrocyte scar usually prevent regrowth.

Names for areas of the body surface in the anatomical position, such as cephalic (head), cervical (neck), thoracic (chest), lumbar (lower back), brachial (arm, shoulder to elbow), antebrachial (forearm), femoral (thigh) and crural (leg, knee to ankle).

The external ear (auricle, ear canal and tympanic membrane) collects sound; the air-filled middle ear holds the auditory ossicles (malleus, incus and stapes) and opens into the throat through the auditory (eustachian) tube; the fluid-filled inner ear holds the cochlea, the vestibule and the semicircular canals.

The five regions of the heart tube, from outflow to inflow: the truncus arteriosus (becomes the aorta and pulmonary trunk), bulbus cordis (most of the right ventricle), primitive ventricle (most of the left ventricle), primitive atrium (front parts of both atria) and sinus venosus (the smooth back wall of the right atrium and the SA node region).

The large intestine runs from the ileocecal valve to the anus: the cecum (a blind pouch with the appendix), the colon (ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid, with the right and left colic flexures at its bends), the rectum (with its rectal valves) and the anal canal (with its anal columns and two sphincters).

The three regions of the small intestine: the duodenum (about 25 cm; receives chyme, bile and pancreatic secretions; duodenal glands secrete alkaline mucus), the jejunum (absorbs most nutrients) and the ileum (absorbs vitamin B12 and recovers bile; ends at the ileocecal valve, or ileocecal sphincter, which opens into the large intestine).

The five regions of the vertebral column, the stack of bones from the skull to the pelvis: 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7), 12 thoracic (T1–T12), 5 lumbar (L1–L5), the sacrum (5 fused) and the coccyx (usually 4 fused).
A condition your body actively holds within a normal range, such as body temperature, blood pressure, blood pH or the level of glucose in the blood.

TRH from the hypothalamus makes the anterior pituitary release TSH, which drives every step of thyroid hormone making and release and makes the gland grow. T4 and T3 inhibit TSH and TRH release by long-loop negative feedback.

A CD4 T cell, set up by the gene-control protein FOXP3, that suppresses other lymphocytes with IL-10 and TGF-beta, by taking up IL-2 and by removing B7 from dendritic cells. It keeps responses to self in check and ends responses after an infection.

Hypothalamic hormones carried by the hypophyseal portal system that make the anterior pituitary release (releasing hormones: TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) or hold back (inhibiting hormones: somatostatin, dopamine) its hormones.

The volume of plasma the kidneys completely clear of a substance each minute: C = (U × V) ÷ P. Inulin clearance equals GFR; creatinine, made steadily from creatine phosphate in muscle, gives a creatinine clearance slightly above GFR and is used to estimate it.

The kidneys' part in acid–base balance: they reclaim filtered bicarbonate, mostly in the proximal tubule, and secrete hydrogen ions that leave bound to phosphate (titratable acid) or ammonia (as ammonium). Each hydrogen ion excreted adds one new bicarbonate to the blood. It takes hours to days.

The filtering end of a nephron, in the cortex: a glomerulus (a tuft of fenestrated capillaries) inside the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule, whose visceral layer of podocytes wraps the capillaries and whose capsular space collects the filtered fluid.

The tube of a nephron that carries fluid from the glomerular capsule: the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop (loop of Henle) with its descending and ascending limbs, the distal convoluted tubule, and the collecting duct that many nephrons share.

A chain of blood-borne steps: kidney cells release renin when pressure there falls; renin turns angiotensinogen from the liver into angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mostly in the lungs, makes angiotensin II, which releases aldosterone, constricts vessels and raises ADH and thirst.

Anything that opposes flow, caused by friction between the fluid and the tube wall and within the fluid. It rises with a narrower radius, a longer tube and higher viscosity, the thickness or internal friction of the fluid.

A fall in blood pH caused by a rise in arterial PCO2 above 45 mm Hg, from hypoventilation: for example an opioid overdose or severe COPD. The kidneys compensate over 3 to 5 days by raising bicarbonate.

A rise in blood pH caused by a fall in arterial PCO2 below 35 mm Hg, from hyperventilation: for example anxiety, pain, fever or high altitude. The kidneys compensate over days by excreting bicarbonate.
Sums of two or more respiratory volumes: inspiratory capacity (TV + IRV), functional residual capacity (ERV + RV), vital capacity (TV + IRV + ERV) and total lung capacity (all four volumes).

Groups of neurons in the medulla oblongata and pons that generate the respiratory rhythm and drive the breathing muscles: the ventral and dorsal respiratory groups in the medulla, and the pontine respiratory group (pneumotaxic center) and apneustic center in the pons.

A negative feedback loop in which chemoreceptors sense a change in pH or PCO2 and the respiratory centers change ventilation. More breathing lowers PCO2 and raises pH; less breathing does the opposite. It acts within minutes but cannot remove fixed acid.

Infection of the respiratory tract. Pneumonia is infection of the alveoli, which fill with inflammatory fluid; tuberculosis is airborne infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which survives in alveolar macrophages, is walled off in granulomas, and can stay latent for years.

The barrier between alveolar air and capillary blood: a type I alveolar cell, the fused basement membranes and a capillary endothelial cell, about 0.5 µm thick in all. Its thinness and huge area let oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across quickly.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: The four non-overlapping volumes that together fill the lungs: tidal volume (one quiet breath, about 500 mL), inspiratory reserve volume (extra air you can breathe in), expiratory reserve volume (extra air you can breathe out) and residual volume (air that can never be breathed out).
The membrane potential of a cell that is not being disturbed: about −70 mV in a typical neuron and about −90 mV in skeletal and heart muscle. It comes mainly from potassium leaking out of the cell.

A net of neurons through the core of the brainstem. Its upward part, the reticular activating system, keeps the cerebral cortex awake and alert; it also filters repeated input and sets background muscle tension.

The D antigen, a red cell membrane protein. Rh-positive red cells carry it; Rh-negative cells do not. Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure to Rh-positive cells, through transfusion or pregnancy.

A tiny particle of protein and nucleic acid, with no membrane, that builds proteins by linking amino acids. Free ribosomes make proteins for the cytosol; ribosomes on the rough ER make proteins for membranes, lysosomes and export.

The 12 pairs of curved bones of the thoracic cage, which also includes the sternum and thoracic vertebrae. Each rib has a head, neck, tubercle, angle, body and costal groove and ends in a costal cartilage. Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, 8 to 12 are false ribs, and 11 and 12 are floating ribs.

The stiffening of muscles after death: ATP runs out, calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm, and myosin heads bind actin but cannot detach, locking the filaments together. It starts within a few hours and passes off over one to three days as the proteins break down.
terms.topicTitle: The sliding filament model and cross-bridge cycle

terms.def: Ribonucleic acid: a single-stranded nucleic acid with the sugar ribose and the base uracil in place of thymine. Messenger RNA carries a gene's message, ribosomal RNA forms much of the ribosome, and transfer RNA brings amino acids to it.

Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis; in a limb it is medial rotation if the front of the limb turns toward the midline and lateral rotation if it turns away. Circumduction moves the end of a limb in a circle, sweeping a cone, by flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence. The scapula's superior and inferior rotation tip its glenoid cavity up and down.

Four muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis; SITS) whose tendons wrap the shoulder joint and hold the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity. The first three insert on the greater tubercle, the subscapularis on the lesser tubercle.
terms.topicTitle: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb

terms.def: A quick estimate of the burned share of body surface in an adult: head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, front and back of the trunk 18% each, each lower limb 18%, genital area 1%. Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted; infants have a larger head share.

A vertical plane that divides the body into right and left parts. The midsagittal plane runs down the midline and makes equal halves; a parasagittal plane runs off the midline and makes unequal parts.

Three pairs of exocrine glands (parotid, submandibular and sublingual) plus many small ones in the mouth lining, which make about 1 to 1.5 L of saliva a day under autonomic control. Saliva is mostly water, with mucus, salivary amylase (starts starch digestion), a trace of lingual lipase, lysozyme, IgA and buffers.
An ionic compound that separates in water into cations and anions other than H+ and OH−, such as sodium chloride. An acid and a base react to form a salt and water.

The way an action potential travels along a myelinated axon: current flows under the myelin and the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, so it seems to leap from node to node. It is fast and uses less energy.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of a muscle fiber, and the sarcoplasm is its cytoplasm, packed with myofibrils, mitochondria and glycogen.

The repeating unit of a myofibril, from one Z disc to the next, and the smallest unit that can contract. Its bands are the dark A band (thick filaments), the light I band (thin filaments only), the H zone (thick only) and the M line at the center.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum of a muscle fiber: a network of tubes and sacs around every myofibril that stores calcium ions. Its wide end sacs beside the T tubules are the terminal cisternae.

The scrotum is the skin-and-muscle sac that holds the testes 2 to 3 °C below core temperature. Each testis is divided into lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperm are made, with interstitial (Leydig) cells between them that make testosterone.

An oil gland in the dermis, usually emptying into a hair follicle, that secretes by the holocrine mode. Its product, sebum, is a mix of lipids and cell debris that keeps hair supple, slows water loss and slows some bacteria and fungi.

Active transport in which a carrier uses one substance moving down its gradient, usually sodium, to move another against its gradient. In symport both move the same way; in antiport they move in opposite directions. The gradient it spends was built by the sodium–potassium pump.

The property of a plasma membrane that lets some substances cross freely, lets others cross only through specific proteins, and keeps others out. The cell can change it by changing its membrane proteins.
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: The state in which lymphocytes do not attack your own tissues. Central tolerance removes self-reactive lymphocytes as they mature (negative selection and clonal deletion in the thymus, a similar test in the marrow); peripheral tolerance silences those that escape, for example by clonal anergy when a T cell binds self antigen without a second, confirming signal.

The pulmonary and aortic valves, at the exits from the right and left ventricles. Each has three pocket-shaped cusps that fill with blood slipping back toward the ventricle and seal the opening; they have no cords or muscles.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: A thin sheet that lets some substances cross and blocks others, also called a selectively permeable membrane. The membrane around each of your cells lets water, oxygen and carbon dioxide cross easily but holds back proteins and most ions.

Sensation is the detection of a stimulus and the delivery of signals about it into the CNS, whether or not you are aware of it. Perception is the conscious awareness and interpretation of a sensation, produced by the cerebral cortex.

The three steps of every nervous system task: sensory input (sensory receptors detect a change), integration (neurons process the input and determine a response) and motor output (signals go to effectors).

A fall in a sensory receptor's response to a stimulus that stays constant. Tonic (slowly adapting) sensory receptors, such as nociceptors and proprioceptors, keep firing; phasic (rapidly adapting) ones, such as lamellated corpuscles, fire at the start and end of a stimulus and signal change.
The sensory (afferent) division carries signals from sensory receptors toward the CNS. The motor (efferent) division carries signals away from the CNS to effectors, the muscles and glands.
In a feedback loop, the cell or structure that detects a change in a regulated variable (also called the sensor). It is a whole cell or structure, not a receptor protein.

Sensory receptors grouped by where their stimulus comes from: exteroceptors (outside the body), interoceptors (internal organs and vessels) and proprioceptors (muscles, tendons and joints). Proprioception is the sense of body position; kinesthesia is the sense of movement.

Sensory receptors grouped by the stimulus they respond to: mechanoreceptors (touch, pressure, vibration, stretch), thermoreceptors (temperature), nociceptors (stimuli that damage tissue), chemoreceptors (particular chemicals) and osmoreceptors (the solute concentration of body fluids). The photoreceptor class responds to light.
The dividing walls of the heart: the interatrial septum between the atria, the thick interventricular septum between the ventricles, and the atrioventricular septum between the atria and ventricles.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: A thin, smooth sheet that lines the ventral body cavity and folds back over its organs: a parietal layer on the cavity wall, a visceral layer on the organ, and a film of watery serous fluid between them that lets the layers slide with little friction. The visceral layer on an organ is often called its serosa.
The clear fluid left when blood clots: plasma without fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins, which the clot used up.
The target value a feedback loop holds a regulated variable near, such as about 37 °C for body temperature. It sits inside the normal range and can shift, for example during a fever.

The 23rd chromosome pair: XX in a typical female, XY in a typical male. Every egg carries an X and each sperm an X or a Y, so the sperm sets the sex; the SRY gene on the Y turns the early gonad into a testis.

The development of male or female reproductive organs from a shared start. SRY turns the gonad into a testis (gonadal differentiation); its anti-Müllerian hormone removes the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, and its testosterone keeps the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts. Without a testis, an ovary forms, the paramesonephric ducts become the uterine tubes and uterus, and the mesonephric ducts break down.

Sideways moves of the dissociation curve. More carbon dioxide and H+ (the Bohr effect), higher temperature and more 2,3-BPG lower hemoglobin's affinity and shift it right, releasing more oxygen at a given PO2; the opposite changes, fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide shift it left.
A short reflex runs entirely within the enteric nervous system in the gut wall. A long reflex carries signals to the brainstem or spinal cord and back through autonomic nerves, such as the vagus.
terms.topicTitle: Organization and regulation of the digestive system

terms.def: An inherited disease in which a single mutation in the beta globin gene makes hemoglobin S. When HbS gives up its oxygen it forms stiff fibers that bend red cells into rigid sickles, which block small vessels and are destroyed early. One copy of the gene causes sickle cell trait, usually without symptoms.

The growth of a signal at each step of a pathway, so that a few messenger molecules produce a large response. One occupied receptor protein can switch on many G proteins, and each step after that multiplies again.

terms.term: signs of upper versus lower motor neuron damage
terms.def: Upper motor neuron damage causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia (brisk tendon jerks), a Babinski sign (the big toe extends when the sole is stroked) and little wasting. Lower motor neuron damage causes flaccid paralysis with lost tendon jerks, marked atrophy and fasciculations. Paresis is partial weakness.

One layer of tall cells, often with microvilli or cilia and with goblet cells that release mucus. It lines the digestive tract from the stomach through the intestines, the gallbladder and the uterine tubes.
One layer of cube-shaped cells with round, central nuclei, specialized for secretion and absorption. It lines kidney tubules, thyroid follicles and small ducts.

Movement of a substance straight through the phospholipid bilayer, down its concentration gradient, with no protein involved. It works for small nonpolar and lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and steroids, and its rate rises in step with the gradient.

One layer of flat cells, giving the shortest path for diffusion and filtration. It lines the air sacs of the lungs; it is called endothelium in the heart and blood vessels and mesothelium on serous membranes.

Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle has fibers linked by gap junctions into sheets that contract together, driven by pacesetter cells and stretch; it lines most hollow organs. Multi-unit smooth muscle has few gap junctions, and each fiber contracts when its own nerve endings stimulate it, as in the arrector pili and the muscles of the pupil.

The sinoatrial node: a patch of autorhythmic cells in the upper back wall of the right atrium, near the superior vena cava. It reaches threshold first, so it is the heart's pacemaker; a rhythm it sets is called sinus rhythm. Bachmann's bundle and the internodal pathways carry its signal quickly across the atria.
terms.topicTitle: The conduction system and pacemaker cells

terms.def: The three kinds of skeletal muscle fiber, sorted by contraction speed and main ATP pathway: slow oxidative (slow-twitch, type I), fast oxidative (type IIa) and fast glycolytic (type IIx). Fast oxidative and fast glycolytic fibers are the fast-twitch fibers.
Muscle tissue of long, cylindrical, striated fibers, each with many nuclei at its edge. It is attached to bones, moves the body and is voluntary.

Cancers of skin cells, mostly caused by UV damage to DNA. Basal cell carcinoma (from basal cells, most common, rarely spreads), squamous cell carcinoma (from keratinocytes) and melanoma (from melanocytes, rarest but deadliest because it spreads early).

The color set by melanin in the keratinocytes, carotene from the diet in the stratum corneum and fat, and blood in the dermis. Erythema is redness from vasodilation, pallor is paleness from less blood in the skin, and cyanosis is a bluish color when much of the blood in the skin has given up its oxygen.

The holes (foramina), canals, fissures and passages through the skull bones that carry nerves and blood vessels. The largest is the foramen magnum in the occipital bone, where the lower end of the brain becomes the spinal cord.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: The explanation of contraction in which thin filaments slide past thick filaments toward the center of the sarcomere, so the Z discs move closer while neither filament changes length. The I bands and H zone narrow; the A band keeps its width.
terms.topicTitle: The sliding filament model and cross-bridge cycle

terms.def: After a meal, segmentation mixes chyme and moves it slowly, with short peristaltic waves. Between meals, the migrating motor complex, triggered by motilin, sweeps residue and bacteria from the stomach to the end of the ileum. The gastroileal reflex increases ileal motility and relaxes the ileocecal sphincter when food enters the stomach.

In smooth muscle, calcium, much of it entering from outside the cell, binds calmodulin; calcium–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates the myosin heads so they can cycle and pull thin filaments anchored to dense bodies. Latch-bridges, dephosphorylated heads that stay attached, hold tension on little ATP.
Muscle tissue of small, spindle-shaped, nonstriated fibers with one central nucleus. It forms the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels and is involuntary; also called visceral muscle.

The match between sodium taken in and sodium excreted, adjusted mostly by the kidneys through aldosterone, ANP and pressure natriuresis. The amount of sodium sets ECF volume; the plasma sodium concentration (normally 135–145 mmol/L) mostly reflects water. Below 135 is hyponatremia, usually too much water; above 145 is hypernatremia, usually too little.

The closing of a voltage-gated sodium channel by its inactivation gate about a millisecond after the activation gate opens. An inactivated channel cannot open again until the membrane repolarizes and resets it.

An ATP-splitting membrane protein (the Na+/K+ ATPase) that moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in per cycle, both against their gradients. It builds the sodium gradient and keeps cell volume steady.
A mixture in which one substance, the solute, is spread evenly particle by particle through another, the solvent. In your body the solvent is almost always water.

A mixture is substances combined physically, without bonds between them. In a solution the particles are tiny and never settle; colloids hold larger particles that still do not settle; in a suspension the particles are large enough to settle on standing.

A somatic reflex acts on skeletal muscle through one motor neuron from the CNS. A visceral (autonomic) reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands through a chain of two motor neurons that synapse in a ganglion outside the CNS, and it can excite or inhibit its target.
The part of the motor division that controls skeletal muscle. One motor neuron runs from the CNS to the muscle, it always excites the muscle, and most of its output is under conscious control.

Somatic motor pathways use one heavily myelinated neuron that always excites skeletal muscle at a neuromuscular junction. Autonomic motor pathways use two neurons meeting in a ganglion, end in varicosities, can excite or inhibit, and act on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, which keep working if the nerves are cut.

The point-to-point map of the body along the primary somatosensory and primary motor cortex, with the legs on the medial surface and the face lowest on the side. Parts with dense sensory receptors or fine control (hands, lips, tongue) get the most cortex, drawn as the homunculus.
terms.topicTitle: Cortical functions, memory, language and sleep

terms.def: The adding together of postsynaptic potentials at the trigger zone. In temporal summation one input fires repeatedly in quick succession; in spatial summation several inputs fire at about the same time. An action potential fires if the sum reaches threshold.

Movements found at only a few joints: supination (palm forward or up) and pronation (palm backward or down, radius crossing the ulna) of the forearm; dorsiflexion and plantar flexion at the ankle; inversion and eversion of the sole; protraction and retraction; elevation and depression; lateral and medial excursion of the jaw; lateral flexion of the trunk or neck; and opposition and reposition of the thumb.

The making of sperm in the seminiferous tubules, about 64 to 74 days long. Spermatogonia (stem cells) divide by mitosis; primary spermatocytes complete meiosis I to give secondary spermatocytes, meiosis II gives haploid spermatids, and spermiogenesis reshapes each spermatid into a sperm.

The spinal cord runs from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris, its cone-shaped end at about L1–L2 in adults. It is wider at the cervical enlargement (supplying the upper limbs) and the lumbar enlargement (lower limbs); below the conus, lumbar and sacral roots hang down the canal as the cauda equina.

Cut across, the spinal cord shows butterfly-shaped gray matter inside (dorsal or posterior horns for sensation, ventral or anterior horns with motor neurons, and lateral horns with sympathetic neurons from T1 to L2) around a central canal, and white matter outside in posterior, lateral and anterior columns. The anterior median fissure marks the front and the posterior median sulcus the back.

Damage to the spinal cord that cuts tracts at one level and destroys the gray matter there. A cervical injury causes tetraplegia (quadriplegia), weakness of all four limbs; a thoracic or lower injury causes paraplegia, weakness of the legs. A hemisection, damage to one half of the cord, causes same-side weakness and position-sense loss with opposite-side loss of pain and temperature.

One of the 31 pairs of nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal) formed where a dorsal root and a ventral root join in the intervertebral foramen. Every spinal nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying both sensory and motor axons.

Measuring the volumes of air breathed in and out, and how fast they move. Forced spirometry gives the forced vital capacity (FVC) and FEV1, the volume blown out in the first second; a low FEV1/FVC ratio shows obstructive disease, and small lungs with a normal ratio suggest restrictive disease.

The largest lymphoid organ, in the upper left abdomen, which filters blood rather than lymph. Its white pulp holds lymphocytes around central arteries; its red pulp removes old red blood cells, platelets and bacteria and holds a platelet reserve.

Bone built as a lattice of thin struts, the trabeculae, with marrow in the spaces and no osteons. It fills the ends of long bones and the inside of other bones; in flat skull bones it is called the diploë. Also called cancellous bone.

A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament. A dislocation forces the surfaces of a joint completely out of contact; a subluxation is a partial dislocation in which they still touch but are out of line.

The three stages of labor, each ended by an event: the dilation stage (true labor to full dilation of the cervix at 10 cm), the expulsion stage (full dilation to birth of the baby) and the placental stage (birth to delivery of the afterbirth, the placenta and membranes). An episiotomy is a cut in the perineum to widen the opening.

The loops this course returns to again and again: body temperature, blood pressure, glucose in the blood and red blood cell production (negative feedback), and childbirth contractions and blood clotting (positive feedback).

Severe, prolonged lack of food energy, in which the body lives on its own tissues. Fat and ketone bodies carry it for weeks while sparing protein; when fat runs out, protein breakdown rises and heart and breathing muscle waste.
An unspecialized cell that can divide to renew itself and can also give rise to specialized cells.

The range of cell types a stem cell's descendants can become: totipotent (every cell plus the supporting tissues of pregnancy), pluripotent (every body cell type), multipotent (several related types), oligopotent (a few) or unipotent (one).

The breastbone: a flat bone in the front midline of the chest with three parts, the manubrium on top, the body in the middle and the small xiphoid process at the bottom. The jugular notch is the dip at its top, and the sternal angle, where the manubrium meets the body, marks the level of the second rib.
A lipid built on four fused carbon rings. Cholesterol, the main one, sits in the boundary around cells and is the raw material for your other steroids.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids
