terms.def: The three triggers for hormone release: a humoral stimulus (a change in an ion or nutrient in the blood), a hormonal stimulus (another hormone) and a neural stimulus (a nerve signal).

terms.term: stratified cuboidal and stratified columnar epithelium
terms.def: Rare stratified epithelia named for cube-shaped or tall surface cells. They line some large ducts, such as those carrying sweat, and parts of the male urethra.

Many layers of cells with flat cells at the surface, built to resist wear. The keratinized form, with dead keratin-filled surface cells, is the epidermis; the nonkeratinized form lines most of the mouth, the esophagus and the vagina.

The contraction of a muscle in response to its own stretch. Stretch fires muscle spindles, whose sensory neurons synapse directly on the motor neurons of the same muscle (a monosynaptic reflex), while interneurons inhibit its antagonist. The patellar reflex (knee jerk) and every other deep tendon reflex are stretch reflexes.

The stretch response of smooth muscle: after being stretched, smooth muscle slowly lets its tension fall back while it stays at the new length. It lets hollow organs such as the bladder and stomach fill with little rise in pressure.
The fine light and dark bands across skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers, produced by actin and myosin stacked in lined-up repeating units. Smooth muscle has no bands and is nonstriated.
The volume of blood one ventricle ejects in one beat: SV = EDV − ESV, about 70 mL at rest.

The three kinds of joint sorted by what joins the bones: fibrous joints (dense connective tissue, no space), cartilaginous joints (cartilage, no space) and synovial joints (bone ends separated by a fluid-filled space lined by synovial membrane).

A nerve is a bundle of axons in the peripheral nervous system wrapped in three connective tissue layers: endoneurium around each axon, perineurium around each bundle (fascicle), and epineurium around the whole nerve.

A sperm has a head, holding a tightly packed haploid nucleus under the acrosome, a cap of digestive enzymes; a midpiece, packed with mitochondria that make ATP; and a tail, a single flagellum that bends to drive the cell forward.

The liver is built of lobules: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, with hepatic sinusoids between the plates and a portal triad (portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch, bile duct) at each corner. Blood flows inward to the central vein; bile flows outward in bile canaliculi to the bile ducts.

A word part added at the end of a root that usually tells what kind of term it is: a condition (-itis, inflamed), a procedure (-ectomy, cutting out), a field (-logy, study of) or a description (-al, pertaining to).
Superficial means toward the body surface; deep means away from the surface, farther inside. Skin is superficial to muscle.
Superior means toward the head or above; inferior means toward the feet or below. Cranial (toward the head end) and caudal (toward the tail end) mean the same in a standing human.
Supine means lying face up, on the back; prone means lying face down. They describe how the body is lying and do not change the meaning of any directional term.
The first line of defense: intact skin and mucous membranes, their secretions (mucus, tears, saliva, stomach acid) and resident harmless microbes, which keep most microbes from entering the tissues.

A film of about 90% lipids, mostly phospholipids, and 10% proteins that type II alveolar cells secrete onto the water lining the alveoli. It lowers surface tension, so the alveoli stay open and inflate more easily.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: The tall supporting cells of the seminiferous tubule, also called Sertoli cells. They wrap and nourish developing sperm, make androgen-binding protein and inhibin, and are joined by tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier, which keeps immune cells and many substances away from cells in meiosis.

The interlocking seams between skull bones, bound by a thin layer of dense connective tissue. The named ones are the coronal (frontal to parietals), sagittal (between the parietals), lambdoid (parietals to occipital) and squamous (parietal to temporal) sutures.
terms.topicTitle: The axial skeleton and the skull

terms.def: Swallowing, in three phases: a voluntary phase (the tongue pushes the bolus into the oropharynx), a pharyngeal phase (a brainstem reflex that seals the nose and airway and squeezes the bolus into the esophagus) and an esophageal phase (peristalsis carries it to the stomach).

Coiled tubular glands, also called sudoriferous glands. Eccrine glands, over almost all skin, open at surface pores and make watery sweat; apocrine glands, in the armpits and groin, open into hair follicles from puberty and make a thicker secretion that bacteria turn into body odor.

The thoracolumbar division: preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn of T1–L2 send short axons through white rami communicantes to the sympathetic chain (chain or paravertebral ganglia) or through splanchnic nerves to the collateral (prevertebral) ganglia: celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric. Long postganglionic axons return to every spinal nerve through gray rami communicantes or run to the organs.
The junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell. The presynaptic (sending) and postsynaptic (receiving) cells are separated by a gap about 20 nanometers wide, the synaptic cleft.
A junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell. The presynaptic neuron sends the signal from its axon terminal; the postsynaptic neuron receives it, usually on a dendrite or the cell body.

The shared parts of a synovial joint: articular cartilage on each bone end, a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid, and an articular capsule with an outer fibrous membrane and an inner synovial membrane. Some add an articular disc of fibrocartilage and intrinsic (in the capsule), extrinsic (outside it) or intracapsular (inside it) ligaments.
A connective tissue membrane, with no epithelium, that lines the cavities of movable joints and releases a thick, slippery fluid that reduces friction.

The loop that carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta and its branches to the capillaries of every tissue except the lung's air sacs, and back through veins and the venae cavae to the right atrium. It works at high pressure.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: Systole is the contraction phase of a heart chamber and diastole is its relaxation and refilling phase. One cardiac cycle is one full heartbeat, from the start of one beat to the start of the next.
terms.topicTitle: Blood flow through the heart and the two circuits

terms.def: A lymphocyte that matures in the thymus (as a thymocyte, passing positive and negative selection) and recognizes, with its T cell receptor, only short peptides held on MHC proteins. Some kill infected cells; others coordinate responses.

The switching on of a naïve T cell in a lymph node, which needs recognition of its peptide in MHC (signal 1), costimulation by B7 binding CD28 (signal 2) and cytokines (signal 3). IL-2 then drives clonal expansion into effector T cells and memory T cells.

A transverse tubule: a narrow infolding of the sarcolemma that runs into the fiber and carries action potentials deep inside. Its inside is open to the extracellular fluid. One T tubule and the two terminal cisternae beside it form a triad.

terms.term: tactile and dendritic cells of the epidermis
terms.def: Tactile (Merkel) cells in the stratum basale press against sensory nerve fibers and signal light touch. Langerhans cells (the epidermal dendritic cell type), mainly in the stratum spinosum, settle in the skin before birth, renew themselves there, and take up foreign material.
Any cell that carries receptor proteins for a particular messenger. Cells without those receptor proteins do not respond, however much messenger reaches them.

Your 20 deciduous (baby) and 32 permanent teeth: incisors cut, canines (cuspids) tear, premolars and molars crush and grind. Each has a crown above the gum and roots in a socket; enamel caps the crown, dentin forms the bulk, the pulp cavity holds vessels and nerves, and cementum covers the root.

A polysynaptic reflex started by Golgi tendon organs, which sit where muscle joins tendon and sense muscle tension. Rising tension inhibits the motor neurons of the same muscle through interneurons and excites its antagonist, damping the muscle's force.
Cords of dense regular connective tissue. A tendon joins muscle to bone, a ligament joins bone to bone, and an aponeurosis is a tendon spread into a flat sheet.

Agents outside the embryo or fetus that can cause birth defects, such as alcohol, some drugs, some infections and radiation. Their effect depends on timing, dose and genes; weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization, when organs form, are the most sensitive time for major structural defects.

terms.term: the bicarbonate to carbon dioxide ratio
terms.def: Blood pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, normally 24 to 1.2, or 20 to 1. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives it: pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PCO2)). Halving the ratio lowers pH by 0.3.

The negative feedback loop that holds blood calcium steady. Cells of small glands behind the thyroid sense low calcium and release a calcium-raising hormone that increases bone resorption, calcium saving by the kidneys and, through activated vitamin D, absorption in the intestine; rising calcium reduces its release.

The negative feedback loop that holds blood glucose, the concentration of glucose in plasma, at about 70 to 99 mg/dL fasting. High glucose makes beta cells release insulin, which lowers it; low glucose makes alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it.

The negative feedback loop that holds body temperature, with the skin as sensor and effector. When the body warms, dermal blood flow and sweating rise and more heat is lost; when it cools, dermal blood flow falls and shivering of skeletal muscle makes heat.
The eleven organ systems: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The four kinds of tissue that build every organ: epithelial tissue (covers and lines), connective (supports and binds), muscle (contracts) and nervous tissue (carries electrical signals).

The defenses that keep acid and pepsin from digesting the stomach wall: an alkaline mucus layer holding bicarbonate, tight junctions, replacement of surface cells every few days, mucosal blood flow and prostaglandins. When Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAIDs weaken it, acid and pepsin can erode the lining and cause a peptic ulcer.

The principle that blood volume is set by how much sodium and water the kidneys excrete, the one loss route adjusted to match intake. Water follows sodium, so keeping sodium keeps fluid in the plasma and interstitial fluid.

The knee joint is a mostly hinge joint between femur and tibia, held by the medial and lateral menisci, the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the tibial and fibular collateral ligaments and the patellar ligament. The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a ball-and-socket joint with a shallow socket rimmed by the glenoid labrum, a loose capsule, and the rotator cuff tendons as its main support.

The positive feedback loop of labor: stretch of the cervix sends afferent signals to the hypothalamus, oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary, and stronger contractions stretch the cervix more. The stretch-to-oxytocin reflex is the Ferguson reflex. Birth ends the loop; it strengthens labor but is not needed for labor to start.

A sharp rise in LH to many times its usual level just before ovulation. It happens when estradiol from the dominant follicle stays high for about two days and switches the hypothalamus and pituitary from negative to positive feedback; ovulation follows about 34 to 36 hours after it begins.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.term: the long refractory period of cardiac muscle
terms.def: In cardiac muscle the absolute refractory period lasts about 200 to 250 ms, because the sodium channels stay inactivated through the plateau. It lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so a new action potential cannot start until the cell is relaxing, and twitches cannot sum into tetanus.
terms.topicTitle: Cardiac muscle cells and their action potential

terms.term: the major organs of each system
terms.def: The main organs of each organ system, such as the brain and spinal cord (nervous), the heart (cardiovascular), the lungs and trachea (respiratory), the stomach and liver (digestive), the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra (urinary), and the gonads (reproductive).
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: The tubes that carry sperm from the testis: the epididymis, where sperm mature and are stored; the ductus (vas) deferens, which runs in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal; and the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the urethra inside the prostate.

The steady rise in osmolarity of the interstitial fluid of the renal medulla, from about 300 mOsm/L at the cortex to about 1,200 mOsm/L at the papilla. NaCl builds most of it in the outer medulla, and urea about half of it in the inner medulla.

The action potential of a skeletal muscle fiber: triggered by the end plate potential, it swings the sarcolemma from about −90 mV to about +30 mV and back in 2 to 5 ms, spreading from the end plate toward both ends of the fiber and down every T tubule.

terms.term: the newborn's first breaths and circulatory changes
terms.def: The changes in the first minutes to weeks after birth as breathing starts: pulmonary resistance falls and systemic resistance rises, the foramen ovale is pressed shut, the ductus arteriosus constricts and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, and the ductus venosus closes. Meconium, the dark first stool made before birth, is passed within about two days.
The concentration of calcium in the plasma, normally about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL total (about 2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L). About half is free calcium ions, the form cells sense and the feedback loop controls.

The negative feedback loop that holds plasma osmolality near 285 to 290 mOsm/kg: a rise is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, which drive ADH release (so the collecting ducts keep water) and thirst (so you drink), and the added water brings osmolality back down.
terms.topicTitle: Body fluid compartments and water balance

terms.def: The sodium–potassium pump keeps the sodium and potassium gradients steady by replacing ions that leak. Its direct effect on the resting voltage is only a few millivolts; if it stops, the gradients and the resting potential fade slowly.

The route taken by proteins bound for secretion, the plasma membrane or lysosomes: made on ribosomes docked on the rough ER, modified in the ER and Golgi apparatus, then carried in vesicles to their destination, ending in exocytosis for secreted proteins.

The ways intact skin keeps water in and microbes, chemicals and UV light out: dead keratin-filled cells joined tightly and sealed by lipid sheets, a dry, constantly shed, slightly acidic surface (about pH 5), germ-killing molecules in sweat and sebum, Langerhans cells, and melanin.

The body's hormonal and nervous response to a threat, described as the general adaptation syndrome: an alarm reaction driven by sympathetic nerves and epinephrine, a stage of resistance carried by cortisol and salt-keeping hormones, and a stage of exhaustion in which prolonged exposure to these hormones does harm.

terms.term: the three main parts of a cell
terms.def: The three main parts of a typical cell: the plasma membrane (the outer boundary), the cytoplasm (everything inside the membrane except the nucleus) and the nucleus (the compartment that stores the cell's genetic instructions).
terms.topicTitle: The cell and its plasma membrane

terms.def: The 12 pairs of nerves that attach to the brain rather than the spinal cord, numbered I to XII from front to back: olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory (spinal accessory) and hypoglossal. I, II and VIII are sensory; III, IV, VI, XI and XII are motor; V, VII, IX and X are both.

Control of core temperature by the preoptic area of the hypothalamus, which matches heat loss to heat production: skin vasodilation and sweating when warm; skin vasoconstriction, shivering and nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat when cold.

How a newborn keeps its body temperature. A large surface for its size, wet skin, little fat and weak shivering make it lose heat fast; it makes heat mainly by nonshivering thermogenesis in brown fat, which uses oxygen and glucose.

Two kinds of skin that differ in their epidermis. Thick skin, on the palms and soles, has five strata including a stratum lucidum, a very deep stratum corneum, friction ridges and no hair. Thin skin, everywhere else, has four strata and usually hair.

A filament made of about 300 myosin molecules. Their tails form the shaft, and their heads stick out toward the thin filaments; each myosin head has a site that binds actin and a site that binds and splits ATP.

A filament of two twisted strands of actin, with the rod-shaped protein tropomyosin lying along its groove and the calcium-binding complex troponin attached to the tropomyosin. At rest tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.
The conscious urge to drink, produced by the thirst center in the hypothalamus when plasma osmolarity rises, blood volume falls or the mouth is dry.
The part of the ventral body cavity above the diaphragm, enclosed by the chest wall. It holds the two pleural cavities and, between them, the mediastinum.
The membrane potential, about −55 mV in a typical neuron, at which enough voltage-gated sodium channels open that sodium entry outpaces potassium exit and an action potential starts.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.def: A family of peptides released by the thymus's epithelial cells that help white blood cells mature in the thymus. How much they act as circulating hormones, rather than locally, is still unclear.
A gland in the mediastinum, behind the upper sternum, where white blood cells of the immune system mature. It is largest in childhood and is gradually replaced by fat after puberty.

Hypothyroidism (too little thyroid hormone: cold, tired, slow) and hyperthyroidism (too much: hot, weight loss, fast heart). Graves disease, an immune protein that switches on TSH receptor proteins, is the commonest cause of hyperthyroidism. A goiter is an enlarged thyroid gland. Congenital (neonatal) hypothyroidism is found by newborn screening.

A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, two lobes joined by an isthmus across the trachea. It is packed with follicles: spheres of follicular cells around thyroid colloid, whose main protein, thyroglobulin, holds the stored hormones. Parafollicular (C) cells lie between the follicles.

Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), lipid-soluble amine hormones made from tyrosine and iodine. T3 is the active form, mostly made from T4 in the tissues. They raise cells' oxygen use and heat production, increase beta-1 receptor proteins in the heart, and are needed for normal growth and brain development.

The two leg bones. The tibia is medial and carries almost all the weight; it has two condyles at the knee, the tibial tuberosity and the medial malleolus. The thin fibula is lateral, is not part of the knee, and ends in the lateral malleolus.
terms.topicTitle: The pelvic girdle and lower limb

terms.def: A continuous band where strands of claudin and occludin proteins stitch the membranes of neighboring cells together. It seals the space between cells, so substances must pass through the cells rather than between them.
A group of similar cells, plus the material around them, that work together to do one job. The study of tissues is histology.
terms.topicTitle: Levels of organization and organ systems

terms.def: A thin sheet of tissue that covers a body surface or lines a body cavity or hollow organ. An epithelial membrane is an epithelium on connective tissue (mucous, serous, cutaneous); a connective tissue membrane has no epithelium (synovial).

The replacement of damaged tissue, either by regeneration (the same kind of working cells divide and replace the lost ones) or by fibrosis (fibroblasts fill the gap with collagen, forming scar tissue). The parenchyma is an organ's working cells.

How a solution changes a cell's volume, set by the solutes that cannot cross the membrane. In an isotonic solution the cell keeps its volume, in a hypotonic one it swells and may burst (osmotic hemolysis), and in a hypertonic one it shrinks (crenation, in red blood cells).

The skin's touch receptors (tactile receptors): sensory nerve endings that detect touch, pressure, vibration, temperature and pain. Free nerve endings are bare nerve tips; encapsulated endings, such as tactile (Meissner) corpuscles in the dermal papillae and lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscles deep in the dermis, are wrapped in a capsule.

The windpipe, from the larynx to its division in the chest. It is held open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage (tracheal cartilages), open at the back, where the smooth trachealis muscle closes the gap against the esophagus. The last cartilage forms the carina, a sensitive ridge where the trachea splits into the primary bronchi.
terms.topicTitle: Trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli and lungs

terms.def: Copying a gene's DNA sequence into RNA in the nucleus. RNA polymerase binds at the gene's promoter and builds a complementary RNA; splicing then removes the introns and joins the exons.

Harm caused by a transfusion; the most dangerous is the recipient's antibodies attacking ABO-incompatible donor red cells, causing agglutination, hemolysis, fever, dark urine, low blood pressure and kidney damage. O negative red cells are the universal donor, AB positive the universal recipient, and a crossmatch mixes the patient's plasma with the donor's cells to check before transfusion.

A stratified epithelium whose dome-shaped surface cells flatten when the organ stretches, so the sheet thins without tearing. It lines the ureters, urinary bladder and first part of the urethra; also called urothelium.
Building a polypeptide on a ribosome by reading the codons of an mRNA in order, with tRNAs bringing the matching amino acids. Several ribosomes reading one mRNA at once form a polyribosome.

Immune destruction of a transplanted organ or tissue, mostly by recipient T cells reacting to the donor's HLA (MHC) proteins: hyperacute (minutes, existing antibodies), acute (days to months, T cells) or chronic (months to years). Tissue typing matches HLA; in graft-versus-host disease, donor T cells attack the recipient.

terms.term: transport in the distal tubule and collecting duct
terms.def: The final adjustments to the urine. The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium with chloride, and calcium under PTH. In the collecting duct, principal cells reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium under aldosterone and reabsorb water under ADH; intercalated cells secrete acid or bicarbonate.

The descending limb of the nephron loop lets water out but little salt; the ascending limb lets salt out but almost no water. In the thick ascending limb, the Na–K–2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) moves 1 Na+, 1 K+ and 2 Cl− into the cells, diluting the tubular fluid to about 100 mOsm/L.

The transport maximum (Tm) is the highest rate at which the tubules can reabsorb a substance once all its carriers are busy; for glucose it is about 375 mg/min. The renal threshold is the plasma level at which the substance first appears in urine, about 180 mg/dL for glucose; glucose in urine is called glucosuria or glycosuria.
A horizontal plane that divides the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) parts. The cut surface it makes is a cross section.

The veins that drain into the superior and inferior venae cavae. Above the diaphragm, internal jugular and subclavian veins form the two brachiocephalic veins, which form the superior vena cava; the azygos vein joins it from the chest wall. Below, the common iliac veins form the inferior vena cava, which receives lumbar, gonadal, renal and hepatic veins.

The route for touch, pain and temperature from the face: first-order neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, second-order neurons in trigeminal nuclei of the pons and medulla whose axons cross and rise to the thalamus, and third-order neurons to the face area of the postcentral gyrus.

A lipid made of one glycerol joined to three fatty acids, the long carbon and hydrogen chains with a carboxyl group at one end; it is the main form of stored fat. Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds and run straight; unsaturated ones have at least one double bond, which bends the chain.
terms.topicTitle: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids

terms.def: A hormone whose target is another endocrine gland, making it grow and release its own hormones. TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH are tropic.

The calcium switch of the thin filament: calcium binds troponin, troponin changes shape and lets tropomyosin roll off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and myosin heads can bind. When calcium falls, tropomyosin covers the sites again.

The movement of a substance from the fluid inside the renal tubule back into the blood of the peritubular capillaries. It crosses the tubule wall through the cells (the transcellular route) or between them through the tight junctions (the paracellular route), which are leaky in the proximal tubule.

The movement of a substance from the peritubular capillaries into the tubular fluid, adding to what was filtered. The tubule secretes potassium, H+, and many organic acids and bases, including drugs such as penicillin.

Ways of describing a broken bone: open (skin broken) or closed, displaced (ends out of line) or not, complete or incomplete (greenstick), by the line of the break (transverse, oblique, spiral) and by the number of pieces (comminuted: three or more).

The six shapes of synovial joint: plane (gliding), hinge and pivot (uniaxial), condyloid and saddle (biaxial), and ball-and-socket (multiaxial). The number of axes is how many lines a bone can move around.

The cord joining the fetus to the placenta, about 50 to 60 cm long at term. It holds two umbilical arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta, and one umbilical vein, which carries oxygen-rich blood to the fetus, cushioned in jelly-like connective tissue.

Changes in how many receptor proteins a target cell carries. Long exposure to high messenger levels causes down-regulation (fewer receptor proteins, weaker response); long exposure to low levels causes up-regulation (more receptor proteins, stronger response).

The two neurons of a voluntary motor command. An upper motor neuron has its cell body in the motor cortex or a brainstem nucleus and its axon inside the CNS; a lower motor neuron has its cell body in the ventral horn or a cranial nerve motor nucleus and sends its axon to skeletal muscle, the final common path.

A loop of reactions in liver cells that combines ammonia, bicarbonate and a nitrogen from aspartate into urea, spending 3 ATP per urea. Urea is far less toxic than ammonia and is excreted by the kidneys.

The passage of urea out of the inner medullary collecting duct, where ADH adds urea carriers, into the interstitial fluid of the inner medulla, where it supplies about half the osmolarity. Some re-enters the nephron loop and circulates again.

A muscular tube, about 25 to 30 cm long, that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder by peristalsis. It is lined by transitional epithelium and enters the bladder at a slant that acts as a one-way valve.

The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside: about 3 to 4 cm long in females and about 20 cm in males. The involuntary internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck; a distinct ring in males, a functional zone in females) and the voluntary external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle, in the pelvic floor) hold urine in.

A hollow, stretchy muscular bag behind the pubic bone that stores urine. Its wall is the detrusor muscle, its lining is transitional epithelium folded into rugae when empty, and the smooth trigone on its floor joins the two ureter openings to the urethral opening.

Urine is about 95% water plus urea, creatinine, uric acid, ions and the yellow pigment urochrome; its specific gravity (density compared with water) is usually 1.005 to 1.030. A urinalysis examines its appearance, a dipstick and a microscope sample; oliguria is under about 400 mL a day and anuria almost none.

The monthly changes in the endometrium, also called the menstrual cycle: the menstrual phase (menses), when falling progesterone makes the functional layer break down and be shed; the proliferative phase, when estradiol rebuilds it; and the secretory phase, when progesterone makes its glands secrete.
terms.topicTitle: Hormonal control of the ovarian and uterine cycles

terms.def: Two muscular tubes, about 10 cm long, from the uterus toward the ovaries (also called fallopian tubes or oviducts). Each has an open end fringed with fimbriae, a wide ampulla where sperm usually meet the oocyte, and a narrow isthmus next to the uterus; cilia and smooth muscle move the oocyte toward the uterus.

The hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ in which an embryo develops, with a fundus, body and cervix, draped by the broad ligament. Its wall has an outer perimetrium, a thick smooth muscle myometrium and an inner endometrium, whose functional layer is shed at menstruation and regrown from the basal layer.

The vagina is a gland-free, acidic muscular tube, 7 to 10 cm long, from the vaginal opening to the cervix, with a hymen at its opening. The vulva is the external genitals: the mons pubis, labia majora and minora, the clitoris, the vestibule and the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands.

Cranial nerve X, the only cranial nerve that reaches the chest and abdomen. It supplies the muscles of the throat and voice box, carries about three quarters of all parasympathetic axons (slowing the heart and stimulating the digestive organs), and brings sensory signals back from the heart, lungs and gut.

Swollen, lengthened, twisted superficial veins, usually in the legs, caused when venous valves become incompetent: blood falls back, pools and stretches the thin wall, which pulls the next valve open in turn.

The contraction of smooth muscle in the wall of an injured vessel, caused by direct injury, chemicals such as thromboxane A2 and serotonin from platelets, and local pain reflexes. It slows flow for up to about half an hour.

Vasoconstriction is narrowing of a blood vessel when the smooth muscle in its wall contracts; vasodilation is widening when that muscle relaxes. Because resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, both change flow sharply.

The blood held in the systemic veins and venules, about 60 to 65 percent of the total at rest. Veins are highly compliant, so they store blood with little rise in pressure, and sympathetic venoconstriction can shift that stored blood toward the heart.

Deep limb veins run beside the arteries and share their names (radial, ulnar, brachial, axillary; tibial, fibular, popliteal, femoral). Superficial veins run under the skin: the cephalic, basilic, median cubital and median antebrachial veins of the arm, and the great and small saphenous veins, which start from the dorsal venous arch of the foot.

The brain's veins drain into dural venous sinuses, channels between the layers of the dura mater with no smooth muscle and no valves. The superior sagittal and straight sinuses drain to the transverse sinuses, then the sigmoid sinuses, which leave the skull as the internal jugular veins. The cavernous sinuses lie beside the sphenoid bone.

The flow of blood back to the heart through the veins, driven by a small pressure gradient and helped by the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump and venoconstriction, with venous valves preventing backflow.

The matching of blood flow (perfusion) to airflow (ventilation) in each region of the lungs. The ventilation–perfusion ratio, V/Q, is about 0.8 for the whole lung; low alveolar PO2 constricts nearby pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), sending blood to better-ventilated alveoli.
The large anterior main body cavity of the trunk. The diaphragm divides it into the thoracic cavity above and the abdominopelvic cavity below.

The four connected fluid-filled chambers inside the brain, left from the hollow of the neural tube: two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle. The interventricular foramina and the cerebral aqueduct join them, and the median and lateral apertures open the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

The action potential of a contractile ventricular cell, lasting about 250 to 300 ms: a fast sodium upstroke (phase 0), a small notch (phase 1), a plateau near 0 mV where calcium entry balances potassium exit (phase 2), repolarization by potassium exit (phase 3), and rest at about −90 mV (phase 4).
terms.topicTitle: Cardiac muscle cells and their action potential

terms.def: Venules drain capillaries and merge into veins, which carry blood toward the heart at low pressure. Veins have a thin tunica media, a thick tunica externa, a wide lumen and, in the limbs especially, venous valves; they are capacitance vessels that hold large volumes of blood.
A small sphere of membrane that carries cargo within a cell. It buds off one membrane and fuses with another.

The balance organs of the inner ear. In the vestibule, the utricle and saccule each have a macula whose hair cells are covered by an otolithic membrane topped with otoliths; they sense head tilt and straight-line movement. The three semicircular canals have a cupula that lagging endolymph bends when the head turns. Their signals drive equilibrium and the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), which turns the eyes opposite to a head turn.

The route from the retina to the cortex: optic nerve, optic chiasm (where fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross), optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and primary visual cortex. Each optic tract and hemisphere handles the opposite half of the visual field.

Vitamins that dissolve in fat, such as D and K, are absorbed with dietary fat in micelles and leave in chylomicrons; vitamins that dissolve in water use carriers. Vitamin B12 needs intrinsic factor from the stomach and pancreatic proteases, and is absorbed in the terminal ileum by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

terms.term: vitamin D synthesis in the skin
terms.def: The making of vitamin D in the skin: UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes into previtamin D3, which body warmth turns into vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol). Extra UV makes inactive products, so sunlight cannot cause an overdose.

Organic molecules needed in small amounts that the body cannot make in enough amounts; most act as coenzymes or other active molecules and supply no energy. The fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored and can build up; the water-soluble ones (the B vitamins and C) are stored little, except B12.

The difference in electrical potential energy per unit of charge between two points, also called potential difference, measured in volts. It exists only where charge is separated; voltages across the membranes around cells are a few tens of millivolts (mV; 1 mV = 0.001 V), written as the inside compared with the outside.
Channels that open when the membrane depolarizes. Sodium channels open fast, then close on their own; potassium channels open slowly and close slowly. Together they shape the action potential.
terms.topicTitle: Electrical signals: graded potentials and action potentials

terms.term: voltage-gated, ligand-gated and mechanically gated channels
terms.def: The three main kinds of gated ion channel, named for what opens them: voltage-gated channels open when the voltage across the membrane changes, ligand-gated channels open when a specific molecule binds, and mechanically gated channels open when the membrane is stretched or pressed.

A reflex coordinated by a network of neurons in the medulla oblongata that expels the contents of the stomach through the mouth. The airway is closed, the stomach and lower esophageal sphincter relax, and the diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract hard to squeeze the stomach.

The colon absorbs about 90% of the roughly 1.5 L of fluid that reaches it each day. Epithelial cells take up sodium actively, chloride follows, and water follows by osmosis; aldosterone increases it. The longer contents stay, the more water is absorbed.

About 9 L of water enter the gut each day, and about 98% is absorbed, most in the small intestine. The gut absorbs sodium (with sugars and amino acids, in exchange for hydrogen ions, or through channels) and chloride, and water follows by osmosis. Calcium absorption depends on calcitriol, and iron absorption is set by need.

The daily match between water gained (drinks, food and metabolic water made by cellular respiration) and water lost (urine, insensible loss through the skin and breath, sweat and feces), about 2.5 L each way. Only drinking and urine volume are adjusted to keep it balanced.
terms.topicTitle: Body fluid compartments and water balance

terms.def: Water-soluble (hydrophilic) messengers cannot cross the plasma membrane, so they bind receptor proteins on the cell surface and act fast. Lipid-soluble (hydrophobic) messengers, such as steroids, diffuse through the membrane, bind receptor proteins inside the cell and act slowly by changing gene expression.

Wave summation is the adding together of twitches when action potentials arrive before the fiber has relaxed. At higher frequencies it becomes incomplete tetanus, then complete tetanus, a smooth sustained contraction. Treppe is the staircase rise in twitch strength in a rested muscle stimulated slowly.

The ways antibodies disable antigens: neutralization (blocking toxins and viruses from binding cells), agglutination (clumping), opsonization (coating for phagocytes), complement activation and directing natural killer cells. The antibody binds; other cells and proteins do the killing.

Vascular resistance is set by vessel length, blood viscosity and, most strongly, vessel radius, because resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius⁴. Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is the resistance of the whole systemic circulation; most of it is in the arterioles.

The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, water balance and thirst, hunger, autonomic output (heart rate, blood pressure, digestion), the daily sleep-wake timing and the body's side of emotion, and it controls the pituitary gland. It acts through autonomic neurons, hormones and drives.

Hyaline cartilage forms articular cartilage on bone ends, the nose tip and the trachea's rings; fibrocartilage forms intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee; elastic cartilage forms the ear flap and epiglottis.

Where each epithelium is found: the epidermis (outer skin) over the dermis, thyroid follicles, alveoli (lung air sacs), the epiglottis and others. Each site's lining matches the wear and exchange it faces.

terms.term: where the body's acid comes from
terms.def: Your acid comes in two kinds. Volatile acid is carbonic acid from the carbon dioxide cells make, about 13,000 to 20,000 mmol a day, removed by the lungs. Fixed (metabolic) acids, such as sulfuric and phosphoric acid from protein, cannot be breathed out; about 50 to 100 mmol a day must be excreted by the kidneys.

The white cell count and the differential count (each type's share). Leukocytosis is a count above about 11,000 per µL and leukopenia one below about 4,500. Leukemia is cancer of blood-forming cells in the marrow; lymphoma is cancer of lymphocytes growing mainly in lymph nodes.

Calcium triggers muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release and clotting steps, forms bone mineral, and from outside cells makes voltage-gated sodium channels harder to open. Hypocalcemia makes nerves and muscles overexcitable (tingling, tetany); hypercalcemia makes them less excitable (weakness, confusion).

terms.term: why the left ventricle wall is thicker
terms.def: The left ventricle wall is about three times thicker than the right because it pumps into the high-resistance vessels of the whole body and must generate about five times the pressure; heart muscle thickens when it works against a heavier load. On average, both ventricles pump the same volume per beat.
terms.topicTitle: Heart valves, septa and internal structure

terms.def: Heart valves are passive: a valve opens when pressure behind it (upstream) is higher than pressure in front of it, and closes when pressure in front becomes higher and blood starts to flow backward.

The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is a polysynaptic reflex in which nociceptor signals excite the flexors and inhibit the extensors of the stimulated limb, pulling it away. In the crossed-extensor reflex, interneurons crossing the cord do the opposite in the other limb, which straightens and bears the weight.

The part of a medical term that carries its core meaning, usually a body part or substance, such as cardi (heart) in cardiology. A root plus a linking vowel, usually o, is a combining form, written cardi/o.

The overlapping stages that close a break in the skin: a clot and scab, inflammation, rebuilding with granulation tissue (new capillaries and fibroblasts), new epidermis and wound contraction, then months of remodeling into a scar. Closed edges heal by primary union; open wounds by secondary union. A keloid is a scar that grows beyond the wound.

Inheritance of genes on the X chromosome. Males have one X, so an X-linked recessive allele, such as the one for hemophilia A, shows in any male who has it and passes from carrier mothers to half their sons; an X-linked dominant allele shows with one copy in either sex.

An inactive enzyme precursor (proenzyme), stored and secreted in a form that cannot digest the cell that makes it and activated only after release, for example pepsinogen becoming pepsin in stomach acid.
